I live with my husband outside Madison, Wisconsin, in the same small house we have been in for thirty-three years.

We have a son in Milwaukee and a daughter in Minneapolis.

I retired three years ago, after twenty-seven years as a property manager at a small real estate firm two blocks from our downtown.

I managed about a hundred and forty small rental properties.

I knew the families. I knew which furnaces were old. I knew which roofs we were going to be on the phone about that winter.

It was steady work for a careful woman.

I am, on paper, in fine shape.

I am on no prescription medications.

I take a multivitamin and a vitamin D and that is the entirety of my pill organizer.

My doctor — Dr. Stewart, a careful woman I have been seeing for thirteen years — tells me at every annual visit that my bloodwork is in the ranges she wants it in.

I walk every morning.

I eat the way a woman my age should eat.

I sleep seven hours a night.

That is the part I want you to hold while you read this.

I want to tell you, plainly, about a quiet question I had been carrying for almost two years.

It was small.

It would not have registered on any chart.

I am not telling you a dramatic story.

I am telling you what one careful woman in her sixties had been noticing quietly about herself, alone, for almost two years, before another woman said one sentence to her on a bench at the community garden in May.

It looked like this.

I have a small plot at our town community garden.

I have been gardening there for five years.

The plot is twenty feet by ten.

I grow tomatoes, peppers, basil, parsley, and a row of beans.

I had been planting it every May in two long Saturday mornings for five years.

For the previous two springs, the same two Saturday mornings of planting had become four Saturday mornings.

I had been needing to come home in the middle and lie down.

I had been needing to leave half the work for Sunday morning, and to come back on Monday for the parts I had not finished.

I had been telling myself it was the heat.

It was not the heat.

I had been telling myself it was the new mulch I had been using, which was heavier than the old one.

It was not the new mulch.

I had been telling myself a great many things.

It looked like the afternoon.

I had been a woman who never took an afternoon nap.

I had not been a napper at fifty. I had not been a napper at fifty-five. I had not been a napper at sixty.

Somewhere in the second year of my retirement, I had started lying down on the couch after lunch.

I had told myself it was retirement.

It was not retirement.

It was the quiet pull of an afternoon I had not felt before, that started somewhere just past sixty-two, and that I had been giving in to once a week, then twice a week, then most days.

It looked like my book club.

I am in a book club that meets once a month at our library on Tuesday evenings.

I had been a four-books-a-month woman for forty years.

We read one for the club. I read three others on my own.

For the previous eighteen months I had been falling asleep on the couch after dinner with the book club book open on my lap.

I had been reading the same paragraph over.

I had been finishing the book club book on Tuesday at five in the afternoon, in a rush, because I had not finished reading it at the natural pace I had used to read at for forty years.

I had not finished three other books in eight months.

I went into Dr. Stewart's office for my annual physical last February.

She did the bloodwork.

Everything was in the ranges she wanted it in.

Not borderline. Not perfect. In the ranges.

She looked at me across her desk.

She said: anything we should be talking about, Nancy?

I told her about the garden.

I told her about the afternoons.

I told her about the book club books.

I told her I was not asking her for an answer. I just wanted her to have the picture.

She listened.

She wrote it down.

She said: I do not see anything on your chart I would do anything about today. But you know your body better than I do. If something changes, or if you want to come back sooner, you call me.

I told her thank you.

I drove home thinking about that conversation.

What I drove home thinking was this.

Dr. Stewart was not wrong.

I was not wrong either.

There is a kind of quiet shift in your sixties that does not show up on the chart.

It is not a thing to panic about.

It is not a thing to ignore.

It is, I decided that afternoon, a thing to pay attention to.

I had been carrying it quietly for two years before I told Dr. Stewart about it.

I had been carrying it quietly for two more weeks before I sat on a bench at the community garden.

The community garden is two blocks from my house.

It has thirty-two plots.

The woman whose plot is next to mine is named Sandy.

She is, I would guess, sixty-seven.

Silver hair, a quiet manner, gardens in slow careful rows the way a woman who has been gardening for a long time gardens.

We had been nodding at each other for three years.

We had said hello and goodbye and complimented each other's tomatoes and asked each other about the rain, the way two women who garden next to each other for three years do.

That kind of friendship is its own thing.

You can have it with another woman for three years at a community garden without ever really knowing very much about her.

The Saturday in May was a Saturday like every other Saturday.

I had been at my plot since seven, planting the last row of tomatoes.

I was tired.

I had been planning to plant the peppers, too, and I knew I was not going to make it.

I went and sat on the long bench at the edge of the garden area.

It was eight-thirty.

I had been planting for an hour and a half.

I was already done for the morning.

I was already going to come back on Sunday.

I sat on the bench with my water bottle.

I was angry at my body.

I had been angry at my body off and on for two years.

Sandy came over.

She had been at her own plot.

She sat down on the bench next to me.

She did not say anything for a long time.

She just sat there with her own water bottle.

Then she said: Nancy, I have been meaning to ask you. Are you alright? You have been on this bench more often this spring than I remember from the other springs.

I sat with that for a moment.

I looked at my hands.

I said: I am not unwell. My doctor is happy with me. The numbers are fine. The chart is fine. I am just tired in a way I was not tired three years ago. The garden tires me out. The afternoons tire me out. The books tire me out. I do not know how to say it any plainer.

Sandy was quiet for a long minute.

Then she said something I have been thinking about every day since.

She said: Nancy. I had been quietly noticing the same thing about myself for almost three years before I decided to do anything about it. I had been sitting on this bench more than I had been planting, and I had been telling myself it was sixty-four. It was not sixty-four. It was something quieter than that.

She told me she had been noticing her own shifts since her early sixties.

Slow morning routine.

The afternoon pull.

Reading less.

She told me she had told herself it was retirement. She told me she had told herself it was the dog. She told me she had told herself a great many things.

Then she said: about four years ago, I added one small thing to my own mornings. I read for a month before I added it. I talked to my doctor and to my pharmacist before I added it. I want to be careful with you about what I say next, because I am one woman and you are looking at one woman and bodies are different.

But I have been more like myself for the last four years than I was for the three years before that. I have been gardening more steadily. I have been finishing my book club books on time. I have been getting through a full Saturday without lying down. I would not tell you it is the beetroot capsule on its own. I would tell you it is one thing I added to everything else.

She said it without performance.

She said it the way a woman in her late sixties says something to another woman on a bench at the community garden where they have been gardening next to each other for three years.

She wasn't selling me anything.

She was just telling me.

I asked her what she had added.

She said it was a beetroot capsule.

She said the brand was called Rosabella.

She said she had picked it because the small company that made it cold-pressed the beetroot at low temperatures rather than processing it with heat, and because her doctor had specifically said how the supplement was processed mattered for what would make it from the field into the capsule.

The morning was getting hot.

She stood up.

She put her hand on my shoulder before she walked back to her plot.

She said: Nancy. Please call your pharmacist before you add anything. That is the only thing I am going to be insistent about. Promise me.

I promised her.

She walked back to her plot.

I sat on the bench for another twenty minutes.

I drove home thinking about Sandy.

I drove the rest of that week thinking about Sandy.

By the weekend, I was thinking about what I was going to do.

I am, by temperament, a careful woman.

A property manager for twenty-seven years is, almost by definition, a careful woman.

I do not add things to my body without understanding what I am adding.

I went home and I started reading.

I read for almost three weeks.

I read about beetroot.

I read about the deep crimson pigment in the root.

It is called betalain.

It is the color that stains your cutting board for three days.

It is also, according to a long and patient body of research the cardiovascular community has been quietly building for decades, one of the more potent antioxidants in the food supply.

I read about the long, slowly built relationship the structure-function research has had with this vegetable.

In the context of supporting healthy circulation.

Supporting cardiovascular wellness.

Supporting the body's own cellular energy.

In people whose numbers are already in the range their doctors want them in.

That last one is the one I had been waiting to find.

Cellular energy.

It is the basement-level work the body does to keep doing its work.

It is not the same thing as energy in a coffee cup.

It is not the same thing as the energy you get from a candy bar at four in the afternoon.

It is the quiet, steady work the body has to do, all day every day, just to keep being the body it has been being.

In people my age, in good health, who are doing all the careful things, that quiet work is something the research community talks about supporting.

Not boosting. Not fixing. Not treating.

Supporting.

In a structure-function way.

For people whose numbers are already in the range their doctors want them in.

That was the shape of the language I had been hoping to find.

I read about the cold-press, too.

The chemistry is straightforward.

The betalain pigment is heat-sensitive.

If you process beetroot the standard way, with heat, you lose some of the compound to the heat.

Rosabella cold-presses at low temperatures because they want as much of the compound as possible to make it from the field into the capsule.

That is a slower way to make a supplement.

It costs them more.

At sixty-four, after twenty-seven years of watching small landlords in our town make small decisions about their own properties, I have come to pay close attention to the small decisions companies make when no one is watching.

Those decisions tell you everything.

The other thing I liked was the simplicity.

Two capsules in the morning with a glass of water.

That is the whole protocol.

I have a husband, a garden plot, a book club, and a couch.

I am not interested in a protocol that requires its own shelf.

Now I want to tell you the most important part of this letter.

I made Sandy a promise at the garden.

I kept it.

Before I added anything to what I was already taking, I called my pharmacist.

His name is William.

He has been the pharmacist at the small independent pharmacy three blocks from our house for sixteen years.

I have been filling things there for as long as we have lived in town.

I called him for a specific reason.

I am on no prescription medications.

I take a multivitamin and a vitamin D.

I called William anyway.

I called because I am a careful woman and because I wanted somebody who knew what was on my record to confirm that adding a beetroot capsule to a multivitamin was the right thing to do at my age.

He pulled up my profile.

He confirmed there were no concerns at the dosage on the label.

He told me to take it in the morning with my coffee the way the bottle suggested.

He told me to call him back if Dr. Stewart ever started me on any prescription medication in the future, because the conversation would be different at that point.

He told me, before he got off the phone, that he wished more of his patients made the call I had just made.

I also called Dr. Stewart's office that week.

I left a message with her nurse, with the same information.

She called me back the next day to tell me Dr. Stewart had no concerns about my adding it at the dosage on the label.

I want to say something now, plainly, to every reader of this letter.

If you are on any prescription medication, especially anything cardiovascular, please make the call before you add anything new.

I made two calls.

I would have made three if I had been on a prescription.

So should you.

The two minutes the call takes is the most important two minutes of your engagement with any supplement.

I started on a Monday in early June.

I set the bottle on the counter next to the coffee maker.

I took the two capsules with my first sip of coffee.

The first two weeks I felt nothing in particular.

I had read enough alongside what Sandy had told me to know that bodies are different.

Some women notice something within the first week or two.

Some women take much longer.

Some women don't notice much at all.

I was prepared to land in any of those camps.

I was prepared to be honest with myself about the result.

The first thing I noticed, around week six, was the garden.

By nine-thirty I had planted the second wave of beans, weeded both rows of tomatoes, and watered the basil that the heat had been hard on.

I had not been to the bench.

I came home at ten-fifteen.

I made myself a sandwich for lunch.

I did not lie down on the couch.

I sat on the back porch with a book for an hour.

I did not say anything about it to my husband.

I did not want to make a thing of it.

I had read enough not to make a thing of one observation.

It was a Wednesday evening.

I was on the couch after dinner.

I was on the second chapter of the book club book.

I read the second chapter.

I read the third.

I read the fourth.

I looked at the clock and it was ten-fifteen.

I had been reading for an hour and a half without falling asleep, without re-reading the same paragraph, without putting the book down on my chest.

I finished the book by Friday.

I finished the next book I picked up by the following Tuesday.

I read four books that month.

The third thing I noticed was Sunday dinner.

My son and daughter-in-law and their two children come down from Milwaukee for Sunday dinner once a month.

I had been hosting them for sixteen years.

For the last two years, I had been needing to lie down on the couch for an hour before they arrived, just to get through the visit.

The Sunday in early October was the first one after I had been on Rosabella for four months.

I made a roast chicken, mashed potatoes, salad, and a small pumpkin pie.

I set the table.

They arrived at one.

I hosted them for three hours.

I cleaned up the kitchen with my daughter-in-law afterward.

We sat in the living room for another hour after the kids went outside to play in our yard.

I went to bed at the normal time that night.

I had not needed to lie down at any point during the day.

I sat in the kitchen at the end of that Sunday and I drank a small glass of water by myself and I let myself notice it.

I want to be careful with what I am telling you.

I am not telling you Rosabella did any of those things on its own.

I had been walking a little more deliberately after my conversation with Sandy.

I had been going to bed at the same time every night.

All I am telling you is that I added one small thing to a long list of things I was newly doing.

The research community talks about it in the context of supporting healthy circulation, supporting cardiovascular wellness, and supporting the body's own cellular energy.

In people whose numbers are already in the range their doctors want them in.

It is not a fix for anything.

It is not a treatment for tiredness, or for aging, or for any of it.

Please call your pharmacist or your doctor's office before you add it.

If you are on any blood pressure medication, cholesterol medication, or anything cardiovascular at all, this is non-negotiable.

I called William.

I called Dr. Stewart's office.

I would not have added anything to a prescription without those calls.

Neither should you.

The people who know your chart will tell you in two minutes whether the supplement is safe for you to add given what you are already taking.

I am a sixty-four-year-old retired property manager in Wisconsin.

I am not the person to ask.

Your pharmacist or your doctor is.

The company has a ninety-day satisfaction guarantee.

If you are not satisfied — for any reason at all, including just changing your mind — they refund you.

It is not tied to anything you have to prove.

If you are not satisfied, you are not satisfied.

That is the whole policy.

The beets are grown on a small operation that harvests on its own schedule.

There are stretches when they are in stock and stretches when they are not.

I mention that not to push you — please do not let anybody push you into a health decision — but so that if you go to the site and they are out, you know why.

That is all I have.

Thank you for reading this far.

I hope something here was useful to you.

I hope, somewhere today, your own Sandy is sitting on a bench at your own community garden, waiting for you to come sit next to her with your water bottle.

scripts.body_meta:
I'm fifty-eight, and for about two years I have been giving each day a little less than I used to give it.

Last fall, a man eighteen years older than me showed me what I had been doing without showing me anything.

I'm fifty-eight years old.

My name is Greg.

I run a custom-cabinetry business out of a shop in the small town outside Pittsburgh where my wife, Linda, and I have lived for thirty-one years.

I started the business at thirty-five. I have nine people who work for me now. Most of them have been with me for more than ten years. Two of them have been with me for more than twenty.

We make kitchens, mostly. Built-ins. Custom libraries. The kind of work where every piece is sized to a house and every piece has to fit.

I am telling you that because the wood I use matters to me, and the place I buy the oak I use most often is a small Amish sawmill in Holmes County, Ohio, run by a family I have been buying from for twenty-three years.

The man who runs the sawmill is named Samuel.

Samuel is seventy-six.

The story I want to tell you is about a Tuesday in September last fall, when I drove out to Samuel's mill for a load of oak, and I came home with a question I had been avoiding for almost two years.

I want to back up.

For about two years before that Tuesday, I had been quietly noticing that the body I had been running my cabinetry business with was not delivering the way it used to deliver.

Not failing. Not declining in any clinical sense. Just less.

I had been getting to the shop a little later. Six-thirty had become seven. Seven had become seven-fifteen on the days I didn't have an early install.

I had been finishing the day a little earlier. Five had become four-thirty. Four-thirty had become whatever the guys can finish without me.

The Saturday work I used to do — drawings, quotes, the small administrative catch-up — had quietly stopped happening.

I was sitting on the couch with my coffee from nine until almost noon on Saturdays. The drawings sat in the truck.

I had stopped going down into the basement on Sunday afternoons to work on small projects for the house.

The deck rail had been waiting for me for a year. The trim around the basement windows had been waiting for two.

I had been going to bed by nine-thirty. I had been a man who could read until eleven and get up at six and feel like myself.

That stopped, in small pieces, over the course of the year I turned fifty-seven.

I was not sick. I was not declining in any measurable way.

My annual physical at fifty-seven was clean. My bloodwork was where my doctor wanted it.

My blood pressure was good. My cholesterol was in range. My weight was where it had been for ten years.

I take no prescription medications.

There was no chart-level problem.

There was just a man who had been giving the days a little less than he used to.

I had been telling myself it was age. I had been telling myself it was twenty-three years of running a business.

I had been telling myself it was the stress, the sleep, the long winter we had had two years in a row.

I had not been telling myself the simpler thing, which was that I had been quietly accepting a level of less that I would have been embarrassed by at fifty.

The Tuesday in September was a normal trip out to Samuel's.

I drive out two or three times a year. The drive is about three and a half hours each way. I load the truck with quarter-sawn white oak boards I have ordered ahead, I have lunch with Samuel and his sons, I drive home.

I have been doing this run since 2001.

I have known Samuel since the year he turned fifty-three.

That last Tuesday, I drove in around eleven.

Samuel was at the back of the mill, helping his oldest son and one of his grandsons get a long board off the carriage. He was wearing the same kind of work shirt and work pants he has worn for twenty-three years.

He looked, from across the yard, exactly like he had looked when I had first started buying from him.

He saw me, walked over, shook my hand, and we went into the small office at the front of the mill to look at the bill of materials.

After we were done with the paperwork, he asked me whether I wanted to walk back and see a piece of curly maple they had been holding for me. I said yes.

We walked the length of the mill yard together.

It is about a quarter mile from the office to the back lot where they were holding the maple.

The yard is gravel.

The day was cool. We walked at the pace Samuel was walking, which was, I noticed about halfway back, a pace I was working harder to keep than I should have been.

I am fifty-eight. Samuel is seventy-six.

I was working to keep his pace.

We looked at the curly maple. Samuel and his son loaded it on the truck with the oak. Samuel and I went back to the small house behind the office where his wife had laid out lunch.

I sat at the table across from Samuel.

He ate the way he has eaten for twenty-three years, which is with the appetite of a man who has been working with his hands since he was twelve years old.

I ate the way I had been eating for about a year, which was not much, because most days my afternoon energy had been running thin and I had been keeping lunches small.

About halfway through the meal, Samuel — who is a quiet man and does not say much at lunch — looked at me across the table and said, in his careful English, Greg, you are not yourself today.

I told him I had been tired.

He said: for how long.

I told him: for about a year. Maybe two.

He chewed for a while. He is a man who does not rush a sentence.

He said: what does your doctor say.

I told him my bloodwork was good. My blood pressure was good. Everything was where my doctor wanted it. There was nothing to fix.

He nodded.

He took another bite. He chewed. He swallowed.

He said one thing more, and then he changed the subject.

He said: Greg, the body that gets you through a long day is the body you are paying attention to. If you have stopped paying attention to it, it will stop getting you through a long day.

He ate the rest of his lunch. We talked about the maple, and about a chair he had been making for his grandson, and about the price of fuel.

I drove the three and a half hours home thinking about Samuel walking the length of his mill yard at seventy-six.

I drove the rest of that week thinking about it.

By the weekend, I had started reading.

I am the kind of man who has been ordering oak from the same sawmill for twenty-three years. I am not a man who jumps at the next thing. I read carefully, slowly, the way I read a set of plans for a kitchen that I am about to build.

I read for almost three weeks.

I read about cellular energy. I read about the slow, invisible decline in the body's machinery that starts somewhere in the mid-forties and accelerates, in small increments, through the fifties and sixties.

I read about the long, patient relationship the cardiovascular research community has had with various plants and compounds, in the context of supporting healthy circulation and the body's own cellular energy.

I read about beetroot specifically. I read about the deep crimson pigment called betalain — the color that stains your cutting board for three days. I read about the dietary nitrates that are naturally present in the root.

I read about the decades of careful, patient research the cardiovascular community has been accumulating on this vegetable, in people whose numbers are already in the range their doctors want them in.

None of what I read was a fireworks story. It was the opposite of one.

The language being used in the careful corner of the research conversation was supports healthy circulation, supports cardiovascular wellness, supports the body's own cellular energy — in people whose numbers are already in range.

Not fixes anything.

Not replaces what your doctor has you on.

Not gives you your forty-year-old body back.

That was the language I had been looking for and had not been finding in the supplement aisle at the drugstore.

I picked one of the brands I had read about, a small company called Rosabella, and I picked it for one specific reason.

The betalain pigment is heat-sensitive. That is the chemistry of the molecule.

If you process beetroot the standard way, with heat, you lose some of the compound to the heat.

Rosabella decided to cold-press the root at low temperatures because they wanted as much of the compound as possible to make it from the field into the capsule.

That is a slower way to make a supplement. It costs them more.

I have been a cabinetmaker for twenty-three years. I have spent twenty-three years paying attention to the small decisions craftsmen make when no one is watching. The cold-press told me something about who was making the supplement.

The other thing I liked was the simplicity. Two capsules in the morning with a glass of water.

scripts.body_meta:
There's a Flight of Stairs at My Granddaughter's School I'd Been Quietly Losing to for Two Years.

There's a flight of stairs at my granddaughter's elementary school.

Two flights, actually — twenty-two steps each, with a small landing between them.

The auditorium where her spring piano recital happens every May is at the top.

For her first three recitals I climbed those stairs without thinking about them.

At her fourth recital, two springs ago, I stopped on the landing.

Just for a moment.

I told myself I was admiring a watercolor that some fifth grader had taped to the wall.

At her fifth recital, last spring, I stopped on the landing again.

And then halfway up the second flight.

By the time I got to the auditorium I sat in my seat for two minutes before I could really focus on the program.

A man at least ten years older than me passed me on the way up.

He didn't stop.

I sat there in the auditorium that afternoon listening to children play "Für Elise" with one hand, and I made myself a small, careful promise.

The next time I saw my cardiologist, I was going to tell her about the stairs.

She looked across her desk at me a week later and said something I think about almost every day now.

She said: "Marilyn. Your bloodwork is in the ranges I want it in. Your medication is doing what we hoped it would do. But you're three years past the change now, and the conversation I want to have with you today is a little different from the ones we've been having."

Then she sat back in her chair and asked me — and these are her exact words — "what your body has been telling you that you haven't been telling me."

I sat there for a long moment.

I am sixty-four years old.

I was a high school guidance counselor for twenty-eight years before I retired.

I have spent most of my professional life asking other people careful questions and waiting for them to answer honestly.

I had not expected to be on the receiving end of one.

But I had walked into her office that morning prepared to answer one.

I told her about the stairs.

That was one thing.

The other thing was the hill to our church.

We've gone to the same small church for thirty-one years.

The parking lot is on the lower lawn. The church itself is at the top of a small slope — maybe forty paces, an incline you wouldn't call a hill if you were younger than fifty.

I had walked that slope every Sunday morning for thirty-one years without registering it.

Sometime in the year before my granddaughter's fifth recital, I had started parking in the upper lot instead, by the office.

It's only twenty paces, on the flat.

I told myself it was easier when I was carrying a casserole for the Sunday lunch.

I had not been carrying a casserole every Sunday for thirty-one years.

I had been carrying my body up a slope that was telling me something I was not in a mood to hear.

There was one more thing I told her too.

The way I sometimes notice my own heartbeat at night now, the way I didn't notice it ten years ago.

Not loudly. Not alarmingly.

Just present in a way it hadn't been present before.

I told her I knew none of it was anything, exactly.

My numbers were in the ranges. The medication was doing its work. The annual EKG had been unremarkable.

I told her I was probably making something out of nothing.

She did not say I was making something out of nothing.

She said: "Your numbers are in good shape, Marilyn. The medication is doing what we wanted it to do. A lot of women in their sixties start paying closer attention to what their bodies are telling them, especially the small physical things they used to do without noticing. That's a healthy instinct. The chart is one piece of information. What you've just told me is another. Both are useful."

She was quiet for a moment after that.

Then she said: "I'm not going to change anything today. Your medication is doing what we want it to do. But if you'd like to think about whether there's one small additive thing you might bring into your mornings — something general, structure-function, well-researched, that supports what your body is already doing — I'd be happy to have that conversation at your next appointment. Or sooner, if you call."

I drove home from her office that afternoon thinking about the difference between a doctor who treats a chart and a doctor who reads a person.

I started reading the next day.

I want to be clear about something before I describe what I read.

I am not a doctor.

I am not a nurse.

I do not have any medical expertise of any kind.

I am a retired high school guidance counselor with a husband, two grown sons, a granddaughter who plays piano, and a relationship with my own body that I have been paying closer attention to in recent years.

What follows is one careful woman's experience told the way I'd tell a friend at the kitchen table.

Nothing more.

I am a careful reader.

Twenty-eight years of working with teenagers and their parents teaches you to be suspicious of anything that arrives loud.

I skipped past the supplement companies promising things no supplement can promise.

I skipped past the protocols and the morning routines and the influencers and the people selling certainty.

I was looking for the careful, quiet, structure-function corner of the conversation.

The thing that kept coming up there was beetroot.

Not beetroot juice. Not the beetroot powders at the health food store.

The active compound in beetroot — a family of pigments called betalains.

The research is real.

It has been built carefully over decades by careful people who have not, to their credit, been making outlandish claims.

The betalains in beetroot are studied in the context of supporting healthy circulation, supporting cardiovascular wellness, and supporting the body's natural antioxidant balance — particularly in people whose numbers are already in the range their doctor wants them in.

That was the shape of the language I had been looking for.

Not "fixes." Not "treats." Not "reverses."

Just supports.

In women whose cardiovascular wellness was part of the long, careful conversation they were having with their own doctors.

One brand kept showing up in the more careful sources.

Rosabella.

The thing I liked about it was a small thing.

Betalains are heat-sensitive — that's just the chemistry of the molecule — and most processing methods involve high temperatures, which is the cheaper and faster way.

Rosabella cold-presses their beetroot at low temperatures.

It costs them more to do it that way.

It takes longer.

They do it anyway, because more of the active compound survives the processing.

After twenty-eight years of telling teenagers to pay attention to what people do rather than what they say, I have come to believe the same thing about companies.

The other thing I liked was the simplicity.

Two capsules in the morning with a glass of water.

That is the whole protocol.

I am sixty-four years old. I have already lived through the years of complicated routines.

I am not interested in another one.

Before I added it, I made two phone calls.

I want to talk about both, because they are the most important part of any honest letter about a supplement.

I am on a low-dose cholesterol medication. I have been on it for eight years.

My doctor and I are happy with how it has been working.

I would not add anything to that medication without checking first whether the addition was sensible — and "sensible" is not a thing I, as a retired guidance counselor in suburban Pittsburgh, am qualified to determine on my own.

I called Dr. Tanaka's office on a Tuesday morning.

I left a message with her nurse with the brand name and the dosage.

She called me back that afternoon.

Dr. Tanaka had said it was a reasonable thing to add, that there were no concerns with the dosage on the label alongside my current medication, and to let her know how I was feeling at our next appointment.

I called the pharmacy where I have been filling my prescription for nine years.

I told the pharmacist on duty what I wanted to add.

She pulled up my profile.

She confirmed what Dr. Tanaka had said — no concerns at the dosage on the label, given the medication and dose I am on.

She told me to take the capsules at the same time I take my morning prescription, with water, the way the bottle suggested.

I want to be plain about this.

Both calls together took me less than ten minutes.

If you are on any cardiovascular medication — a cholesterol medication, a blood pressure medication, a blood thinner, anything — those minutes are the most important minutes you will spend on the supplement.

The people who know what's on your chart will tell you in two sentences whether adding something is safe for you.

I am a retired guidance counselor in suburban Pittsburgh.

I am not the person to ask.

They are.

I started on a Monday in late April.

I put the bottle on the counter next to the coffee maker.

I took the two capsules with my first sip of coffee, right alongside my prescription.

I did not feel anything in particular for the first two weeks.

I had read enough to know I shouldn't expect to.

A supplement is not a drug. It doesn't switch on the way a drug switches on.

It is something the body uses, slowly, in the work the body is already doing.

What I noticed, I noticed in two specific moments.

The first one was at my granddaughter's end-of-year recital in June.

Same school. Same auditorium on the second floor. Same two flights of stairs.

I climbed them without stopping on the landing.

It wasn't that I climbed them quickly.

I didn't.

I climbed them the way I had climbed them at sixty-one, before I started quietly stopping on landings.

I got to the auditorium and I sat down in my seat and I noticed, with my purse in my lap, that I was not catching my breath.

I did not say anything to my husband.

He was already engrossed in the program.

I made a quiet note. I kept paying attention.

The second moment was on a Sunday morning in early August.

I was at the church parking lot.

I had a casserole in my hands — a real one this time, a chicken and wild rice for the women's group lunch.

I started toward the upper lot by the office, where I had been parking for over a year.

Then I stopped.

I turned around.

I walked back to the car.

I drove down to the lower lot and parked there instead.

I carried the casserole up the slope.

I did not stop.

I got to the top and I stood on the church porch for a moment and I noticed, with the casserole still in my hands, that I had walked up the slope I had been quietly refusing for a year and a half.

I did not tell anybody at church.

I went inside and put the casserole on the women's group table and sat down for the service.

That was the morning I let myself notice it.

I want to be careful with what I am saying here.

I am not telling you that Rosabella climbed those stairs or carried that casserole.

I had been doing other things alongside the supplement.

I had been walking a little more deliberately after my conversation with Dr. Tanaka.

I had been taking the steps in our own house at home, on purpose, three times a day, rather than avoiding them.

Something had shifted in me the afternoon I drove home from her office in April that had nothing to do with a capsule on a saucer.

There were several things changing at once.

The way there are when a careful woman finally tells a careful doctor the thing she has been carrying alone for two years.

What I can say is that I added one small thing to a list of small things I was newly doing.

I kept everything else exactly the same — including the medication Dr. Tanaka has me on.

And the months that followed were qualitatively different from the eighteen months that preceded them.

I saw Dr. Tanaka in October.

New bloodwork. New EKG.

She read the results for a few minutes.

Then she looked up.

She said: "Your numbers are in the same good place they've been. But you look like someone who hasn't been measuring her own breath lately."

I told her about the stairs and the casserole.

I told her about the beetroot.

I told her I'd called the office before I started.

She nodded.

She said: "That was the right way to do it. Antioxidant support in this range is well-researched. Keep going."

She did not change my medication.

She did not change anything else.

She told me she'd see me in March.

I drove home from her office that afternoon thinking that there is a quiet, careful conversation happening between a woman's body and her doctor in the years after the change.

And that the bloodwork only tells half of it.

The other half is what the body tells you on the stairs.

I'm telling you this because I think you might be a woman where I was two springs ago.

Post-menopausal.

In fine shape on paper.

On a medication that's doing its job.

With a quiet, persistent awareness that something has shifted in the way your body handles the small physical work of your day — the stairs, the slopes, the things you used to do without noticing them.

If that's you, please don't ignore what your body is telling you just because your chart is fine.

The chart is one piece of information.

Your body is another.

A good doctor wants both.

Mine asked me directly, and I'm grateful she did.

If yours hasn't, you can be the one to bring it up.

If you decide to think about adding a structure-function supplement to what you're already doing, please make the call before you start.

If you're on any cardiovascular medication — cholesterol, blood pressure, blood thinner, anything — this is not optional.

Call your doctor's office.

Call your pharmacist.

The two minutes it takes is the most important two minutes of your engagement with anything you put in your body.

The brand I added to my morning is Rosabella.

Two capsules with water, alongside my prescription, with my coffee.

1,300 milligrams of organic beetroot per serving, cold-pressed at low temperatures.

It is not a fix for anything.

It is not a substitute for hormone therapy or any cardiovascular medication.

It is not a treatment for menopause or for post-menopausal anything.

It is one small thing some women add to the long list of things they are already doing for themselves, alongside everything else.

Bodies are different.

Some women notice something within the first two weeks.

Some women take a couple of months.

Some women don't notice much at all.

That is the truthful version, and I would rather you hear it from me now than be disappointed later.

P.S. Rosabella has a ninety-day satisfaction guarantee.

Any reason at all.

You don't have to prove anything to anyone — not to them, not about your numbers, not about how you feel.

If you tried it and you're not satisfied, you're not satisfied.

That is the whole policy.

I appreciate that kind of policy at sixty-four.

The cold-pressing takes longer than the conventional methods, so they sometimes run out between harvests.

I keep an extra bottle in the cupboard now.

I learned to stay one bottle ahead.

Call your doctor's office and your pharmacist before you add anything new to a cardiovascular medication.

Not because anything bad will happen — probably nothing will.

I Went on a Wildflower Hike Alone Because My Husband Was Too Tired to Come. A Woman on the Trail Said Six Words I Haven't Forgotten.

We'd signed up for the walk three months earlier.

It was Frank's idea.

A guided wildflower hike at a state park about forty minutes from our house.

Two hours through the woods with a naturalist who knew every plant by its Latin name and its common name and which Native American tribe had used it for what.

Frank had circled the date on our kitchen calendar.

He'd told me about it at dinner.

He'd told me about it again two weeks later when the registration confirmation came in the mail.

He'd said: "This is the kind of thing we should be doing more of."

I'd agreed.

We were both 65.

We'd been talking for a year about how we needed to start doing things again.

Frank had been a birdwatcher his whole adult life.

When we were first married, he used to wake me up at 4:30 in the morning on Saturdays to drive out to the lake before dawn to listen for warblers.

I'd grumble.

I'd drink my coffee in the car.

I'd sit in the cold marsh with him for two hours while he wrote things in a notebook.

I never loved it the way he did.

But I loved him, and he loved it, and that was enough.

He stopped going somewhere in his early sixties.

Not all at once.

He started saying he was too tired the night before.

Then he started saying he'd go next weekend.

Then he stopped putting it on the calendar at all.

His binoculars sat on the bookshelf in our living room and gathered dust.

His field guides were stacked next to them, the bookmarks still in the pages from his last trip.

The vintage car he'd been restoring in our garage — a 1972 Buick he'd bought from a man in Indiana — hadn't moved in fourteen months.

The dust on the hood was thick enough I could write my name in it if I wanted to.

I didn't write my name in it.

I tried not to look at it most days.

The wildflower walk was the first thing he'd put on the calendar in over a year.

When he'd signed us up, I'd let myself hope.

I'd thought maybe this was the start of something.

Maybe he was coming back.

The Saturday of the walk, I woke up at 6:30.

I made coffee.

I packed two water bottles and two granola bars and a small bag with a sandwich for the road home.

I came back into the bedroom to wake Frank up.

He was awake.

He was lying on his back, looking at the ceiling.

He said: "Honey, I don't think I can do it today."

I sat down on the edge of the bed.

I said: "Frank, you picked this one."

He said: "I know. I'm sorry. I just can't."

He didn't look at me when he said it.

He looked at the ceiling.

He looked at it the way a man looks at a ceiling when he can't look at his wife.

I sat there for a long minute.

I had three things I wanted to say.

I didn't say any of them.

I said: "Okay. I'll go."

He said: "You don't have to."

I said: "I'm going."

I stood up.

I kissed him on the forehead.

I left.

I cried in the car for the first ten minutes of the drive.

Not big crying.

The quiet kind, where you keep driving and you keep your hands on the wheel and you let it happen because there's nobody to see it.

By the time I got to the trailhead I'd cleaned myself up.

I parked.

I sat in the car for two minutes before I went in.

I almost turned around and drove home.

I didn't know why I was there alone.

I didn't know why I was going on a wildflower walk that I hadn't picked, on a Saturday morning when my husband was lying on his back in our bedroom looking at the ceiling.

But I'd told him I was going.

And I'd already gotten dressed for it.

So I got out of the car.

The group at the trailhead was maybe twelve people.

Mostly couples in their fifties and sixties.

A young couple with hiking poles who looked serious about it.

A grandfather and grandson, the grandson maybe nine.

And me.

And a woman about my age standing by herself on the other side of the gravel parking area.

She was wearing a green windbreaker and good walking shoes.

She had a small backpack.

She was looking at her phone the way you look at your phone when you're alone in a place where everyone else is in a pair and you'd rather be looking at anything than at the couples.

I recognized the posture.

I was doing the same thing.

The naturalist gathered us.

He introduced himself.

He gave the safety talk and the don't-touch-the-poison-ivy talk and the please-stay-on-the-trail talk.

He started walking.

We followed.

The woman in the green windbreaker fell in next to me about ten minutes into the trail.

Not on purpose.

The path narrowed and the couples paired up and the two of us ended up walking side by side because there wasn't really another option.

We didn't talk at first.

We just walked.

The naturalist stopped every few hundred feet to point at something.

A trillium.

A bloodroot.

A jack-in-the-pulpit that he said was actually a female because the spadix was the right shape.

We listened.

We nodded.

We moved on.

About twenty minutes in, the woman next to me said: "My husband was supposed to come today."

She said it quietly.

She wasn't looking at me.

She was looking at the trail ahead.

I said: "Mine too."

She turned and looked at me then.

She had kind eyes and the kind of crow's-feet that come from a lifetime of smiling at things.

She said: "Oh."

And that was all she said for a minute.

We kept walking.

After a while she said: "What does yours like? Out here, I mean. What was he hoping to see?"

I said: "Warblers. He's a birdwatcher. Was a birdwatcher. He used to be."

She nodded.

She didn't ask what had changed.

She didn't need to ask.

She said: "Mine's a math professor. He's retired now. He used to lead these walks at our community college. Plant identification. He could tell you the family of any flowering thing within sixty seconds. Now he doesn't go on walks anymore."

I said: "I'm sorry."

She said: "Me too."

We walked for a while in silence.

The trail curved up a small rise and dipped into a hollow where there were violets growing in great drifts on both sides of the path.

The naturalist stopped.

He talked about violets.

Yellow violets, white violets, the common purple, the rare bird's-foot violet with leaves cut like a chicken's foot.

The grandson found a bird's-foot violet by accident and the naturalist made a big deal of it.

The grandson glowed.

I watched the grandson glow.

I thought about Frank at our kitchen table fifteen years ago teaching our own grandson to identify the birds at the feeder.

I thought about how my own grandson is twelve now and barely sees Frank because Frank is too tired most weekends to drive the hour out to our son's house.

I thought about how Frank doesn't even know what his grandson is into anymore.

The woman in the green windbreaker said, quietly, next to me: "Are you alright?"

I said: "I don't know."

She said: "I wasn't either, for a long time."

We walked for another half hour without talking about it.

She told me her name was Helen.

I told her mine.

She told me she lived about an hour from where I lived, on the opposite side of the state park.

She told me her husband's name was Walter.

She told me they'd been married for forty-three years.

She'd been a high school librarian for thirty-one years.

She'd retired in 2019 thinking she and Walter would do all the things they'd been waiting to do.

It didn't happen.

She said it like that.

"It didn't happen."

She didn't elaborate.

She didn't need to.

After a while she said: "Can I tell you something? You don't have to do anything with it. I just want to tell you because I'm seeing my own face from a few years ago on you and I wish someone had told me what I'm about to tell you."

I said: "Tell me."

She said: "There's a quiet kind of disappearing that happens to men sometimes when they get into their sixties. It's not a heart attack. It's not a fall. It's not anything you can put on a chart. The bloodwork looks fine. The blood pressure is fine. The doctor says everything's fine."

"They just start dimming. They sit in the chair earlier in the evening. They stop picking up the hobbies. They sleep more and rest less. They go on fewer walks. They stop reading the books they used to read. They stop calling the people they used to call. They become a quieter version of the man you married."

"And the worst part is that the world has a name for it that lets everyone stop asking questions. The world calls it aging."

She stopped on the trail.

She turned to me.

She said: "Sometimes it is aging. Sometimes it really is. But sometimes it's just that nobody — not the doctor, not the wife, not the man himself — has looked underneath the word aging in a long time."

She put her hand on my arm.

She said the six words that I haven't forgotten in nine months.

She said: "Your husband isn't gone. He's tired."

I want to tell you that I had something articulate to say back.

I didn't.

I just stood on the trail and looked at her and tried not to cry in front of a stranger.

She squeezed my arm.

She said: "Come on. The group's getting ahead."

We started walking again.

After a few minutes she said: "I'll tell you what I did. Not because you should do it. Because you asked, and I'd want someone to tell me. I read for a long time about what happens to the body's energy systems as it ages. I'm not going to pretend I understood all of it. I'm a librarian, not a scientist. But I learned that there's a category of things that go on inside the body that don't always show up on the standard bloodwork. The way the cells handle stress. The way the smallest blood vessels keep doing what they're supposed to do. The way the body manages its own fuel."

"I talked to Walter's doctor about it. He's a good doctor. He didn't dismiss me. He told me that a few things he considered reasonable as additions to what Walter was already doing. He gave me a short list. He told me to look at it, pick what made sense, and let his office know what I added."

"One of the things I added was a beetroot supplement."

"I'd had beetroot in salads my whole life and I'd never thought of it as anything more than a vegetable. But beetroot has been studied for decades for circulatory wellness and antioxidant balance. Walter's doctor said the research on it was solid. He had no concerns about it being added to Walter's routine."

She paused.

She picked her way over a root in the path.

She kept going.

"What I learned is that not all beetroot supplements are the same. Most of them are processed with high heat. The active compounds inside the beet — the ones the research is actually about — are heat sensitive. They don't survive the fast, cheap processing. A lot of what makes the root worth taking gets cooked away."

"I spent a whole afternoon reading labels and processing methods. I found one that did it the slow way. Cold-pressed at low temperatures. It costs more. The bottles are smaller. But what's in the capsule is closer to what's actually in the beet. You can see it in the color of the powder. It's a deep, dark crimson — almost purple. That's the compounds the cold-pressing preserves."

She said the brand name.

I'd never heard of it.

I asked her to spell it for me.

She did.

I wrote it on a corner of my trail map with the pen the naturalist had handed out at the start.

She smiled at me when I did that.

She said: "I'm not selling you anything. I'm an old librarian and I work part-time at a thrift store for my church. I just had a conversation a few years ago at a quilting class with a woman I'd never met before who told me what she'd done for her husband. I went home and tried it. So I'm passing the favor on."

We walked the rest of the trail with Helen telling me about Walter the way you tell someone about a person you love.

He'd started taking the supplement six months after the conversation she'd had at the quilting class.

She'd been honest about all of it.

She didn't tell him it was a miracle.

She didn't tell him it would change his life.

She told him she'd talked to his doctor and that his doctor was alright with him trying it.

She told him she just wanted him to try one thing for ninety days alongside everything else he was already doing.

He'd agreed.

The first month, she said, she hadn't noticed anything.

She'd almost stopped.

She said: "I want to be honest about that part. The first few weeks I thought I'd just bought myself an expensive vegetable in a bottle."

The second month, Walter started taking longer walks.

She didn't ask him to.

He just started doing it.

The third month, he opened one of his old field guides one Saturday morning.

He didn't say anything about it.

He just sat at the kitchen table with his coffee and his guide and looked at the pictures.

The fourth month, he started writing in his notebook again.

He'd kept the same kind of notebook for forty years.

He'd stopped writing in it three years before any of this started.

He started again.

She said: "I'm not telling you Walter is twenty-five years old again. He's not. He's 68 and he's tired sometimes and he still falls asleep in his chair after dinner some nights. But he's in the world again. He's doing things again. He's calling the friends he used to call. He's coming on these walks again — most of the time. He didn't come today because he had to drive his sister to a dental appointment. But he wanted to come. That's the part that matters."

She looked at me.

She said: "I'm not telling you any of this is the beetroot. I changed a couple of other things too. We started eating dinner earlier. We started taking walks together in the evening. I stopped saying we should and started saying let's just and I dragged him along most of the time. There were a lot of small things. The beetroot was one of them. I don't know with certainty what did what."

"What I know is that I added one thing to a man who was disappearing into his chair, and a lot of small things started shifting in the same direction."

"That's the most honest version I can give you."

We came out of the woods at the trailhead at 11:30.

The grandson was clutching a worksheet the naturalist had given him with all the plants he'd identified marked off.

The young couple with the hiking poles were sweating.

The other couples were comparing photos on their phones.

Helen and I stood by the trailhead sign.

I said: "Thank you."

She said: "Don't thank me. Just go home and look at him. The way you'd look at him if you were a stranger meeting him for the first time. See what a stranger would see."

I said: "I will."

She hugged me.

I hugged her back.

She walked to her car.

I walked to mine.

I never saw her again.

I drove home with my trail map on the passenger seat and the brand name written in the corner.

Frank was on the couch in the living room when I came in.

The TV was on.

He was asleep with his mouth slightly open.

It was 12:15.

I stood in the doorway and I looked at him the way Helen had told me to.

I saw a man who was smaller than the man I'd married.

Tireder.

Quieter.

Further away.

His binoculars on the bookshelf with dust on them.

His field guides next to them.

His grandson's birthday card from March still on the side table because he hadn't gotten around to mailing one back.

I sat down in the chair across from the couch.

I watched him sleep for a long time.

When he woke up he saw me sitting there.

He said: "How was the walk?"

I said: "It was good. I met somebody."

He said: "Yeah?"

I said: "Yeah."

He said: "What did you talk about?"

I said: "I want to tell you about it. But first I want to tell you something else. I think there's something I want us to try. Together. I want to call your doctor first."

He looked at me.

He sat up on the couch.

He said: "Okay."

That was all he said.

That was enough.

I called Frank's doctor on Monday.

I told the nurse I'd been reading about beetroot supplements and wondering if it would be alright to add one to what Frank was already doing.

She put me on hold.

She came back about three minutes later.

She said the doctor had no concerns about Frank adding it to his routine, that beetroot was a reasonable thing to consider for circulatory wellness, and that he just wanted us to keep him in the loop.

I asked her if I could email him the supplement facts panel of the one I was thinking about, just so he could see it.

She said please do.

I did.

He emailed back the next day.

He said it looked fine.

I ordered Rosabella that night.

I want to be careful about what I tell you next.

I'm not going to tell you Frank felt it in seventeen minutes.

I don't think it works like that.

I'm not going to tell you anything dramatic happened in the first week.

It didn't.

What I can tell you is what we noticed over about three months.

The first month, Frank kept taking it because he'd told me he'd give it ninety days and Frank does what he says he'll do.

Somewhere in week five, he started reading again in the evenings.

Not for long.

Maybe twenty minutes before bed.

But the field guide that had been on the side table for fourteen months started moving.

I'd find it on the kitchen counter one morning.

The bookshelf the next.

The bedroom another.

It was traveling around the house with him.

Week eight, he opened the garage on a Saturday morning.

He didn't work on the Buick.

He just stood next to it for an hour.

He wiped the dust off the hood with a rag.

He sat in the driver's seat and turned the key just to listen to the engine.

He came inside afterward and didn't say anything about it.

I didn't say anything about it either.

Somewhere around week ten, he asked me if I'd come with him to the lake at dawn on Saturday.

He hadn't asked me that in four years.

We went.

He sat in the marsh and wrote in his notebook.

I drank coffee in the car.

It was cold and it was beautiful and he came out of the marsh at 7:30 with two new species written down in handwriting that was a little shakier than it used to be but was his.

His handwriting.

The kind of handwriting Frank does.

His doctor saw him at his regular six-month checkup about ten weeks in.

He took his blood pressure.

He drew labs.

He went through the standard checklist.

He said Frank's numbers were in better shape than they'd been in a couple of years.

He didn't make a big deal of it.

He told Frank whatever he was doing, to keep doing it.

Frank told him about the beetroot.

The doctor said: "Yeah, your wife emailed me about that. Good. Keep at it."

That was the whole conversation about it.

That was all it needed to be.

I want to be careful about what I'm claiming here.

I am one woman.

Frank is one man.

I'm not a doctor and I'm not pretending to be one in any of what I've just told you.

Beetroot wasn't the only thing we changed.

We started eating dinner earlier.

We started taking walks together in the evening.

I stopped accepting tiredness as a complete answer.

I asked him more questions.

There were a lot of small things.

The supplement was one of them.

I don't know with certainty what did what.

What I know is that I went on a wildflower walk alone in May because my husband was too tired to come, and I came home with a name written on the corner of a trail map, and ten months later my husband sat in our marsh at dawn writing in a notebook for the first time in four years.

That's the version I have.

That's all I have.

If you're a woman whose husband has been dimming for a while and you've been calling it aging because that's what everyone calls it — talk to his doctor.

Always start there.

Whatever you add to what he's already doing should be a decision his doctor is in the loop on.

If his doctor is open to it, beetroot is a reasonable thing to look at.

It's been studied for decades.

It's not exotic.

It's just been processed badly by most of the brands selling it.

Rosabella is the one Helen told me about on a wildflower trail last May.

It's the one I bought.

It's the one Frank still takes every morning with a glass of water.

I'm not the right person to tell you what to do with your husband's body.

But I am a woman who waited too long to take any of this seriously.

And I had to be told by a stranger on a hiking trail what I should have been telling myself for two years before that.

If you're reading this, maybe you've just been told.

P.S. Two capsules with a glass of water in the morning.

That's the whole protocol.

Don't change anything else he's doing.

Not the medications.

Not the diet.

Not the routine.

Just add this and pay attention to what shifts.

P.P.S. Talk to his doctor or pharmacist before he starts.

This is the first step, not a footnote.

If he takes any prescription medication — especially for blood pressure, cholesterol, or his heart — the conversation with his doctor matters more than anything I have to say here.

P.P.P.S. Rosabella has a 90-day money-back guarantee.

If you're not satisfied for any reason, every penny back.

No questions asked.

That's a sensible policy for a supplement.

It gives you the time you actually need to see whether it helps.

P.P.P.P.S. Rosabella is a small operation.

They harvest and bottle on their own schedule.

I keep an extra bottle in the house now because I don't want to be the woman who runs out and has to wait.

They have a multi-bottle option I went with myself.

Worth a look.

P.P.P.P.P.S. I've gone back to that state park three times this year.

I've walked the same trail twice.

I haven't seen Helen.

I don't know if I ever will.

If she's reading this somewhere — thank you.

You said six words to a stranger on a wildflower trail in May and you gave me back the man I married.

I hope someone gives you the same gift someday, whether you need it or not.
