scripts.body_meta:
A woman in the seat next to me at a community-college pottery class told me, very casually, why her hands had stopped bothering her.

I went home that night and thought about it for a week.

I am sixty-four years old. My name is Patricia, but I have been Pat to everyone I love since I was about six.

I retired three years ago from the regional library system in our part of central Ohio, where I had been a children's librarian for thirty-one years.

My husband, Doug, retired the year after me from the maintenance department of the city schools, where he had been the head of operations.

We have one daughter, who lives in Columbus with her own family, and three grandchildren we see most weekends.

We live in the same house we have lived in for thirty-six years, on a quiet street with old maples and neighbors who have mostly been here as long as we have.

I am telling you all of that because the story I want to tell you is small, and small stories are easier to follow if you know who the small story is happening to.

I started having achy hands about five years ago.

It was not a sudden thing. None of this has been a sudden thing.

It started the way these things start — one morning I noticed my hands felt a little stiff when I went to open a jar of peach preserves at breakfast.

I have been opening jars for fifty years. I noticed the stiffness because the jar took two tries instead of one, and because the second try involved my whole shoulder in a way that the first try used to handle on its own.

I did not think much of it.

I am a librarian, after all, and I had read enough about getting older to know that hands stiffen a little at sixty. I thought about it for the rest of the morning and then I forgot about it for almost a year.

Over the course of that year, though, I noticed it again. And then again. And then more often than that.

By the time I was sixty-one, I was waking up in the morning with hands that took about half an hour to feel like my hands.

I was reaching for jars two-handed.

I was finding that the small repetitive tasks of a life — knitting, which I have done since I was twelve, and the small bits of mending that come up when you live in an old house, and the dishes after a Sunday dinner with twelve people — were each leaving me with a quiet ache that lingered into the next morning.

I went to my doctor about it at my annual physical.

She is a careful woman, my doctor, in her early fifties, and she has been our family doctor since our daughter was in middle school.

She examined my hands. She asked me a number of careful questions. She ran some additional bloodwork.

She looked at the results and told me what she always tells me when she tells me good news — that everything was in the ranges she wanted to see it in.

She told me my hands looked, to her examination, like the hands of a sixty-one-year-old woman who had been using them carefully for sixty-one years.

She told me there was nothing she would treat at this stage, that this was the kind of thing many women her age and mine live with, and that she would keep an eye on it.

She was right. I want to say that clearly.

She was right that there was nothing to treat, and she was right to be conservative, and I do not have a complaint about how she handled the conversation. She did her job well.

But.

She had told me my numbers were in the ranges she wanted. She had told me there was nothing she would treat. She had told me I was, in every clinical sense, fine.

And I had gone home from that appointment to the same house with the same jars of preserves and the same knitting basket and the same dishes after Sunday dinner, and the achy hands were still my achy hands, and they were going to keep being achy hands, and the medical conversation about them was apparently over.

This is the gap I want to tell you about.

The gap between the chart is fine and the body that I live in still hurts in small ways that I have started to plan my days around.

It is a particularly quiet gap to live in, because there is no acute problem to solve and no one to complain to about it.

You learn to use both hands on the jar. You learn to do the knitting in smaller sessions. You learn to keep the dishes for the next morning.

You adjust.

I adjusted for two more years.

The achy hands stayed about the same.

The achy hands were joined, eventually, by an achy left hip that talked to me when I got out of the car after a long drive, and an achy lower back that talked to me when I worked in the garden for more than an hour.

By the time I was sixty-three I had three quiet conversations going on with three different parts of my body, and they had all of them become part of the daily texture of my life.

I want to be clear that none of this stopped me from doing anything.

I gardened. I knitted. I took the grandchildren to the park. I helped my daughter with the things she needed help with. I traveled with my husband. I lived my life.

The aches were just there, all the time, in the background, like the hum of an old refrigerator.

The thing I want to tell you about happened in the fall, about a year and a half ago, at the community-college pottery class I had signed up for partly because I had always wanted to and partly because my daughter had suggested it as something that might be good for my hands.

The reasoning was that pottery would keep my hands warm and moving and engaged, and that the instructor would be able to teach me techniques that did not strain the small joints.

My daughter is thoughtful in this particular way. I love her for it.

The class was on Tuesday evenings, in a basement studio at the community college fifteen minutes from our house. There were eleven of us — mostly women, mostly in our fifties or sixties, the kind of people who sign up for a pottery class on a Tuesday evening in the fall.

I sat next to a woman I had not met before.

Her name was Joan. She was, I would guess, sixty-eight or so, and she had silver hair pulled back in a long braid and the kind of hands that told you, before she said anything, that she had been working with them for a long time.

We exchanged the small pleasantries you exchange with the woman at the next wheel on the first night of a pottery class.

We learned each other's names. We talked about the grandchildren. We talked about whether either of us had done pottery before, which neither of us had.

We agreed, partway through the first session, that we were both terrible at centering the clay — which is the first thing you have to learn and which is genuinely much harder than it looks.

It was around the third or fourth class that I mentioned, in passing, that my hands had been bothering me a little more than usual that week.

I said it almost as an apology — I had been making a worse mess than usual at the wheel — and Joan looked over at my hands and asked, in the gentle way some older women ask things, how long my hands had been bothering me.

I told her. The abridged version: five years, started small, got steadier, three quiet conversations now with three different parts of my body, doctor said nothing to treat, I had adjusted.

She nodded. She did not interrupt me while I was telling it.

When I was finished, she said: I had the same conversation about my hands with my own doctor about four years ago, and my answer to it was about the same as yours.

I asked her what she meant.

She said: I adjusted. I learned to live with it.

And then she said something that I have been thinking about ever since.

She said: About three years ago, I started taking one small thing in the mornings — a beetroot capsule, of all things — and I want to be careful about what I say to you about it, because I do not want to overstate anything, but I have been doing it for three years now, and somewhere in the second year I noticed that my hands had stopped being the first conversation I had with my body every morning.

They are still my hands. They are still sixty-eight years old. They still talk to me when I have been doing something with them for a long time.

But the morning conversation is different than it used to be.

She told me she had not changed anything else about her life.

She told me she was still on the same prescriptions she had been on for years — a low-dose blood pressure medication and something for her thyroid — and that she had specifically called her pharmacist before she added the beetroot, to ask whether it would play nicely with what she was already taking.

Her pharmacist had told her it would, and to keep doing what she was doing.

She told me the small company she had been buying it from is called Rosabella, that she had picked it because they cold-pressed the beetroot at low temperatures rather than processing it with heat, and that she had been ordering the same bottle every six weeks for three years.

She said it casually.

She was not selling me anything. She was a woman at the next wheel telling me what she had been doing, the way women that age tell you things — without performance, just the facts of a life.

I went home that night and told my husband about it.

He asked me what I was going to do.

I told him I was going to think about it.

I thought about it for a week. Then I started reading.

I read for almost three weeks.

I am a librarian — was a librarian — and reading carefully is what I do.

I read about beetroot. I read about the deep crimson pigment called betalain — the color that stains your cutting board for three days — and about the dietary nitrates that are naturally present in the root.

I read about the long, patient relationship the research community has had with this vegetable for decades, in the context of supporting healthy circulation, supporting cardiovascular wellness, and supporting the body's own natural inflammatory response, in people whose numbers are already in the range their doctors want them in.

None of what I read was a fireworks story.

It was the opposite of one.

It was the kind of careful, slowly built body of evidence that I, as a librarian, recognized — the kind that comes from researchers who are not making outlandish claims and who are content to let the work accumulate over a long time.

I picked Rosabella, the brand Joan had mentioned, and I picked it for the reason she had given and for one other reason I came to on my own.

The reason Joan had given was the cold-press.

The betalain pigment is heat-sensitive. That is the chemistry of the molecule. If you process beetroot the standard way, with heat, you lose some of the compound to the heat.

Rosabella decided to cold-press the root at low temperatures because they wanted as much of the compound as possible to make it from the field into the capsule.

That is a slower way to make a supplement, and at my age I have come to pay attention to the small decisions companies make when no one is watching, because those decisions tell you everything.

The reason I came to on my own was the simplicity.

Two capsules in the morning with a glass of water.

I am sixty-four. I have grandchildren and a garden and a knitting basket and a husband who likes his breakfast on the table at the same time every morning.

I am not interested in a protocol that requires its own shelf.

Before I started taking it, I called my pharmacist.

I called him because that is what Joan had done, and because the doctor and the pharmacist between them are the people who know what is on my chart, and I am not the kind of woman who adds anything to her morning routine without asking.

The pharmacist's name is Stephen and he has been at the small independent pharmacy in our town for the better part of twenty years.

I told him what I was thinking about adding. I told him about the over-the-counter pain reliever I take some mornings when my hands are particularly stiff.

He pulled up my profile, looked at the small things I am on — a thyroid medication I have been on since my mid-fifties, and the over-the-counter — and told me he had no concerns about adding a beetroot supplement in capsule form.

He told me to keep doing what I was doing on the medication side.

He told me, specifically, not to take more of the over-the-counter on the assumption that the beetroot would somehow balance it out — because that would be the kind of small change that should involve my doctor's office and not me on my own.

He told me to call him back, or to call my doctor, if anything changed.

I want to say something now that I am going to say several times before this letter is over, because it is the only thing in this letter that matters more than anything else.

If you are on any medication — prescription, over-the-counter, anything — call your pharmacist or your doctor's office before you add anything new to what you are already taking.

Especially if you take an over-the-counter pain reliever on any kind of regular basis, the way many women my age do.

Do not, under any circumstances, change a prescription or an over-the-counter routine on your own on the strength of what some retired librarian in Ohio wrote in a letter you found on the internet.

The people who know your chart will tell you in two minutes whether what you are thinking about adding makes sense for you.

I called Stephen. I would call him again tomorrow if I were adding anything else. The two minutes it takes to ask are worth every second.

I was adding it to what I was already doing.

Not stopping the thyroid medication. Not changing how often I took the over-the-counter when I needed it. Not adjusting anything else.

I started on a Monday.

The first two weeks I felt nothing in particular, and I want to tell you that honestly because the temptation in a letter like this one is to compress the timeline and pretend something dramatic happened on day three.

Nothing dramatic happened on day three.

I had read enough alongside what Joan had told me to know that bodies are different — some people notice something within the first week or two, some people take much longer than that, some people don't notice much at all — and I was prepared to land in any of those camps.

What I noticed, I noticed slowly, in pieces I did not connect at the time.

The first thing I noticed was the morning warm-up.

I have, for about four years, had a half-hour at the start of every day during which my hands were not quite my hands yet.

After a few weeks, I noticed that I had opened the cabinet for the coffee filters one morning without thinking about whether my hands were going to cooperate, and I realized halfway through the motion that they had cooperated, and that there had been no negotiation.

I made the coffee, drank it, and went on with my day.

It was not until that afternoon that I thought back and realized what had happened.

The second thing I noticed was the knitting.

I have been knitting in twenty-minute sessions for about three years, because longer sessions had become more than my hands wanted to give me.

Sometime in the second month, I sat down with my knitting after dinner one evening and the next time I looked at the clock it had been forty-five minutes.

I had not noticed my hands during those forty-five minutes, which is its own kind of news at sixty-four.

I put the knitting down because I was tired, not because my hands were tired.

The third thing I noticed was the morning conversation Joan had described.

I want to use her words for this because I do not have better ones.

My hands had been the first conversation I had with my body every morning for four years.

Somewhere in the second or third month of taking the beetroot capsule, that conversation got quieter.

They are still my hands. They are still sixty-four. They still talk to me when I have been pulling weeds in the garden for an hour.

But the morning conversation has changed.

I want to be careful with what I am telling you, because I am writing this to people I do not know and I do not want to overstate anything.

I am not telling you Rosabella did any of that on its own.

I had been doing the pottery class for almost a year by the time I noticed anything, and the pottery class itself had been good for my hands — keeping them warm, keeping them moving, building small motor skills.

I had been walking more in the year leading up to this, because Doug and I had started taking the dog out twice a day after his second knee acted up.

I had been making a point of stretching for ten minutes in the mornings, on a tip from my daughter.

There were several things changing at once, the way there are when a person decides, finally, to pay attention to something that has been quietly bothering them for years.

All I am telling you is that I added one small thing to a long list of things I was already doing, kept everything else exactly the same, and a quiet stretch of months followed that had not been preceded by an equally quiet stretch.

That is the honest version. I would not trust anyone who gave you a cleaner one.

I saw my doctor at my next annual, about eight months in.

She did the same examination she does every year. She looked at my hands, asked her careful questions, and ran the bloodwork.

The bloodwork was where she wanted it, in the same ranges it had been the year before.

She told me to keep doing what I was doing.

I told her about the pottery and the walking and the stretching and the beetroot.

She nodded the way she nods when she is processing something. She did not push back on any of it.

She told me to come back in a year.

That is the whole story.

I am not, as I said, the kind of woman who writes letters to strangers.

But I have been thinking about Joan at the next wheel ever since that Tuesday in the fall, and about the small kindness of telling another woman, casually, without performance, what you have been doing.

If Joan had not said anything to me, I would still be opening the peach preserves two-handed in the morning and adjusting around my hands the way I had been doing for four years.

I do not know what Joan is doing now. I see her about every other week at the same pottery class — we have both signed up for the spring semester — and we talk about the grandchildren and the centering of the clay and the things women our age talk about at a pottery wheel.

I have told her, once, that I had taken her advice and that I was grateful.

She nodded the way she did and said, I am glad.

And we had gone back to our wheels.

If you are reading this and you are living with the kind of low-grade, quiet, daily aches I have been describing — and you have been told by your doctor that there is nothing to treat, and you have adjusted, and the body you live in is just achier than it used to be in small ways that have become part of your day — I want to say a few things to you carefully.

I do not know you. I do not know what your doctor has said. I do not know what you are taking.

Bodies are different. Some people notice something within the first week or two of adding something like this. Some people take much longer. Some people don't notice much at all.

That is the honest version, and anyone offering you a cleaner one is selling you harder than I am.

Here is how I think about Rosabella now, in the words I would actually use.

It is something the body uses.

The research community talks about it in the context of supporting healthy circulation, supporting cardiovascular wellness, and supporting the body's own natural inflammatory response — in people whose numbers are already in the range their doctors want them in.

It is not a fix for anything.

It is one small thing you add to the long list of things you are already doing for yourself.

Please call your pharmacist or your doctor's office before you add it.

If you are on any medication at all — prescription or over-the-counter — and especially if you are on a regular over-the-counter pain reliever, this is non-negotiable.

The people who know your chart will tell you in two minutes whether what you are thinking about adding makes sense for you.

I am a retired children's librarian in Ohio who met a woman at a pottery wheel. I am not the person to ask. Your pharmacist or your doctor is.

The company has a ninety-day satisfaction guarantee. If you are not satisfied — for any reason at all, including just changing your mind — they refund you.

It is not tied to your bloodwork. It is not tied to anything you have to prove to anybody.

If you are not satisfied, you are not satisfied. That is the whole policy.

The beets are grown on a small operation that harvests on its own schedule, which means there are stretches when they are in stock and stretches when they are not.

I mention that not to push you — please do not let anybody push you into a health decision — but so that if you go to the site and they are out, you know why.

That is all I have. Thank you for reading this far.

I hope something here was useful to you. And I hope, somewhere in the country today, Joan is at her wheel making something beautiful with hands that have been carrying her for sixty-eight years.

— Pat

P.S. I want to come back to the cold-press for a second, because I rushed past it. The betalain pigment — the deep red, the part the research community keeps circling back to — is heat-sensitive. If you process beetroot the standard way, with heat, you lose some of the compound to the heat. Rosabella chose the slow way. Cold-press, low temperatures, more of the compound through to the capsule. It costs them money and time. They made the choice anyway. That was a piece of why I picked them, and at sixty-four it is the small things that tell you who you are dealing with.

P.P.S. Two capsules. In the morning. With a glass of water. That is the entire protocol. No powder to mix, no afternoon dose to remember, no schedule taped to the inside of the cupboard door. I keep the bottle on the counter next to the coffee. Doug and I have earned a simple morning at this point.

P.P.P.S. I am going to say it one more time, because I have to. Please. Call your pharmacist or your doctor's office before you add anything new to what you are already taking. Especially if you are taking an over-the-counter pain reliever on a regular basis, the way many women my age do. They have your whole picture. I have written you a letter. There is a difference, and the difference matters. The two minutes it takes to ask are worth every second.

P.P.P.P.S. The guarantee, again, in case you skimmed. Ninety days. Any reason at all. You do not have to prove a single thing — not to them, not about your numbers, not about how you feel. If you tried it and you are not satisfied, you are not satisfied, and they send the money back. That is the whole policy and it is a small-company policy, the kind of thing companies used to do when companies still answered the phone.

P.P.P.P.P.S. The thing Joan said at the pottery wheel — my hands had stopped being the first conversation I had with my body every morning — has been with me for a year and a half now. It was a small sentence, said casually, by a woman I had only just met. I think about it almost every day. I think about how many small kindnesses get exchanged between women of a certain age, at a pottery wheel, at a grocery store, in line at the pharmacy, in waiting rooms, that we never tell anyone about. I do not know what the equivalent of Joan is in your life. But I hope you find her. I hope someone says a small sentence to you that gets you to start paying attention. And I hope, in a year, you find yourself doing something you used to do without thinking about it — opening a jar, knitting for forty-five minutes, getting through a Sunday's dishes — and you realize, halfway through, that you have not been thinking about it at all. I hope that is for you. That is the whole reason I wrote this letter.

— P.

scripts.hook_line: She Was Standing at the Pharmacy Counter Arguing With Herself. I Almost Didn't Say Anything. Then She Turned Around.
scripts.body_meta:
She Was Standing at the Pharmacy Counter Arguing With Herself. I Almost Didn't Say Anything. Then She Turned Around.

I was waiting for a prescription to be filled on a Tuesday afternoon in October.

Nothing special about the Tuesday. Nothing special about the prescription. Tom takes something for his cholesterol — has for the past four years — and every ninety days I drive to the pharmacy on Merchant Street, drop off the paper, and wait. Sometimes I bring a book.

Sometimes I walk the aisles and look at things I don't need. Sometimes I just sit on the little bench near the blood pressure machine and watch other people do the same thing.

That Tuesday I was doing the aisle walk. Not buying anything. Just moving.

I had turned down the supplement aisle — which I don't usually do because I find it overwhelming, all those bottles making all those promises in very small type — when I noticed the woman at the far end.

She was holding two bottles. One in each hand. Reading the back of the left one. Then the back of the right one. Then the left again.

Then she put the left one down. Then she picked it up. She set them both on the shelf, stepped back, looked at them side by side like she was judging a lineup, and then picked up the left one again.

She wasn't blocking the aisle. She wasn't bothering anyone.

She was just standing there in her own quiet world, turning something over and over in her hands, and it was unmistakably the body language of a person trying to make a decision she doesn't quite feel equipped to make.

I know that look because I've had that look. I had it in this exact aisle about eighteen months ago, standing in almost the exact same spot, doing almost the exact same thing.

I was going to walk past her. It wasn't my business.

But she turned around.

She looked at me, then at the bottles in her hands, then back at me, in the particular way people do when they've decided that a stranger's opinion is better than another hour of their own uncertainty.

"Can I ask you something?" she said.

"Of course."

She held both bottles out slightly, the way you'd hold up two paint chips. "Do you know anything about beetroot supplements?"

Her name was Carol. We ended up on the bench near the blood pressure machine — hers and mine, two strangers with our respective plastic bags from the prescription window not yet in our hands — and we talked for the better part of twenty minutes.

Carol was sixty-two. Her husband Dennis was sixty-four, just retired from the fire department after thirty-one years. Big man. Good shape, relative to what a fire department career does to a body.

Not overweight. Walked every morning. Had changed what he ate about two years prior when his cholesterol numbers first started to concern his doctor — less of this, more of that, the usual conversation. He'd lost weight. He was consistent about it.

But his numbers hadn't cooperated the way his effort deserved.

His last panel had come back, and his doctor had looked at it and told him the diet and the walking were clearly doing something — she could see it — but the numbers were still trending in a direction she wasn't comfortable with.

She'd mentioned that if the next panel didn't show improvement, she was going to recommend starting a medication.

"He doesn't want to go on a medication," Carol said. She said it without any drama, just as a fact. "Not because he's stubborn — I mean, he's a little stubborn, thirty-one years on the fire department, you know — but he's watched friends go through it and the experience wasn't what they hoped for. He just wants to try everything he can first. You know?"

I did know. Tom had sat in that same chair and had almost the same conversation with almost the same framing four years ago, before his doctor ultimately recommended he start something.

"So what did his doctor say about trying a supplement?" I asked.

Carol shook her head. "I haven't asked her yet. I wanted to know what I was even looking at before I walked in there with a bottle and wasted everyone's time. I didn't want to seem like I'd been watching YouTube videos."

I laughed at that. "That's very considerate."

"I have a thing about not wasting people's time."

"Still," I said, "I'd ask before you start anything. That's the step that matters most. Whatever Dennis tries — any supplement, anything new — his doctor should know about it first. Not because she needs to approve every decision he makes, but because she's managing the full picture and she should have all the information. Especially with his numbers where they are. Especially if medication ends up being part of the picture down the road."

Carol nodded. She had the nod of a woman who had already thought about this and just needed to hear it said out loud by someone other than herself.

"That's what I figured," she said. "I just wanted to understand what I was looking at first."

So I told her.

I told her what I knew about beetroot, which is more than a person probably expects to know and less than someone who's read every study knows.

I'd spent the better part of three months reading about it when Tom and I were trying to figure out whether there was anything useful to add to what he was already doing. Not replace. Add to.

The short version is this: beetroot contains two things that have attracted a serious amount of research attention over the years.

Betalains, which are the pigment compounds that give beetroot its deep red color, have been studied for decades as antioxidants — compounds that support the body's natural defenses against oxidative stress, which is a normal process in the body that can accumulate over time.

And dietary nitrates, which are naturally occurring compounds in beetroot that researchers interested in cardiovascular wellness have paid a lot of attention to.

Which is why, when I was doing my reading, I specifically looked for a supplement that handled the processing at low temperatures — cold-pressed, not cooked down.

The point being to preserve what was actually in the beet rather than processing it in a way that works against you.

Carol was listening carefully. She had the kind of attention that people give you when they've been trying to find this information somewhere and haven't been able to land on anything they could trust.

"So what's in those two bottles?" she asked.

I looked at them. One was a generic store brand — I couldn't find anything on the label about how it was processed. The other was a brand I didn't recognize. I told her honestly that I didn't know either of those specifically.

I told her the one Tom and I had settled on was called Rosabella — organic beetroot, 1,300 milligrams per serving, two capsules in the morning with a glass of water, cold-pressed at low temperatures to preserve the betalains.

"The label says it supports healthy cholesterol levels already within the normal range," I told her. "Not that it lowers cholesterol. That language matters. It's a supplement that supports healthy function — it's not a medication.

That's an important distinction, and a brand that's honest about it is one I feel better about."

Carol looked at me for a second.

"That's actually what I want," she said. "Dennis's numbers are heading somewhere his doctor doesn't want them to go.

They're not catastrophic. He's not broken. I just want something that supports what his body is already trying to do while he keeps working at the rest of it."

"That's exactly what we were looking for too," I said.

I wrote the name down on the back of her pharmacy receipt because that's what she had in her hand. Rosabella. I underlined it.

"Look it up when you get home," I said. "Make sure it says what I said it says. And then call Dennis's doctor's office before he starts it. Not an appointment — just the nurse line.

Tell the nurse what it is, what's in it, ask if there's any reason it would be a concern given where his numbers are and whatever else he might be on or considering. That call takes five minutes. It's the step I was glad I took."

Carol looked at the receipt. Then at the bottles on the shelf. Then she put them both back.

"I was standing there for forty-five minutes," she said.

"I could tell."

She laughed. It was the laugh of someone who's been carrying something just a little too long and has finally been able to put it down somewhere.

My name was called about ten minutes later. I picked up Tom's prescription, and Carol and I said goodbye the way you say goodbye to a stranger you've just had a real conversation with — warmly, and with the mutual understanding that you're probably not going to see each other again.

I drove home thinking about Dennis. About the gap between doing everything right and watching the numbers not respond the way the effort deserves. That gap is a particular kind of frustration. You can't argue with it. You can't outwork it.

You just sit in the doctor's office hearing that the walking and the diet are helping and that the numbers are still not where she wants them, and you drive home feeling like the goalposts keep moving.

Tom had been in that gap. In some ways he still is, because cholesterol is complicated and bodies don't follow straight lines.

But his last panel gave his doctor something she hadn't had to say in a few years — that his numbers were in better shape than they'd been in a while.

She was careful about it. She said the walking, the diet changes, the consistency — she wanted to attribute it appropriately, because he'd done real work and that work deserved real credit.

But she also asked, at the end of the appointment, what if anything had changed recently. Tom mentioned the Rosabella.

She said it was a sensible thing to add and the research on beetroot for cardiovascular wellness had been accumulating for a long time. She wanted to see the next panel before drawing any firm conclusions. That's the right answer. That's what a careful doctor says.

I want to be honest with you the way I was honest with Carol: Rosabella is not a treatment for anything. The label says it supports healthy cholesterol levels already within the normal range, and that's the honest framing for what it does.

It's two capsules in the morning with a glass of water. It's added to whatever else you're already doing — the walking, the diet, the medications if that's where things have gone — not in place of any of it. Not a replacement. An addition.

Tom's doctor knows he's taking it. That mattered to me.

I made the call before he started — a five-minute conversation with the nurse — and she said it was fine and to mention it at the next appointment. That one call is what made me comfortable. It's what I'd tell anyone to do first.

Before anything else. Before you look up the website. Before you order a bottle. Call the office. Tell them what it is. Ask.

That's the step.

I've thought about Carol a few times since that Tuesday. I don't have her number and she doesn't have mine. I don't know if she called the doctor's office the next morning like she said she would.

I don't know if Dennis started something, or if the next panel came back differently, or if his doctor ended up recommending a medication and he made peace with it. I don't know any of that.

What I know is that she was standing in a supplement aisle for forty-five minutes holding two bottles she didn't understand, because she loved her husband and she wanted to do something and she didn't know what the right something was.

I know what that feels like from the inside.

I was that woman eighteen months ago. I found my way through it slowly, by reading more than I wanted to read and asking my husband's doctor more questions than I thought were worth asking, and eventually landing on something I felt good about.

She didn't have anyone to tell her. And then, on a Tuesday afternoon in October, she turned around, and she did.

If you're in a similar place — the numbers have been moving in a direction they shouldn't, you've been doing what you're supposed to do, your doctor has mentioned something on the horizon — I'm not here to tell you what to do.

I'm just a person who found something useful and is passing it along the way Carol's stranger passed it along to her.

Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before you add anything new. Especially if there's already medication in the picture, or if there might be soon.

That call comes first, always. Then, if they say it's fine: two capsules with a glass of water in the morning. Not instead of anything. In addition to everything.

Give it real time before you decide anything. Some people notice something shift within the first week or two — a little more ease in the morning, an energy that isn't quite so thin by the afternoon.

Others take longer. Bodies are different. A lot of what happens is quiet. Be patient with yours.

P.S. Tom's doctor asked at his last appointment what he'd changed. He listed the walking, the diet — the things he'd been doing for three years — and then he mentioned the Rosabella. She said she'd seen good research on beetroot for cardiovascular wellness and that it was a sensible choice. She wants the next panel before she draws any conclusions, which is exactly what she should say. She's been his doctor for eleven years. She knows he's adding this to his routine, not substituting it for anything. That's the conversation I wanted him to have before he started. I'm glad he had it.

P.P.S. The thing about doing everything right and watching the numbers not respond is that it does something to a person over time. Tom went quiet about it for a while. He'd come home from appointments and not say much and I'd ask how it went and he'd say "same thing" and that would be the end of it. What shifted, slowly, wasn't just whatever was happening on the panel. It was that he had something to do. Something he hadn't tried yet. The supplement gave him something to try. And having something to try gave him something back that the silence had been taking. I don't know how to quantify that. I know it was real.

P.P.P.S. Here's the practical version of everything I just said: call your doctor's office first. That's the step. Nurse line, five minutes, tell them what it is and ask if it's okay given everything else in the picture. If they say yes — two capsules, glass of water, morning. Don't change anything else you're doing. Just add this one thing. It's added to whatever else you're already doing — not replacing any of it. Give it a few weeks before you decide anything about it. Some people notice something within the first week or two. Others take longer. Bodies are different. Be patient with yours.

P.P.P.P.S. Rosabella has a 90-day money-back guarantee. If you're not satisfied for any reason, every penny back. No questions asked. I think that's a fair policy for a supplement — it gives you enough time to actually find out whether it's doing anything for you, rather than having to decide in two weeks. Take the time.

P.P.P.P.P.S. Rosabella is a small operation. They harvest and bottle on their own schedule, so I keep an extra bottle on hand just in case. I started taking it too, a few months after Tom did. His doctor's reasoning stayed with me — the research on antioxidant support and cardiovascular wellness wasn't just for people whose numbers were already moving. You don't have to wait until something is visibly wrong to start paying attention to what's working.

scripts.main_pain_point: Declining kidney function (eGFR 42, Stage 3) marching toward dialysis exactly like her father, despite years of supplements and generic medical advice.
scripts.hook_line: My eGFR was 42 and declining. Three years on every kidney supplement available. CoQ10. Turmeric. Herbal blends. All failed. Two different hibiscus teas failed. Then I found out why — and my eGFR went from 42 to 58 in 9 months.
scripts.body_meta:
My eGFR was 42 and declining. Three years on every kidney supplement available. CoQ10. Turmeric. Herbal blends. All failed. Two different hibiscus teas failed. Then I found out why — and my eGFR went from 42 to 58 in 9 months.

My father died at 68.

I'm 59.

Three weeks ago, my doctor closed the exam room door.

The click echoed.

She sat down. Pulled up my chart without looking at me.

"Sandra. We can't wait anymore. Your eGFR is 42. We need to start discussing fistula placement and dialysis access. You're entering Stage 4."

My throat constricted. The walls tilted.

Dialysis.

My father went through it. Eleven years of declining kidney function leading to the same endpoint.

His energy went first. Exhaustion hitting by noon. Just sitting in his recliner. Every day. Shuffling around like an old man at 58.

The kidney function tests that got worse. And worse. And worse.

Creatinine climbing. GFR dropping. Year 6: Stage 3. Year 9: Stage 4.

Year 11: Dialysis three times a week. His arm with the fistula. Swollen. Purple. Painful.

A man who used to run marathons couldn't walk to the mailbox without gasping for breath.

My mother's words at the funeral, barely audible over my own sobs: "The doctors never found anything to actually stop it. They just managed the decline until there was nothing left to manage."

Eleven years of watching his kidneys fail.

My father died anyway. His kidneys failed despite doing everything the doctors said.

I sat in my car in the parking lot. Couldn't turn the key. Just gripped the steering wheel.

The lab results crinkled in my jacket pocket. I pulled them out. Stared at them.

eGFR 42. Creatinine 1.9. Stage 3 kidney disease.

My hands shook.

My husband was unloading groceries when I walked through the door. "Hey. How was your checkup?"

The words stuck. I handed him the lab results without speaking.

eGFR 42.

The grocery bag hit the floor. Eggs shattered. Milk carton split. He didn't notice. Both hands covered his mouth. Tears streaming down his face.

"No." His voice broke. "Sandra, I watched what happened to your father. Stage after stage. That fistula. I can't. I can't watch you go through that. I can't-"

He couldn't finish. Turned away. Shoulders shaking.

That night I lay awake. The ceiling fan rotated. Over. And over. And over.

Red numbers glowed on the clock: 11:52 PM.

Rolled over. 12:41 AM.

Again. 1:38 AM.

At 2:23 AM I gave up. Went downstairs. Sat at the kitchen table. Opened my laptop.

The screen's blue glow hurt my eyes.

I typed: how to stop kidney function decline naturally

The search results loaded.

My chest tightened.

Every site: Low protein diet. Low sodium. Drink water. Control blood pressure.

The exact advice I'd been following for three years. The exact advice my father followed for eleven years.

I clicked deeper. Medical journals. Why do kidney supplements fail to stop progression?

Article after article.

"Oxidative stress and antioxidant depletion in proximal tubular cells is a primary driver of progressive nephron loss in CKD..."

"Despite evidence that cellular antioxidant depletion accelerates kidney disease progression, most clinical guidelines do not address this mechanism..."

"Dietary protein restriction and blood pressure management reduce load on declining nephrons but do not address the cellular antioxidant depletion causing nephron death..."

My father's face flashed in my mind. The dialysis center. Three times a week. Four hours per session.

I searched: CoQ10 turmeric kidney disease results

Studies loaded.

CoQ10: "modest antioxidant activity, limited bioavailability in kidney tubular cells..."

Turmeric: "anti-inflammatory properties, poor cellular penetration in renal tissue..."

Alpha lipoic acid: "some antioxidant activity, insufficient to reverse oxidative damage in established CKD..."

A forum post: "My wife has been on every kidney supplement out there for two years. eGFR still declining. Doctors say just manage it."

My heart hammered against my ribs. I closed the laptop. Rubbed my face with both hands.

What do I do?

I wasn't going to follow my father's path without trying everything first.

Three days.

Five days.

Seven.

My husband found me at my desk one evening, surrounded by printed medical journals. "Sandra. What are you doing?"

"Researching."

"The doctors said-"

"The doctors said my father needed to manage his decline too. Didn't stop it. Just made his last years a slow march to dialysis."

His chin trembled. "But what if there's nothing else? What if you lose function waiting?"

"What if I go through dialysis like he did? What if I spend 11 years declining and die anyway, just more slowly and more painfully?"

He had no answer.

That weekend I searched everything. Natural kidney support. Clinical studies. Research papers.

Hibiscus appeared everywhere. Studies on kidney cell protection. Antioxidant activity in nephron tissue. Research from multiple universities showing measurable eGFR stabilization.

Real universities. Real science. Not fringe pseudoscience.

Monday morning I ordered the highest-rated hibiscus tea on Amazon. 4.2 stars. Over 6,000 reviews.

Seven weeks later. My eGFR: 41. Still declining.

I tried a different brand. Specialty health food store. Marketed specifically for kidney support.

Nine weeks. Never missed a day.

eGFR: 41. No change.

My follow-up appointment was in three weeks. Then two. Then one.

Every time I felt that exhaustion, the foamy urine in the morning, the swelling in my ankles by afternoon — I saw my father. The dialysis chair. The fistula. Stage by stage by stage.

Ten days before my appointment, I stood in a health food store. Supplement aisle. Endless kidney support products.

All useless.

Two women talking one aisle over.

scripts.body_meta:
I watched a man in a Carhartt jacket put back a gallon of milk at the gas station because the total at the pump had already eaten what he came in with.

He didn't argue.

He just nodded at the clerk like they'd already had the conversation a hundred times.

I was standing two people behind him, holding a bag of dog food and a quart of motor oil for our Buick, and I watched him slide that milk back into the cooler with the kind of care a man uses when he's pretending nothing is wrong.

He set it in the same spot. He turned the label so it faced out, the way you'd put a book back on a library shelf.

Then he walked out into the lot. He sat in his truck for a long minute before he started the engine. The truck was clean. Older, but clean. A man who took care of his things.

I knew that man.

I didn't know his name. But I knew him. I'd been married to a version of him for forty-one years.

My name is Maggie. I'm sixty-four. I drove a school bus in our county for twenty-six years and I retired last spring because my back finally said enough. My husband is Frank. He's sixty-seven. He spent his whole working life as a union electrician, climbing into the rafters of grain elevators in February and pulling new wire through finished homes in July. He has hands the size of dinner plates and a laugh that used to fill the kitchen.

I'm not a doctor. I'm not anything fancy. I'm just a wife who has sat across from the same man at the same kitchen table every morning for four decades and I notice things.

I notice when his eggs get cold because he's too tired to lift the fork. I notice when his thumb shakes for half a second before it stops. I notice when he holds the coffee mug differently than he used to.

I noticed the day his hands stopped wrapping all the way around the mug.

It was a Tuesday in March, three years ago.

He didn't say anything. I didn't say anything. But I saw it. The mug was the same mug. His hands were not the same hands.

You don't get to be married to a man for forty-one years and miss something like that.

I'm going to tell you a story.

I'm going to tell you about Frank and what I watched happen to him, and what I finally figured out after I stopped trusting people in white coats more than my own eyes.

I'm telling you because the man in the Carhartt jacket at the gas station could have been Frank.

It could have been your husband.

It could have been you.

And I don't want you to wait as long as we did.

Frank and I met at a wedding in 1983. Mutual cousins. He had a mustache then. I had a perm. We danced one slow song and he stepped on my foot and apologized seven times and I knew before the song was over.

We were married eight months later in a Lutheran church in our hometown and he was wearing the same suit his father wore in 1958.

He went straight from high school into the apprentice program at the local union hall. By the time he was thirty he was the man they sent up on the worst calls. Frozen substations. Lightning damage at three in the morning. The bad jobs.

He could read a wiring diagram the way some people read the newspaper.

He came home from work every night smelling like burned dust and coffee, and he'd kiss me on the cheek before he washed his hands, and he'd ask what I'd put in the slow cooker.

That was our life.

We raised two kids in a house he wired himself. Our son David is a county sheriff's deputy two towns over. Our daughter Karen teaches third grade and has two boys of her own. The youngest, our grandson Toby, just turned two.

Toby is the whole reason I'm writing this.

I have to start before the trouble started, because if I don't, you won't understand what I mean when I say my husband used to be a different man.

When Frank turned fifty-five, he could still throw a fifty pound bag of feed onto the back of the truck without making a sound. He could shovel the driveway after a foot of snow and come in pink-cheeked and ready for breakfast.

He worked through the day, came home, ate, watched a few innings of the Cardinals game, and walked the dog before bed.

He never sat still.

He fixed our neighbor's broken porch light for free. He drove our nephew to baseball practice when our brother-in-law was working nights. He kept a list of widows in town and once a week he'd swing by one of their houses and ask if they needed anything moved, lifted, or fixed.

That's who he was.

I am telling you all this not because I want you to be impressed by my husband. I want you to picture him clearly. Because the man I just described is not the man who set our grandson back down on the floor at Easter.

The slide started slow.

It always does. That's part of why I missed it for so long. If a man falls off a cliff, you see it. If a man walks down a long, slow hill for nine years, you don't notice he's at the bottom until you turn around and look up.

I'm going to walk you through those nine years.

I'm going to tell you what I saw every year. Some of it is small. Some of it is the kind of thing a person might dismiss. But put together, it's a map. And I want you to have the map, in case you're standing on one of the steps right now and don't know it.

Year one was 2016.

Frank was fifty-eight.

He had his yearly physical in February. Our family doctor at the time was a man named Dr. Henley. Older, kind, talked slow. He told Frank his numbers were "the best in the county." Said it twice. Said Frank could be a poster on the wall.

Frank's only complaint that year was that his left calf cramped at night. Not bad. Just enough to wake him up some nights.

Dr. Henley said to drink more water. Eat a banana before bed. The pills can do that sometimes, he said. Nothing to worry about.

Frank had been on Lipitor for two years at that point. He started taking it after a routine check turned up a borderline reading. His own father had died of a heart attack at sixty-six. So Frank took the pill. He was disciplined about it. He took it with breakfast. Every morning. Forty milligrams.

That was year one.

Just a little cramp. Just a banana before bed.

Year two was 2017.

Frank started skipping his second cup of coffee.

For thirty-five years, Frank drank three cups of coffee in the morning. Black. No sugar. He poured the second one before he'd finished the first. It was a rhythm, like a metronome.

In the summer of 2017, he started leaving the second cup half-finished.

I asked him about it. He said his stomach felt off. He said maybe he'd been pushing himself too hard.

He had not been pushing himself too hard. He had been pulling fewer overtime shifts that year because he said he was tired by Wednesday. He'd never been tired by Wednesday in his life.

Dr. Henley's appointment that year went the same as the year before.

"Your numbers are wonderful, Frank. Whatever you're doing, keep doing it."

I sat in the corner of the exam room. I always went with Frank. He said he liked the company. The truth was, I'd started going because I wanted to hear what the doctor said with my own ears.

I asked Dr. Henley about the cramps and the tiredness.

He said, "Some of that's just being fifty-nine. Some of that is muscles. We can switch to a different statin if it gets bad, but the numbers are too good to fuss with right now."

The numbers were too good to fuss with right now.

I wrote that down in a little notebook I started keeping. I have the notebook in front of me as I write this.

Year three was 2018.

Frank turned sixty.

We threw him a party in the backyard. Our daughter Karen brought a sheet cake from the grocery store. Our son David grilled brats. Frank stood in the corner of the yard with our brother-in-law Dale and talked about nothing for an hour.

After everyone left, Frank sat down in his recliner. He didn't get up for two hours. He fell asleep with his shoes on.

That was new.

Frank had never been a man who napped. He used to make fun of his own father for napping.

That fall, he stopped going up on the roof to clean the gutters. He hired a kid from down the street to do it. Twenty dollars. Frank said it was time to start letting younger men do that kind of work.

I think now that he stopped going up on the roof because he didn't trust his legs.

He never told me that. He wouldn't have.

Year four was 2019.

Frank started forgetting things.

Little things at first. Where he set his keys. The name of an actor in an old western. Whether he'd already taken his pill that morning.

He started leaving notes for himself on the counter. "Took Lipitor 6:40 AM." "Trash out Tuesday." "Karen called."

He'd never needed notes before.

I bought him a pill organizer. The kind with seven little compartments. He used it without comment.

In June of 2019 he forgot our anniversary.

We'd been married thirty-six years. I came down the stairs that morning and the kitchen was empty. No card on the table. No flowers. No nothing. Frank was on the porch reading the paper.

I didn't say anything. I made coffee.

Around lunchtime he looked up from the paper and his face went pale.

"Maggie. Oh, Maggie. I'm so sorry."

He drove to the grocery store and came back with flowers and a card and the look on his face was not the look of a man who forgot an anniversary. It was the look of a man who didn't know how he could have forgotten an anniversary. It was scared.

I told him it was fine. I told him I was tired anyway and it didn't matter.

That night I sat in the bathroom and cried for ten minutes with the fan on so he wouldn't hear.

Not because he forgot. Because I had started to suspect, in some small back room of my mind, that something was wrong with my husband that nobody was naming.

The appointment with Dr. Henley that year was different.

Dr. Henley was retiring at the end of the summer. His replacement was a younger doctor named Dr. Maren. She was maybe forty. Sharp glasses. Soft voice. Smart.

She read Frank's chart in front of us. She looked at the lipid panel.

"Mr. Hofstetter, these are some of the best numbers I've seen this month. Whatever you're doing, you should bottle it."

I leaned forward in my chair.

"He's tired all the time. He forgot our anniversary. He can't remember the names of people he's known for thirty years."

Dr. Maren looked at me with a kind of soft patience that I now understand was the most dangerous look in medicine.

"That's pretty normal at sixty, Mrs. Hofstetter. Especially in men. We all slow down. Have you thought about whether there might be some depression here? Some grief about retirement coming? Frank, are you sleeping well?"

Frank said he was.

Dr. Maren said if the brain fog kept up, Frank might want to see a therapist.

That was the first time someone suggested a therapist.

I will tell you it was not the last.

Year five was 2020.

Everyone remembers 2020 for the same reason. I remember it for that reason too. But I also remember it because that was the year Frank stopped carrying our grandson.

Our grandson Toby wasn't born yet that year. I'm talking about our older grandson Ethan, who was four.

Ethan would run at Frank with his arms in the air. Grandpa, up. Up, up. Frank used to scoop Ethan up like he weighed nothing.

One Sunday at our daughter's house, Ethan ran at Frank, and Frank knelt down instead of lifting him. Hugged him at eye level. Made it look like a choice.

I watched.

Karen watched.

Karen didn't say anything to me until we were doing dishes after dinner. She said, quiet, "Mom, is Dad okay?"

I told her he was fine.

I lied to my own daughter.

That spring his hands started to ache. Not pain like a hammer hit them. Pain like the inside of the muscle had a low-grade fever. He'd flex his fingers all day long, opening and closing them like he was trying to wake them up.

He stopped fixing things around the house.

That was a big one.

For forty years, when something broke, Frank fixed it. The garbage disposal. The screen door. The starter on the lawnmower. He didn't call repairmen. He was the repairman.

In May of 2020 the garbage disposal stopped working. Frank looked at it for about three minutes, said his hands weren't up to it that day, and went and got the phone book.

I stood in the kitchen and watched him pay a man a hundred and ten dollars to fix a thing my husband used to fix in his sleep.

I didn't say a word.

You don't say a word at moments like that. You file them away. You add them to the notebook.

Year six was 2021.

Frank lost weight.

Not a lot. About fifteen pounds across the year. Enough that his belts had to go in a notch. Enough that I noticed his cheekbones in the bathroom mirror in a way I hadn't before.

He wasn't trying to lose weight.

He just didn't seem to want food the way he used to.

He'd push half his dinner around the plate. He'd say it was good. He'd put the leftovers in the fridge and they'd still be there four days later.

His skin got thinner. The veins on the backs of his hands stood up like ropes.

In August of 2021 he had his annual physical with Dr. Maren.

She measured him. Weighed him. Drew his blood. Listened to his heart.

She came in with the results and her face was warm and reassuring.

"Frank, your numbers are excellent. Your LDL is at one twelve. Total cholesterol is one ninety-one. Triglycerides are great. The Lipitor is doing exactly what it's supposed to do. We won't change a thing."

I asked her, "Why is he losing weight?"

She said, "Some men just shrink a little in their sixties. As long as he's eating and the blood work is clean, I wouldn't be alarmed. We can talk about a dietitian if you want."

I asked her, "Why are his hands hurting?"

She said, "There can be some muscle ache with statins, but at his dose, and looking at his numbers, the risk isn't worth changing course. Maybe a heating pad. Maybe some gentle stretching."

I asked her, "Why is he forgetting things?"

She said, "Mrs. Hofstetter, has he considered therapy? Or even just journaling? A lot of men have a hard time with this phase of life. He may need someone to talk to."

I sat in the chair. I felt my face get hot.

I said, "He has me to talk to."

She smiled at me the way doctors smile at people who don't know better.

"Sometimes a professional can help with what a spouse can't."

I'm going to be honest with you. I almost said something I would have regretted.

Frank put his hand on my knee. He has always known how to settle me down with a single touch.

We walked out of that office and he didn't say anything in the car. We drove the twenty-three minutes home in silence and when we pulled into the driveway he just sat there in the passenger seat looking at his hands.

He said, "Maggie. I don't feel like myself."

I said, "I know."

He said, "But the numbers."

I said, "I know."

We sat in the driveway for a long time.

Year seven was 2022.

This is the year I started losing him a little.

His personality changed. Not all at once. In drips.

He was always a funny man. Dry. Iowa dry. He could deliver a punchline so flat you wouldn't know it was a joke until five seconds after. He'd been like that since I met him.

The jokes stopped.

He'd sit in the recliner and watch the news and not say anything. He'd answer questions when I asked them. But he wouldn't start conversations.

He used to call me from his truck on his way home from work, just to say he was thinking of me. Just to ask what I was making.

Those calls stopped years before, when he retired. But the impulse stayed. He used to text me from the grocery store. Pictures of weird products. A bag of Halloween candy in July. A bird that had landed on a shopping cart.

He stopped texting that year.

He just shopped and came home.

In October of 2022 our grandson Toby was born. Frank cried when he held him. Real crying. Shoulders shaking. He hadn't cried like that since his mother died.

When he handed Toby back, his arms were trembling. He had to set the baby down on the couch instead of handing him to Karen.

He laughed about it. Said his arms were rusty.

Karen laughed too.

I didn't laugh.

I went home that night and I added one more line to the notebook.

Year eight was 2023.

Frank slept fourteen hours a day for most of February.

He'd go to bed at nine. He'd sleep until eight. He'd come downstairs, eat a half a slice of toast, and fall asleep in the recliner by ten thirty.

He'd wake up around three in the afternoon, eat soup, and be ready to go back to bed by seven.

I asked him if he was depressed. He said he didn't think so. He said he just felt like his body was running on a battery that wouldn't hold a charge.

That's how he put it. A battery that wouldn't hold a charge.

I made another appointment with Dr. Maren.

She listened. She nodded. She took notes.

She drew his blood.

She came back with the results.

"Frank, I have to tell you, your numbers look great. Your cholesterol management is honestly textbook. I wish all my patients were as compliant as you are."

I said, "Dr. Maren. I am not asking about his cholesterol. I am asking about the fact that my husband is sleeping fourteen hours a day."

She said, "I hear you. I do. But I can only treat what the labs tell me to treat. The labs tell me Frank is doing well. If there were something serious going on, we'd see it in the bloodwork."

I said, "Maybe you're looking at the wrong bloodwork."

She got quiet.

Then she said, very gently, "Mrs. Hofstetter, I think both of you might benefit from talking to someone. We have a referral list for behavioral health services. There's no shame in it."

That was the third time I'd been told to send my husband to a therapist.

The third time someone in a white coat had looked at him fading in front of their eyes and suggested I'd been imagining it.

I took the referral list. I folded it. I put it in my purse. I never looked at it again.

We left.

I drove home with my hands tight on the wheel.

Frank dozed in the passenger seat.

I remember thinking, very clearly: nobody is going to help him. Nobody who is paid to look at his chart is going to look at him.

I didn't know yet what I was going to do about that. But something in me had changed.

Year nine was last year.

2024.

Easter weekend.

Karen and her husband Mark and their two boys came up for the holiday. We dyed eggs at the kitchen table. Ethan, now eight, was the master of the wax crayon. Toby, just under two, mostly ate the wax crayons.

We had ham. We had scalloped potatoes. Karen brought a cherry pie.

After lunch the whole family went out into the yard for pictures.

Karen wanted a picture of Frank and Toby. Just the two of them. Grandfather and grandson.

Frank crouched down and held his arms out. Toby toddled over and grinned that big two-year-old grin.

Frank reached down to pick him up.

I want you to picture this carefully, because I will see it for the rest of my life.

Frank got his hands under Toby's arms.

He bent his knees.

He started to lift.

He got Toby maybe a foot off the ground.

And then his arms gave out.

I don't mean he set Toby down. I don't mean he hesitated. I mean his arms shook and his shoulders dropped and he had to set Toby back down on the grass before he dropped him.

Toby's face crumpled. He thought he'd done something wrong. He thought Grandpa didn't want to pick him up.

He cried. Hard. The way only a two-year-old can. He toddled away to find his mother.

Frank stayed crouched in the grass.

He didn't get up.

He stayed there for what must have been a full minute, staring at his own hands like they belonged to a stranger.

Then he stood up slowly and said he needed the bathroom.

I watched him walk across the yard.

His shoulders were rounded forward. His feet didn't lift the way they used to. He looked twenty years older than he was.

He went inside.

He went into the downstairs bathroom and shut the door.

I sat in the kitchen at the table where I sat every morning of our marriage and I started a stopwatch on my phone.

I don't know why I did that. I just felt I needed to count something.

He was in there twenty-two minutes.

When he came out his eyes were red. He didn't look at anyone. He went into the living room and sat in his recliner and pretended to watch a basketball game even though it was Easter and there was no basketball on.

I went over and sat on the arm of his chair and put my hand on his shoulder.

He didn't speak.

He covered my hand with his.

His hand was so light.

I wanted to tell you that we sat there for a while and then I figured everything out and saved him.

That is not how it happened.

What happened is that I went to bed that night and I lay in the dark and I made a decision.

I decided that no matter how many doctors told me his numbers were good, I was going to find out what was wrong with my husband.

I didn't know where to start. I'm not a doctor. I drove a school bus. I read paperback mysteries and the newspaper and that was about it.

But I knew people. I'd lived in this county for sixty years. And I knew that somewhere in this world, there had to be someone who would look at Frank instead of at his chart.

So that's what I did.

I'm going to tell you what I found.

Some of it I learned in a library. Some of it I learned on a borrowed laptop with my reading glasses pushed up on my forehead at one in the morning. Some of it I learned from a woman at our church who used to work in a hospital pharmacy in Chicago.

I'm going to tell it to you in plain words. Because I am not a doctor. And I want you to understand it the same way I understood it. Not from a textbook. From a kitchen table.

The first thing I learned is that your body does not just make cholesterol because it's lazy.

Your body makes cholesterol because cholesterol is one of the most important things in your body. Every cell wall uses it. Every hormone needs it. Your brain is loaded with it. When your body makes cholesterol, it's doing a job.

The body uses a path to make cholesterol. Think of it like a kitchen with a long counter. The body puts a few ingredients on one end of the counter and slides them down. As it slides, the ingredients change. By the time the dough gets to the other end, it has turned into cholesterol.

That counter has a name. The science books call it the mevalonate pathway.

Most people will never hear that word in their life. I hadn't.

Here's the part that stopped my heart.

The body uses that same counter to make something else.

It makes CoQ10.

CoQ10 is not a vitamin in a pill bottle. It is a real thing your body makes on its own. It is the spark plug for every cell in your body. Especially your muscles. Especially your heart muscle. Especially your brain.

Your cells have little engines inside them called mitochondria. They are the power plants. They are what turn food into energy. They are what let you stand up, walk, think, lift a grandson.

The mitochondria run on CoQ10.

No CoQ10, no energy. No energy, no strength. No strength, no lifting a two-year-old at Easter.

Now here's what statins do.

Statins shut down that counter.

They were designed to. That's the whole point. They block the mevalonate pathway so the body makes less cholesterol.

But they don't shut down just the cholesterol end of the counter.

They shut down the whole counter.

When the counter is shut down, the body can't make CoQ10 either.

That's not a side effect that the statin labels make a big deal about. It is also not new information. There are studies on it going back over thirty years. There are mainstream cardiology papers that talk about it. You can find it in the regular medical literature if you go looking.

I went looking.

I read until my eyes burned. I went to the library and printed papers and read them at the kitchen table with a highlighter.

The story was the same in every paper.

When CoQ10 gets low, muscles ache. Not always sharp pain. Sometimes a deep tired ache that doesn't go away.

When CoQ10 gets low, energy drops. Not regular tired. The kind of tired where you sleep fourteen hours and still feel empty.

When CoQ10 gets low, the brain fogs over. The right word stops coming. The names of people you've known forever go missing.

When CoQ10 gets low, grip strength drops. Hands stop wrapping around the coffee mug the way they used to.

When CoQ10 gets low, weight comes off because the muscle is being slowly starved.

Every single symptom I had been writing in that little notebook for nine years.

Every single one.

And not one of them would ever show up on a lipid panel.

The doctor was reading the wrong test.

She wasn't lying to me. She wasn't being cruel. She was reading the test she was trained to read.

The test does not measure what was happening to my husband.

It was like trying to find out if a house has termites by checking the temperature of the kitchen.

I sat at the kitchen table the night I figured it out and I cried so hard the dog came over and put his head on my foot.

I cried because for nine years I had been right.

I cried because for nine years I had been told I was wrong.

I cried because we had wasted nine years.

I want to be clear about something here.

Frank's doctors were not bad people. They were trained the way they were trained. The system rewards them for getting the lipid panel to look a certain way. The system does not reward them for asking why their patient can no longer lift a two-year-old.

The lipid panel is the report card. The patient is the kid.

The system has been grading the report card and ignoring the kid.

I had spent nine years assuming that if something serious were wrong, the report card would show it. The report card never showed it. The report card was never going to show it. The report card was not built to.

The patient was telling me. With his hands. With his sleep. With his weight. With his silence at the dinner table.

I had been reading the wrong page.

Then I got up. I wiped my face. I poured a glass of water. And I started looking for what to do about it.

I want to be careful here. I am not telling you to stop your medicine. I am not a doctor. Frank's eventual decisions about his medication were made between him and a new doctor we eventually found three counties over, a man near retirement who actually listens.

What I am telling you is what I learned about supporting the body when the body has been running on empty for years.

The first thing I learned is that your body needs help putting CoQ10 back. Some people use a CoQ10 supplement. Frank tried that. It helped a little.

But the help that surprised me most came from a different place.

It came from tea.

Specifically, from a kind of tea I had only ever heard of in passing.

Oolong.

Now, listen. I am from Iowa. I drink coffee. I have never been a tea person. The closest thing to tea in my house growing up was the bag of Lipton my mother kept for when somebody had a fever.

But I kept reading.

And what I learned about oolong tea is not what you'd expect.

The leaves of the oolong plant are loaded with things called polyphenols. Think of polyphenols as quiet little workers that go through your body and put out the small fires that the bigger systems can't see.

There are things in your body called free radicals. They are the trash that gets produced when your cells burn fuel. A few free radicals are normal. Too many free radicals damage the inside of your blood vessels. They damage your muscles. They damage your mitochondria.

Polyphenols are like cleanup crews for free radicals. But not all polyphenols are the same.

The polyphenols in oolong tea, and especially in the whole-leaf kind, are what the research calls selective. That means they go after the bad free radicals without messing up the good signaling molecules the body needs. They don't carpet-bomb. They aim.

That mattered to me. Because Frank's body had been carpet-bombed for nine years.

The oolong leaf also has two specific compounds in it that kept showing up in the papers I read. They are called EGCG and theaflavins. The studies on them are not folk wisdom. They are real studies in real journals on cardiovascular and metabolic health. There are over two thousand peer-reviewed papers on these compounds across green and oolong teas. I am not going to ask you to take my word. You can look. I did.

The third thing I learned was about a hormone called adiponectin. Adiponectin is what your fat cells send out into the bloodstream to keep the rest of your body humming. Healthy adiponectin levels are linked to healthy cholesterol behavior, healthy blood sugar behavior, and healthy inflammation levels. The oolong tea polyphenols help support healthy adiponectin levels naturally.

It was starting to add up.

I was looking for something that could help Frank's body do what the medication had been keeping it from doing. Something that worked with the body, not against it. Something that could deliver the polyphenols and the EGCG and the theaflavins consistently.

Here's what I found out next.

Most tea you buy at the grocery store is junk.

I don't mean that to be rude. I mean it factually. The tea bags at most stores are made from broken leaves and tea dust, what the industry calls fannings. Those fannings get crushed and exposed to air for so long that most of the polyphenols are gone before the box even hits the shelf.

The active compounds in tea are alive when they're whole. When you grind them up and stuff them in a paper bag, they lose their punch.

To get the real medicine of the leaf, you need whole-leaf tea. Carefully processed. Carefully dried. Carefully packed.

That kind of tea is hard to find. And I'll tell you, when I first started looking, I almost gave up. Most of what's marketed as oolong is the same fannings just labeled fancier.

I also learned something interesting along the way that I want to share with you.

In countries where oolong tea is the daily drink — parts of southern China, parts of Taiwan, parts of Japan — heart disease rates are noticeably lower than they are here. The researchers who study this argue about why. Some say it's diet. Some say it's lifestyle. Some say it's the tea itself.

I don't have to win that argument to notice that the same populations drinking real, whole-leaf oolong every day are also the populations not filling the cardiology waiting rooms.

That was not nothing. That was actually a piece of common sense I had been missing.

Then I found PiPi Tea.

A friend from church sent me a link. Her brother in California had been drinking it for two years for blood pressure and he swore by it. He said it was the only oolong he'd ever had that smelled like a real plant instead of a paper bag.
