scripts.body_meta:
I found a man slumped over the steering wheel of an idling Buick at the end of my driveway last Tuesday morning, and I almost called the coroner before I called 911.

I want to tell you that whole story.

Because what I learned from it ended up being the most important thing anyone's said to me about my own husband in 14 years of marriage, and I'd be a coward if I kept it to myself.

My name is Loretta. I'm 58 years old, I live on a dead end street in Erie, Pennsylvania, and I drove a city bus for 31 years before my back finally told me it was done.

I retired in March. My husband Dale retired the year before. We thought we were going to have these long slow mornings together with coffee and the crossword and maybe a dog finally.

Instead I spent that first summer watching him sit in his recliner with the blinds half closed, and I started to understand that retirement wasn't the gift everybody told us it would be.

Dale is 61. He worked at the GE plant in Erie for 38 years, the locomotive division, the one they kept saying was going to close any minute and then somehow never did. He came home every night smelling like metal and diesel and that particular kind of factory sweat that doesn't wash out of a t shirt no matter what you do.

He was strong his whole life. The kind of strong where he could carry both grandkids on his shoulders at the same time and not break stride.

But somewhere around 56, something started to slip.

It wasn't dramatic. It was the kind of slow that you don't notice until you're already on the other side of it.

He stopped wanting to go fishing on Saturdays. He stopped going down to the basement to work on his model trains, and he had hundreds of dollars worth of unpainted boxcars sitting on that workbench gathering dust.

His doctor told him his blood pressure was creeping up. Then it wasn't creeping anymore, it was just up. They put him on one pill. Then a second pill. Then they added a third one for water retention, and his ankles still puffed up by 4 PM every day like little loaves of bread.

I'd watch him sit on the edge of the bed in the morning trying to find the energy to put his socks on, and I'd pretend I wasn't watching.

That's the part that nobody tells you about long marriages. You learn to look away from the things that scare you, because looking at them too directly makes them real.

Anyway.

Last Tuesday morning I was making coffee and I looked out the kitchen window and I saw a car at the end of our driveway. Just sitting there. Engine running. Exhaust coming out the back in those little gray puffs because the morning was cold.

It was a maroon Buick LeSabre, the kind my dad used to drive, and I knew it belonged to Walter from two doors down.

Walter is 67. He's a retired electrician. His wife Diane passed two years ago from pancreatic, and ever since then he's been one of those men who waves but doesn't really stop walking.

I figured he'd pulled in to drop off a card or a casserole dish or something. So I waited. I made my coffee. I sliced a banana for Dale.

Five minutes went by. Walter didn't come up.

I went out on the porch in my robe and slippers, and I called his name, and he didn't move.

I walked down the driveway and I saw him through the windshield, slumped sideways against the door, his face this awful gray color I had only ever seen on one other person in my entire life and that was my mother in her hospital bed the morning she died.

I started screaming his name and pounding on the window.

He didn't open his eyes. But his hand twitched.

I ran back to the house, I called 911, I told the dispatcher I had a neighbor having a stroke or a heart attack in his car and I couldn't get the door open because he had locked it from the inside.

Dale came out in his socks. We both stood there banging on that window while the dispatcher talked in my ear.

The ambulance got there in 11 minutes. The fire department got there first and they used some kind of tool to pop the lock, and they pulled Walter out and laid him on the asphalt of my driveway and worked on him for what felt like an hour but was probably 4 minutes.

They got him stable. They loaded him in the ambulance. One of the paramedics, a young guy with a red beard, told me his pressure had been so high they were honestly surprised he was still talking.

He said, ma'am, this happens way more than you'd think with men this age. They feel it coming on, they get in the car to drive themselves to the hospital because they don't want to make a fuss, and they don't make it.

He said it real plain, like he'd said it a hundred times before. Like it was just a fact about the world.

Walter is okay. He's home now. They kept him for 4 days and they sent him home with two new prescriptions and a sheet of paper about salt.

But I haven't slept right since that morning.

Because I know my husband. And I know that if Dale felt his heart pounding through his chest at 6 in the morning, he wouldn't wake me up. He wouldn't call 911.

He would put his pants on and get in his truck and try to drive himself to the hospital because he wouldn't want to be a burden.

And if I'd been in the shower that morning, or out walking, or asleep, I might have lost Walter.

I might lose Dale the same way.

That's the thought that's been sitting in my chest for the last 9 days like a stone I can't swallow.

So I started reading.

I'm not a researcher. I drove a bus. But I know how to use a library card and I know how to ask my niece, who is a nurse practitioner in Pittsburgh, the questions I should be asking.

I called her that Wednesday morning. I told her about Walter. I told her about Dale's three pills and his puffy ankles and the way he sits on the edge of the bed in the morning like he's bracing for something.

She was quiet for a long time on the phone.

Then she said something that knocked the wind out of me.

She said, Aunt Loretta, those pills don't fix anything. They just push the numbers down. The thing that's actually broken is the wall inside his blood vessels, and nobody is doing anything about that wall.

I said what wall.

She said the lining. The inner wall of every blood vessel in his body. It's a living tissue. It's supposed to make a molecule called nitric oxide that tells the vessels to relax, the way a tense shoulder finally drops when you take a hot shower. When that wall is healthy, it makes plenty of that molecule, and the vessels stay loose, and the blood flows easy.

She said when you're in your 30s and 40s, the wall is mostly fine. But years of stress and processed food and the kind of slow inflammation everybody has and nobody talks about, all of that wears the wall down. Year by year. Layer by layer.

And once the wall can't make enough of that relaxing molecule, the vessels stay tight. The blood has to push harder to get through. The heart has to work harder. And every beat puts more pressure on the wall, which wears it down faster.

She said that's the cycle. That's why blood pressure tends to get worse and worse no matter how many pills they pile on.

I asked her, well what do you do for the wall.

And she said, that's the thing nobody talks about, Aunt Loretta. The pills don't go anywhere near the wall. Beetroot helps a little because it adds some nitric oxide from the outside, but the body already knows how to make its own. The issue isn't supply. It's that the factory is rundown.

Then she said, there is something I've been telling some of my older patients about. It's not a drug. It's a fruit from India. It's been used for thousands of years over there. There's research now that it supports the inner wall of the blood vessels in a way nothing else really does.

She said the name. Amla.

I wrote it down on the back of an envelope. A M L A. I asked her to spell it again.

She told me there are compounds in it called emblicanins. They aren't fancy. They've been in this fruit forever. But what the research is starting to show is that they support the cells in that inner vessel wall, and when those cells are functioning better, they can start making more of their own nitric oxide again. The way they did when you were younger.

She said it's not a magic bullet. It's not a replacement for his medication. But it's the only thing she's seen that works on the wall itself instead of just pushing the numbers down from the outside.

And she said something that I've been thinking about every day since.

She said, Aunt Loretta, the pills are like putting a clamp on a leaky pipe. Amla is more like fixing the pipe.

I sat there at my kitchen table holding that envelope and I started crying. Because for 9 years I've watched Dale shrink. I've watched him stop fishing and stop painting his train cars and stop going to his nephew's birthday parties because the drive felt like too much. I've watched the doctor add pill after pill and never once tell us about any wall.

I felt like somebody had finally given me a map.

She told me about a brand called Alevia. She said it's the one she trusts because it's a clean amla extract, no fillers, third party tested, and she said she'd been telling her own father in law about it.

I ordered a bottle of Alevia Amla that same afternoon.

It came in 4 days. A little blue bottle. Nothing flashy. Two capsules in the morning with breakfast.

I didn't tell Dale at first. I just put it on the counter next to the coffee maker and I said babe, my niece told me to start taking these, my pressure has been creeping up too, want to take them with me.

He said sure. He's a sweet man. He said sure.

The first week, nothing happened that I could put a finger on.

The second week, he started waking up before me. That hadn't happened in maybe 4 years. I'd come downstairs and the coffee would already be made and he'd be standing at the kitchen window looking at the bird feeder.

I didn't say anything. I didn't want to jinx it.

The third week, he went down to the basement on a Saturday. He was down there for 3 hours. I crept halfway down the stairs and I saw him sitting at his workbench with a tiny paintbrush, painting a black stripe on a little orange boxcar.

He looked up at me and he kind of smiled, and he said, I forgot how much I liked this.

I had to go back upstairs because I was about to lose it.

By the end of the second month, the puffiness in his ankles had eased up. Not gone, but eased. His doctor saw him for a regular check and said his numbers had moved in the right direction and asked what he was doing different. Dale said, my wife's making me take some kind of berry.

The doctor laughed. Then he wrote it down.

I'm not going to tell you Alevia Amla is a miracle and I'm not going to tell you it cured anything, because it isn't and it didn't.

What I'm going to tell you is what I see with my own eyes.

I see my husband putting his socks on without sitting down halfway through. I see him walking out to the mailbox without that little hitch in his stride. I see him answering the phone when his brother calls instead of letting it go to voicemail.

I see a man who is starting to come back from somewhere far away.

And every time I look out the kitchen window at the end of my driveway, I think about Walter slumped against that door, and I thank God it wasn't Dale, and I thank my niece for telling me about the wall.

I want to say a few things directly, in case you're still reading.

If your husband is on three blood pressure pills and his ankles still swell, the pills aren't fixing the wall.

If you've been told this is just aging, ask yourself why some 70 year olds run marathons and some 55 year olds can't carry the groceries.

If you've tried beetroot and garlic and magnesium and fish oil and you're still where you started, it's because none of those things support the inner wall directly. They're working on the wrong layer.

Amla works on the layer everything else misses.

Alevia is the company my niece pointed me to. They make a clean amla extract. One bottle is a month. They have a 90 day money back guarantee, which means if you take it for 3 months and you don't notice anything, you can send the empty bottle back and they refund you. No paperwork. No phone tree.

I'm not affiliated with them. I'm a retired bus driver in Erie. I'm just a woman who almost lost her neighbor and is trying not to lose her husband.

If you want to look at it, the link is below.

Take it for 90 days. That's what my niece told me. Give the wall time to do what it's supposed to do.

P.P.S. I keep that envelope with A M L A written on the back of it in the kitchen drawer with the coupons. Some days when Dale is down in the basement painting his train cars I take it out and I look at it. It's just a word on an envelope. But it's the word that gave me my husband back.

scripts.body_meta:
The first time I gave a man CPR, I was holding a 3/8 inch copper elbow joint in my left hand.

That's the detail my brain keeps going back to. Not the noise his head made when it hit the concrete floor. Not the way his glasses skidded across the aisle and stopped against a display of zip ties. Not the woman two aisles over who screamed.

The elbow joint.

I was still holding it when I knelt down. Still holding it when I started compressions. I didn't even realize until somebody, an off duty EMT it turned out, gently took it out of my hand and set it on the floor next to me. He said "I got the count, you keep pumping."

This was a Saturday morning in March. Hennessey's Hardware on State Street in Erie, Pennsylvania. The same hardware store I've been walking into every Saturday morning for 22 years.

The man I was working on was Walt Hennessey. 67 years old. Owner of the store. Father of three. Grandfather of seven. The guy who sold me my first pipe wrench when I was 24 and still had hair.

He didn't die that day. I want to tell you that up front because what I'm about to share is not a tragedy. It's the opposite. But I need you to understand what it felt like in those 11 minutes before the ambulance got there. Because that's the thing that changed me.

Let me back up.

My name is Dale. I'm 56. I run a one truck plumbing operation out of my garage in a neighborhood called Glenwood, north side of Erie. My wife Marlene works at the hospital, billing department, has for 19 years. We've got two grown kids. Our boy Tyler is in the Coast Guard. Our daughter Becca lives in Pittsburgh with her husband and our two grandsons.

I'm not a hero. I want that on the record. I'm just a guy who took a CPR class in 2007 because Marlene made me when our kids were little, and a refresher in 2014 because the union required it, and I'd never used it once. Not on a doll. Not on a person. Not anywhere.

When somebody collapses in front of you, your brain does this thing where everything gets very loud and very quiet at the same time. The fluorescent lights buzzed louder. The little radio behind the counter playing classic rock got muffled, like somebody put a pillow over it. I could hear my own heart in my ears.

And I could hear Walt's wife Diane screaming his name from the front register.

She'd been ringing up a roll of weather stripping for some other customer when she heard the thud. She came around that counter so fast she knocked over a display of work gloves. She got to him about the same time I did.

I'd been standing there 30 seconds earlier. Just standing there in the bolt aisle. Looking for a 3/8 inch elbow joint for a kitchen sink job I had scheduled for Monday. Walt had been three feet away from me, restocking a shelf, talking about the Bills game. Mid sentence.

He said "you watch the second half last week, Dale, I think Allen's gonna" and that was it.

That was the whole sentence.

He didn't finish it. He just went down. Knees first. Then sideways. His shoulder hit the corner of the shelving unit and he kept going. By the time his head met the concrete, his eyes were already closed.

I don't remember deciding to move. I just remember being on the floor. Diane was screaming. Somebody was on the phone. The off duty EMT, a guy named Carlos, came running from the paint section.

I started compressions. Carlos counted. Diane held Walt's hand and said "Walter, stay with me, Walter, you stay right here."

The ambulance took 11 minutes. I know because I asked later. It felt like an hour and it felt like 30 seconds. Both. Somehow.

Walt was breathing on his own again before they loaded him in. Not awake, but breathing. The paramedic, a young woman with a long braid, looked at me as they were lifting him and said "you saved his life. Whatever you did before he got here, you saved his life."

And then they were gone.

I stood in the parking lot of Hennessey's Hardware on a Saturday morning in March, holding a 3/8 inch elbow joint, watching an ambulance turn left onto State Street with its lights on.

I drove home. I don't remember the drive. I remember walking into our kitchen and Marlene was at the table doing the bills and she looked up and saw my face and she said "what happened, what happened, Dale."

I sat down. I didn't say anything for a minute.

Then I told her. And then I cried for the first time in I don't know how many years. Not because I was scared. Because of how close it had been. How fast it had been. How one minute Walt was talking about a quarterback and the next minute his wife was screaming his name on the floor of his own store.

That night I couldn't sleep. I lay in bed and stared at the ceiling and I thought about Walt. And I thought about my own father, who died of a heart attack in his garage at 61. Just dropped in the middle of changing the oil on his old Chevy. My mom found him next to the car with the dipstick still in his hand.

I'm 56. I'll be 57 in November. My dad made it to 61.

That math kept me up.

I have a thing about my health that I've never really talked about with anybody. I'm a plumber. I've been a plumber for 31 years. I do my own brakes. I climb on roofs. I'm under sinks all day. The body, my body, is just the truck I drive to do the job. I don't think about it. I don't want to think about it.

The last time I'd had a real physical was 4 years before. The doctor, a younger guy named Patel, told me my cholesterol was higher than he'd like. He used the word "borderline." He gave me a paper. He said "let's talk about this in 6 months."

I never went back.

The paper sat on my dresser for about a month and then it got moved to a drawer and then I stopped seeing it at all.

After Walt collapsed, I opened that drawer. I had to dig. I found the paper underneath an old watch and a stack of receipts and a pocket knife I'd been looking for since 2022.

The numbers on it didn't mean a lot to me. I just remember Patel circling one and writing the word "high" next to it in pen.

The next Saturday, I went to see Walt at his house. He'd been home from the hospital for three days. They'd put a stent in. He was sitting in a recliner in his living room with the Penguins game on mute and a cat on his lap.

He looked smaller than he'd looked the Saturday before.

Diane brought us coffee. She kept touching his shoulder every time she walked past, like she was making sure he was still there.

Walt looked at me for a long time before he said anything. Then he said "Dale. I owe you my life."

I said "you don't owe me anything, Walt."

He said "Diane and I have been talking. About a lot of things. About the store. About retirement. About what could have happened."

He paused. He took a sip of his coffee. Then he said "the cardiologist who saw me, Dr. Bhatia, she told me something I didn't know. She said this didn't happen Saturday morning. She said this happened over 20 years. The Saturday morning was just when it finally added up."

I didn't say anything. I just listened.

He said "she pulled up my numbers from a physical I had four years ago. Numbers I didn't pay attention to. She circled them on the screen with her finger and she said 'this is when it started showing. You had four years to do something. Nobody told you what to do.'"

He looked at me.

He said "Dale. I'm gonna say something to you and you can take it or leave it. You and I are about the same. You eat like I eat. You move like I move. You worry about your truck more than you worry about your insides. I know because I'm the same guy. And I almost died on the floor of my own store two weeks ago."

He stopped. He set his coffee down.

He said "go get your numbers checked. Today if you can. Monday if you can't. Don't put it off. Please."

I drove home. Marlene was on the porch with our dog Murph, an old beagle who's mostly blind now. She looked at me and didn't ask. She just opened the door.

That Monday I called Patel's office. They got me in Wednesday.

The numbers were worse than they'd been 4 years ago. Not catastrophic. But worse. Patel was kind about it. He didn't lecture. He said "Dale, you came in. That's the hardest part. We can work with this."

He talked about a few things. He talked about a statin. He said "we can try that. Some guys do great on it. Some guys don't tolerate it well. Up to you."

I told him I wanted to think about it.

He said that was fine. He said "but Dale. Don't think about it for 4 years."

I drove home. I sat in our kitchen. Marlene came in and sat across from me and she had that look she gets when she knows we're about to have a conversation that matters.

She said "what did he say."

I told her.

She didn't say anything for a long time. Then she said "Dale. I love you. I want you here when Tyler comes home. I want you here when Becca's boys are 16. I want you here when we're 75 and we're driving each other crazy in this house. I want you here."

I said "I want me here too."

She got up. She walked over to the cabinet above the microwave where she keeps her vitamins and her hospital lanyard and a stack of stuff. She pulled down a small green bottle.

She said "I want to tell you about something. I haven't talked about it because I didn't know if you'd care. But you might care now."

She set it on the table.

Alevia. Amla. I'd never heard of either word in my life.

She said "one of the nurses on the cardiology floor at the hospital, Tina, she's been taking this for about a year. She told me about it. I started taking it three months ago. I didn't say anything because I wanted to see if I felt different first."

I said "and."

She said "and I do."

I picked up the bottle. Turned it over in my hands. Read the label.

She said "Tina told me about it because we were talking one day at lunch about her father in law. He'd had a cardiac event a few years back. He started taking this and his doctor was happy with how his follow up numbers looked. She wasn't selling me on it. She was just telling me about it."

I said "what is it."

She said "it's a fruit. From India. They've been using it for thousands of years. There's actually research on it. Real research. I looked. I'm not telling you it's a magic pill. I'm telling you it's a thing my body seems to like, and you might want to look into it."

I sat at the table that night and I went down a rabbit hole.

I'm not a scientific guy. I install water heaters. But I can read.

What I learned is that amla is the fruit of a tree called Phyllanthus emblica. The Indian gooseberry. It's small, green, and apparently incredibly sour. People in India have been chewing on it for as long as anybody can remember.

But what I cared about wasn't the history. What I cared about was the part where modern researchers had actually studied it.

There are clinical trials. Not five. Not ten. There's a body of research on people, real people, taking standardized amla extract. And the things that show up over and over again in those trials are the things I was now thinking about every time I went to bed.

Lipid markers. Inflammation markers. Endothelial function, which is a fancy way of saying how well the lining of your blood vessels is doing its job.

Here's the part that made me put down my phone and just sit there for a minute.

The way researchers think amla works isn't by attacking one thing. It's by supporting how your body handles the chronic, low grade stress that builds up in your blood vessels over years. The oxidative stress. The inflammation. The slow accumulation of damage that, in Walt Hennessey, took 20 years to add up to a Saturday morning on the floor of his own store.

Amla has a high concentration of polyphenols. Specifically a class called hydrolyzable tannins, plus a marker compound called beta glucogallin that some of the studied extracts standardize for. These compounds have been associated, in human trials, with healthier lipid profiles and lower inflammatory markers like hsCRP.

Translation, because I had to translate it for myself. The plumbing inside your chest. The pipes. They get gunked up over time. Not from one bad meal. From decades of small things. Pressure, friction, oxidation, inflammation, the residue of a life.

Amla has been shown to support the body's ability to handle that residue.

It doesn't unclog anything. I want to be clear. I'm not saying that. The research doesn't say that. What the research shows is that this fruit helps create the kind of internal environment where your cardiovascular system isn't working against itself every minute of every day.

For a guy like me, who'd spent 4 years not opening a drawer because he didn't want to read what was on a piece of paper, that was something I could understand.

I told Marlene I wanted to try it.

She said "I figured."

I started on a Tuesday. Two capsules. With breakfast. Same time as my coffee. I set a reminder on my phone because I've never taken anything daily in my life and I knew I'd forget.

The first week, nothing. I felt the same. I told Marlene I wasn't sure if anything was happening.

She said "Dale. You're 56. You're not gonna feel different in 6 days. Give it time."

The second week, I noticed I was sleeping deeper. Not longer. Just deeper. I'd been waking up at 3:42, 3:51, 4:03, every single night, for years. I just thought that was what being 56 felt like. That stopped happening as much.

The third week, my wife told me my color was different. She said "you look pinker. In a good way. Less grey."

I didn't know what to do with that.

By the end of the first month, I noticed something on a job. I was finishing up a basement laundry hookup over in Millcreek, carrying my tool bag back up two flights of stairs to my truck, and I got to the top and I wasn't out of breath.

That was new.

I'd been telling myself for a year that the stairs at jobs were getting to me because I was getting older. They weren't getting to me anymore. Not in the same way.

I kept going.

Around week 7, I went back to Patel for a recheck. He'd told me 8 weeks would be a fair window to see if any lifestyle changes were doing anything.

I'd made some other changes too. I'd cut back on the gas station breakfast sandwiches. Marlene had been making me oatmeal. I was walking Murph the beagle in the morning before work, even when it was cold. Small stuff. Nothing dramatic.

But the amla was the daily thing.

Patel pulled my numbers up on his screen. He looked at them. He looked at me. He looked at them again. He said "Dale. What did you do."

I told him. All of it. The walking. The oatmeal. The amla.

He nodded slowly. He said "I can't tell you which one of those things is doing what. But whatever you're doing, keep doing it. These numbers are noticeably better. Not perfect. But noticeably better. In 8 weeks."

I drove home. I called Marlene. She was at lunch at the hospital.

I said "the numbers are better."

She said "Dale Donovan, I told you so."

That was 8 months ago.

I'm still on the amla. Same two capsules every morning with my coffee. Marlene's still on hers. Tina, the nurse who told her about it, she's still on hers.

Walt Hennessey is back at the store full time. Not Saturdays anymore. Diane made him give those up. But Tuesdays through Fridays, he's there, behind the counter, telling somebody about the Bills game. He turned 68 in July. He told me at his birthday party that he'd started taking amla too. His cardiologist, Dr. Bhatia, knew about it. She'd told him there was decent research behind it and to go ahead.

I don't talk about this stuff much. I'm a plumber. I'm a private guy. I'm not the type to post on Facebook about my health.

But I'm posting this because of the drawer.

Because of the paper that sat in my drawer for 4 years.

Because there are guys out there reading this who have a paper just like mine. Who got told by some doctor in some appointment that something was borderline. Who walked out and meant to do something about it and never did. Who keep telling themselves they'll deal with it next year.

I'm telling you. Don't wait for somebody to collapse in front of you to take it seriously.

scripts.body_meta:
I pulled my mother of the bride dress out of the garment bag on a Tuesday afternoon in March and the world stopped making sense for about ten minutes.

It was navy. Beaded at the shoulders. The kind of dress you buy when your only daughter is getting married and you want to look like the woman she remembers, not the woman she's become.

I bought it 4 months before the wedding. Tried it on in the store. Cried a little in the dressing room because it fit. Because I looked like myself in it. The tailor took it in half an inch at the waist and that was that.

The wedding was 18 days away.

I stood in my bedroom in Knoxville with the dress laid out on the bed and I tried to step into it the way I'd stepped into a thousand dresses over 62 years. Right foot first. Pull up to the waist. Arms through. Reach back for the zipper.

My right knee wouldn't bend.

Not all the way. Not enough to lift my foot over the hem of the dress. I stood there in my underwear holding navy fabric in both hands and I tried again. And again. The third time I sat down on the edge of the bed and I cried the way you cry when you finally admit something to yourself you've been refusing to admit for 2 years.

My body had been quitting on me. And the wedding was 18 days away.

I'm going to tell you the rest of this story because I'm 62 years old and I never thought I'd be the kind of person who writes a thing like this on Facebook. But what happened in the next 18 days reorganized something in me, and if there's one other woman out there sitting on the edge of her bed wondering how she's going to make it through her daughter's wedding, this is for her.

My name is Linda. I'm a retired 4th grade teacher. I taught at the same elementary school in West Knoxville for 31 years before I hung it up in 2022. My husband Ray is a retired UPS driver. We've been married 38 years. We have one daughter, Caroline, who teaches high school English in Asheville and was, that Tuesday in March, eighteen days away from marrying a man named Mason who fixes timber frame houses for a living and calls me "ma'am" in a way that doesn't feel forced.

The knee thing started in 2023. Or maybe earlier. Truthfully I think it started earlier and I just told myself I was tired.

I'd come home from the school after a day on my feet and I'd take a hot bath and the bath would help. Then the bath stopped helping. Then I noticed I was using the railing to get up the stairs to bed. Then I noticed I was using both hands. Then I noticed Ray would offer me his arm in the parking lot of the Kroger and I'd take it without thinking about it.

I went to my doctor in the spring of 2024. Sat on the crinkly paper. Told him my knees hurt when I bent them and my hips felt stiff in the morning and my hands were starting to ache when the weather changed.

He looked at me over his glasses and said, "Linda, you're 60 years old. This is what 60 feels like. Stay active. Lose 5 pounds. Take Aleve when you need it."

I drove home in my Camry and I didn't cry but I wanted to. Because I'd been a 4th grade teacher for 31 years and I knew what it sounded like when somebody was telling me to be quiet.

So I did the thing women my age do. I bought the cushioned shoes. I bought the topical cream. I bought the pillow that goes between your knees at night. I tried glucosamine. I tried turmeric. I tried collagen powder in my morning coffee even though it made the coffee taste like wet cardboard.

Some of it helped a little. None of it helped enough.

And the calendar kept moving toward Caroline's wedding.

She'd asked me to walk her down the aisle with Ray. Both of us. One on each side. She said she wanted both her parents because Ray's the one who taught her to ride a bike and I'm the one who taught her to read. She said it on FaceTime in October when they got engaged and I cried into my hand and told her of course, of course, of course.

That was October. By March I was sitting on the edge of my bed in my underwear and I couldn't lift my foot high enough to step into a dress.

I called Ray from the bedroom. He was downstairs watching the basketball game. He came up. Saw me sitting there. Saw the dress on the bed. Didn't say anything for a minute.

Then he said, "Honey, we'll figure it out."

That's a thing he says. We'll figure it out. He's said it our entire marriage. When the basement flooded in 1998. When Caroline got mono her senior year and missed a month of school. When my mother died in 2019 and I couldn't stop crying for three weeks. We'll figure it out.

But that night, lying in bed next to him in the dark, I didn't see how we were going to figure it out. Because the wedding wasn't going to wait. And my knees weren't getting better. And the dress was hanging on the back of the closet door like a navy ghost reminding me of what I used to be able to do.

I called Caroline the next morning and didn't tell her. I asked her about the seating chart instead. She talked for 20 minutes. I made the right sounds in the right places.

Then I called the alterations woman who'd done the dress. Told her I might need to come back in for some adjustments. She said sure, bring it by, but I could hear the question in her voice. The dress had fit 4 months ago. What kind of adjustments?

The kind where my body had changed shape because I couldn't bend.

I drove the dress over to her shop in Bearden the next afternoon. Her name is Marlene. She's been altering wedding dresses for 30 years. I'd known her since Caroline was in middle school because she did the alterations on Caroline's prom dresses too.

I walked into the back room of her shop. Hung the dress up. Started to step into it. Got my left foot in. Couldn't get my right foot in. Had to sit down on the little upholstered stool and breathe.

And then I started crying. Right there in Marlene's back room with the navy dress on the floor at my feet and the smell of steam press in the air. I cried the kind of crying where you can't catch your breath. Where your shoulders shake. Where you're 62 years old and you've held it together your whole life and you don't have the energy to hold it together anymore.

Marlene didn't say a word for about 90 seconds. She closed the door to the back room. Sat down on the stool across from me. Handed me a tissue from a box on her sewing table. And she waited.

When I could finally talk I told her. About the knees. About the doctor. About 31 years on my feet teaching 4th graders. About Caroline. About the aisle. About 18 days.

Marlene let me finish. Then she said something I wasn't expecting.

She said, "Linda, my mother in law had the same thing. And I'm going to tell you what she told me."

Her mother in law was named Rosa. 78 years old. Lived in a little house in Oak Ridge with her husband and a yard full of tomato plants. Marlene said Rosa had been having trouble with her hands and her knees for years. The kind of trouble where you can't grip a coffee cup before noon. The kind where stairs become a calculation.

Rosa had been to four different doctors over four different years. Every one of them said the same thing. It's age. Take Aleve. Stay active. Lose 5 pounds.

And then Rosa's sister came to visit from out of state. Saw what was happening to Rosa. Sat at her kitchen table and told her about something she'd been taking for the last 6 months that her own daughter, who's a nurse, had told her about.

It was Amla.

I had never heard of it. I want you to understand that. I'd been raised in East Tennessee, taught 4th grade for 31 years, eaten the same breakfast for the last 20 years, and I had never once in my life heard the word Amla.

Marlene said Rosa started taking it in the fall and by Christmas she was bringing tomato plants up from the basement on her own. Marlene said Rosa called her on the phone one Saturday morning and said, "Marley, I unscrewed the lid on the pickle jar."

That was the line that got me. The pickle jar.

Because that morning, before I drove to Marlene's shop, I'd been standing at my kitchen counter trying to open a jar of strawberry preserves and Ray had come in and taken it from me without saying anything and opened it and handed it back. And I'd felt something flicker in my chest that I hadn't been able to name until Marlene said the word pickle jar.

It was shame. The quiet, daily shame of needing your husband to open a jar.

Marlene wrote the word Amla on the back of a receipt and handed it to me. She said, "Linda, I'm not a doctor. But I've watched my mother in law go from a woman who couldn't button her own blouse to a woman who's making sauce out of fresh tomatoes again. And it didn't cost her much. And it didn't hurt her. So I'm telling you what I would tell my own sister."

I took the receipt. Folded it into my purse. Drove home.

That night, after Ray went to bed, I sat at the kitchen table with my laptop and I went down a research rabbit hole that lasted until 1:47 AM.

Here's what I learned. And I'm going to do my best to explain it the way I understood it, because I'm a 4th grade teacher and I think in 4th grade language and that's the only way it sticks.

Amla is a fruit. It grows on a tree in India and parts of Southeast Asia. They've been using it as food and medicine over there for something like 3,000 years. The English name for it is Indian gooseberry but it doesn't taste like a gooseberry. People who've actually eaten one say it's sour and bitter and chalky and you only eat one if you're being told to.

But the fruit itself is loaded with stuff. Vitamin C. Polyphenols. Tannins. Compounds with names I can't pronounce. The thing that interested me, the thing I kept reading about, was what those compounds seem to do inside the body when it comes to inflammation.

Here's the simple version, the way I understood it after about 4 hours of reading. Inside our joints there are tissues that take a beating over time. Decades of standing, walking, kneeling on classroom floors to tie shoelaces. The cushioning between the bones gets thinner. The tissue around the bones gets irritated. And when that tissue is irritated, your body sends inflammatory signals to the area, kind of like sending firefighters to a small kitchen fire. The problem is, when the firefighters keep showing up year after year and the fire never quite goes out, the firefighters themselves start causing damage.

That's what chronic inflammation does. It's protective in the short term and corrosive in the long term.

What Amla seems to do, based on the research I was reading, is help the body manage that inflammatory load. The compounds in the fruit are associated with lower markers of inflammation in human studies. They're linked to better antioxidant activity in the body, which matters because oxidative stress and inflammation feed each other in a cycle that gets worse over time.

In plain English. The fruit has been studied in people. The people who took it had lower levels of the chemical messengers that drive inflammation. And lower inflammation, particularly the slow chronic kind, is associated with how your joints feel when you wake up in the morning. How your hands feel when you try to open a jar. How your knees feel when you try to step into a dress.

I'm not telling you Amla cures anything. I'm not a doctor and I'm not making that claim. What I'm telling you is what I read at 1:30 in the morning on a Wednesday in March, and what I decided to try, and what happened next.

I ordered a bottle of Alevia Amla on Wednesday morning. It came on Friday.

I want to tell you about Alevia for a minute because the reason I picked it over the other options I'd been looking at matters. There's a lot of cheap Amla powder out there. I'd seen the kind you scoop into a smoothie. The kind that comes in giant bags from places I'd never heard of. I didn't want that. I wanted something I could trust, something with the right form of the fruit, something I could take with my morning coffee and not think about.

Alevia Amla comes in a capsule. The bottle is small. The dose is what the research uses. They have a 90 day money back guarantee, which mattered to me because if I was going to spend 18 days hoping a fruit was going to help me walk my daughter down the aisle, I wanted to know I could send it back if nothing happened.

I took my first capsule on Friday morning at 7:15 AM, standing in my kitchen, in my robe, with a cup of coffee.

Nothing happened on Friday. Nothing happened on Saturday. Sunday I went to church and walked from the parking lot to the sanctuary and noticed I wasn't gripping Ray's arm as hard as I had been the week before. But I told myself I was imagining it.

Day 6 was the first morning I noticed I'd gotten out of bed without thinking about it.

That's a strange thing to write. But for 2 years I'd been waking up and the first thing I'd do, before I opened my eyes, was take inventory. How bad are my knees today. How bad are my hands. How long is it going to take me to get from the bed to the bathroom. That morning I just got up. Walked to the bathroom. Halfway there I realized I hadn't done the inventory.

Day 9 was the morning I opened the strawberry preserves myself.

Day 11 was the morning Caroline called me about the rehearsal dinner seating chart and I walked around the kitchen the whole time we were on the phone instead of sitting down at the table like I'd been doing for months.

Day 14 I drove back to Marlene's shop with the dress.

I walked into the back room. Took the dress off the hanger. Stepped into it. Both feet. Pulled it up to my waist. Reached behind my back. Got the zipper most of the way up and Marlene zipped the rest.

Marlene didn't say anything. She looked at me in the mirror with her hands on the back of the zipper and her eyes were wet.

I stood there in navy with the beaded shoulders and I looked at myself and I saw the woman my daughter remembered.

Day 18 was the wedding.

We stood at the back of the church, Caroline between us, Ray in his good suit with his eyes already wet and Caroline in her dress that her grandmother would have wept over. The doors opened. The music started. And I walked my daughter down the aisle on knees that had decided, for that day at least, to remember what they used to do.

I'm not going to tell you my knees are perfect now. They're not. I'm 62 years old and I taught 4th grade for 31 years and the body keeps a record. What I'll tell you is that I've been taking Alevia Amla every morning since that Friday in March and I'm a different person than I was sitting on the edge of the bed crying into a navy dress.

I take the stairs without the railing. I open jars. I knelt down in the garden last weekend to plant tomatoes and got back up without thinking about it.

Ray said something a few weeks ago that I keep coming back to. He said, "You sound like yourself again."

I didn't know I'd stopped sounding like myself.

If you're sitting where I was, on the edge of a bed somewhere, with a dress or a fishing pole or a pair of garden gloves you don't think you can use anymore, I want to tell you what Marlene told me.

There's a fruit. It's been around for 3,000 years. It's not magic and it's not a miracle and I'm not promising you anything. But it helped my mother in law open a pickle jar. It helped me walk my daughter down the aisle. And the company that makes Alevia Amla will give you your money back for 90 days if it doesn't help you the way it helped me.

That's a fair deal. It was a fair deal for me and it'll be a fair deal for you.

If you want to try it, here's where I got it.

P.S. The dress is hanging in the closet now. I keep meaning to put it back in the garment bag and I keep not doing it because every time I see it I remember what it felt like to zip it up. I don't think I'm going to put it away for a while.

P.P.S. The 90 day money back guarantee is the thing that finally got me to click the button. I want to say that out loud. I'd been burned before by supplements that did nothing and cost me $80 and sat in the cabinet for a year. With Alevia, if it doesn't work for you, you send it back. That's it. That's the whole arrangement. They believe in their product enough to put their money where their mouth is, and I respect a company that does that.

scripts.body_meta:
I almost killed a family on Interstate 40 last Tuesday.

I want to say that out loud because I have not said it out loud and I am 56 years old and I have been driving a truck for 31 years and I have never come close to what I came close to at 4:17 in the morning outside Little Rock.

I was eastbound on I-40 hauling a load of paper products to a distribution center in Memphis. Standard run. I'd done it 200 times. I left Oklahoma City at 11 PM. I'd had a 6 hour break before that. I was not over my hours. I was not low on sleep on paper.

Somewhere around mile marker 152 I zoned out.

I don't know how long. Could have been 2 seconds. Could have been 6. What I remember is the rumble strip on the right shoulder waking me up and then seeing the back of a minivan in my headlights about 80 feet ahead going 20 miles per hour slower than I was going.

I jerked the wheel. I hit the brakes. The truck shifted. I got it straight. I missed the minivan by less than the length of my own hood.

The driver was a woman. I saw her face in her mirror as I went past her in the left lane. There were car seats in the back. I could see the outline of a child sleeping in one of them.

I drove for another 4 minutes and then I pulled into the Pilot at the West Memphis exit and I sat in the cab and I shook for 22 minutes.

I'm going to tell you what happened in that truck stop because what a waitress named Earlene told me at 4:47 AM on a Tuesday morning probably saved more than my CDL. And I think there's somebody else out there reading this who needs to hear it.

My name is Wayne. I'm 56 years old. I drive for a midsize carrier out of Memphis. Long haul, mostly Texas to Tennessee, some runs up to St. Louis when they need me. I've been married to my wife Carla for 33 years. We have two grown daughters, one in Knoxville and one in Jonesboro, and a granddaughter named Riley who's 6 and thinks my truck has a name and asks me what Big Blue is doing every time I call her.

I started driving in 1994. I was 24 years old and I'd just gotten Carla pregnant with our oldest and I needed to make money and a guy I knew said the trucking school in Jackson was hiring out their graduates faster than they could train them. I went. I learned. I got my CDL. I have not had a moving violation in 28 of those 31 years. The two I had were in 1996 and 1998 and they were both speeding tickets in Arkansas, which if you've ever driven through Arkansas you understand.

I'm a careful driver. I'm a boring driver. I run my pre-trip inspection like I'm being graded on it. I take my breaks. I sleep when I'm tired. I do not push.

But I'd been losing time.

That's the only way I know how to put it. I'd been losing pieces of trips. Not falling asleep. Not nodding off. Just sort of going somewhere else for a few seconds and coming back and not knowing how I got from one mile marker to the next. It started maybe 8 months ago. Carla had asked me a couple of times if I was sleeping okay. I'd told her I was fine. The doctor had checked me out for sleep apnea last fall and the test came back negative.

But I'd been tired in a way that felt different than tired. Tired like my brain wasn't getting enough of something. Tired like the lights were on but somebody had turned the dimmer down to about 60 percent and forgotten to turn it back up.

I'd been blaming it on the road. On 31 years of bad coffee and worse food. On the fact that I was 56 and my back hurt and my knees hurt and I was 22 pounds heavier than I'd been at 50.

I had not been blaming it on anything that I could actually fix.

When I pulled into that Pilot at 4:17 AM I was wearing the same flannel shirt I'd put on in Oklahoma City and my hands were shaking and I called Carla and she didn't answer because it was 2:17 AM her time and she's a heavy sleeper and we've had an agreement for 30 years that I don't call in the middle of the night unless something is on fire.

I sat in my truck for those 22 minutes. I thought about the woman in the minivan. I thought about Riley. I thought about Carla waking up to a phone call that was not from me.

Then I got out and I went inside the Pilot to get coffee.

The diner part of the Pilot was almost empty. There was one trucker at the counter eating eggs. There was one couple in a booth who looked like they'd been driving all night to somewhere they didn't want to go. And there was a waitress behind the counter who was probably 58 or 59 with grey hair pulled back in a low ponytail and a name tag that said Earlene in cursive.

She looked at me when I walked in. Did not say hello. Did not ask me what I wanted. She picked up the coffee pot and a clean cup and she walked over to a booth and put the cup down and pointed at it and said, "Sit."

I sat.

She poured the coffee. Sat down across from me in the booth. Put both her hands flat on the table.

She said, "What just happened to you, baby."

I have not been called baby by anyone except my wife in 33 years. Something in the way she said it broke me open in a way that the 22 minutes in the cab had not been able to.

I told her. I told her about the minivan. About zoning out. About the rumble strip. About the woman's face in the mirror. About the car seats. I told her I had a 6 year old granddaughter who calls my truck Big Blue.

I cried at a Formica table at 4:47 in the morning in front of a stranger named Earlene and I did not feel embarrassed about it because it was the first honest thing I had done in 8 months.

She let me finish. She poured me more coffee. She did not speak until I was done.

Then she said, "My brother drove for Yellow for 26 years. Lost his route in 2019 because he failed a roadside test for not being able to do the heel-to-toe walk. He'd been zoning out for two years. Told nobody. Wouldn't go to the doctor. Almost killed himself running off a bridge in Tupelo."

I was listening. I was holding the coffee cup with both hands.

"He thought it was the road. We thought it was the road. The doctor thought it was the road. It wasn't the road, baby. It was something else."

She told me his name was Roy. He was 61 by the time he lost his job. He went to live with their mother for 4 months because he couldn't pay his bills. He was depressed. He was tired. He was not the man Earlene had grown up with.

Then his daughter, who was a pharmacist in Tennessee, started reading about something. She brought it up to him on a Sunday at his mother's kitchen table. He did not want to hear it. He'd had enough people tell him what was wrong with him.

But she kept at him.

What she'd been reading about was a fruit called Amla.

I'd never heard the word in my life. Amla. It's a small green fruit that grows on trees in India. The English name is Indian gooseberry. People have been using it as food and medicine in South Asia for over 3,000 years.

Earlene said her brother started taking it about 4 months after he lost his job. Something one of the studies his daughter showed him said had to do with cellular energy. Said something about how the cells in your body produce energy and what happens when those cells are running on a low battery. Said that the fruit had been studied for what it does to oxidative stress and inflammation, which are the two things that wear those cells down faster than the calendar should.

She said her brother had not been a tired old man. He had been a man whose cells were producing less energy than his life required. And nobody, not the doctor, not the company medical, not the sleep specialist who'd run him through the apnea test, had been looking at it.

She said by the time her brother had been on Amla for 7 weeks he was driving a delivery route again. Local. Smaller truck. But he was driving. And he'd passed the heel-to-toe walk.

She said, "Baby, I'm not telling you a fruit is going to fix you. I'm telling you what fixed my brother. And what my brother had was the same look you got on your face when you walked through that door."

I asked her how to spell it.

She wrote it down on the back of a paper menu. A. M. L. A.

I drove the rest of the way to Memphis that morning at 60 miles an hour with both hands on the wheel and the radio off. I dropped my load. I drove home. I told Carla everything when she got back from work that night. She cried. Then she sat down at the kitchen table with our laptop and she started reading.

I'm going to tell you what we read because I think a lot of guys my age are dealing with what I was dealing with and they don't have an Earlene in their life to put a hand on the table and call them baby.

Inside every cell of your body are tiny structures called mitochondria. They're the part of the cell that makes energy. Your body has trillions of them. They're in your muscles. They're in your heart. They're in your brain. The brain alone uses about 20 percent of all the energy your body produces, even though it's only about 2 percent of your weight.

When your mitochondria are working well, you feel sharp. You feel awake. You can drive a truck through Arkansas at 4 in the morning and stay focused on the road.

When they're under siege, when oxidative stress and chronic low grade inflammation are wearing them down faster than they can recover, they make less energy. They make it less efficiently. And the body keeps demanding more, but the supply isn't there. So your brain dims. Your reaction time stretches. You zone out for 4 seconds at a stretch and you don't know why.

Your bloodwork is fine. Your sleep test is fine. The doctor doesn't know what to look for because the problem is one layer deeper than what the standard tests measure.

Amla, from what we read, has been studied for its effects on the very things that wear mitochondria down. It's high in antioxidants and polyphenols that have been associated with reduced oxidative stress. It's been linked to lower markers of inflammation. There's research that suggests it influences a pathway called AMPK, which is sort of a master energy switch in the cells. When AMPK is active, your cells get pushed toward producing energy more efficiently and your mitochondria get supported in doing what they're supposed to do.

I'm not telling you this because I'm a doctor. I'm telling you what I read with my wife at our kitchen table after I almost killed a family on the interstate.

Carla ordered Alevia Amla that night. I want to tell you why we picked Alevia over the other options.

I'd looked at the cheap Amla powder on Amazon. The kind with the giant bag and the no name brand. Carla wouldn't let me. She said for something I was going to be putting in my body twice a day at 56 years old after a near miss on the interstate, we were going with the company that used the right form of the fruit, the one used in the actual studies, in a dose that lined up with the research. Alevia had a 90 day money back guarantee. That's what closed it for me. If a fruit doesn't do anything for me in 3 months, I get my money back. That's a fair deal.

The bottle came on Friday. I took my first capsule on Saturday morning at 6:30 AM with my coffee. I told my dispatcher I needed two weeks off. I had the time built up. He didn't ask why.

The first 9 days I felt nothing. I told Carla. She told me to keep going.

Day 14 I went out to the driveway to clean out the cab. I'd been putting it off for 4 months because I didn't have the energy. I cleaned the whole cab in 3 hours. Vacuumed it. Wiped down the dash. Pulled out trash I'd been ignoring since June. I came inside and Carla looked at me and said, "Wayne, you look different."

Day 22 I took Riley to the park. We were there for 2 hours. I ran. I actually ran. I have not run after a 6 year old in 4 years. She thought it was the funniest thing she'd ever seen.

Day 31 I went back on the road. Same run. Oklahoma City to Memphis. Eastbound through Arkansas overnight.

I drove the entire 8 hour stretch with my brain on. I did not lose a second. I did not zone out. I pulled into Memphis at 5:42 AM and I went to find a Pilot off the 240 and I bought a coffee and I sat in the cab and I called Carla because I needed to hear her voice.

I have been on Alevia Amla for 4 and a half months as I'm typing this. I have not had a single zone out in 4 months of running my regular route. My dispatcher told me last week I'm running tighter ETAs than I was running 5 years ago. I asked Carla to start taking it too. She has been on it for 9 weeks. She told me last Sunday she has not needed an afternoon nap on the weekend in 6 weeks, which for Carla is something close to a miracle.

I drove past the Pilot at the West Memphis exit two weeks ago. I went inside. Earlene was there. She remembered me. She poured me a coffee and sat down across from me and I told her what had happened.

She cried. Wouldn't let me pay for the coffee. Told me her brother Roy was driving a regional route now and had been off everything but Amla for a year.

If you're a man my age and you've been telling yourself that the fog and the fade and the slow draining of your battery is just part of getting older, I am here to tell you that it might not be. It might be one layer deeper than your doctor knows to look for. And there is a fruit that has been used for 3,000 years that has been studied for the very thing that's happening underneath everything else.

I am not a man who writes things on Facebook. My wife is typing this for me as I dictate it because I do not know how to do this on my own. scripts.body_meta:
The Christmas card I mailed to my cousin Patty in November came back to my house in February with a yellow sticker on it that said DECEASED.

I'm going to start there because that's where it started for me, and because if I try to ease into this I'll never write it.

I came in from the mailbox on a Wednesday afternoon. It was raining. I had on my husband's old Carhartt jacket because I'd run out without my coat, and I had the mail in one hand and a bag of groceries from Kroger in the other. I dumped both on the kitchen counter and I started sorting the mail the way I always do, and there it was. The card I'd sent back at the beginning of November, in my own handwriting, with a yellow forwarding sticker slapped over Patty's address.

DECEASED. Return to sender.

I stood at that counter for a long time. The groceries sat there. A bag of frozen peas slowly thawed against my elbow. I didn't move.

My name is Cheryl. I'm 57 years old. I live in a town called Findlay, Ohio, in a 2 story house on a street where I've lived since 1998. I work as a billing supervisor for a regional medical group. My husband Tom is 60 and he sells industrial pumps for a company out of Toledo. We have 2 grown sons, Adam and Ryan, both married, both out of state.

My cousin Patty was 53.

We grew up across the street from each other in Lima. Our mothers were sisters and they raised us almost like twins. Patty was 4 years younger but she always seemed older to me because she had this calm, settled quality even as a kid. She married a quiet man named Glen who worked for the post office. They never had children. They had a small house on a corner lot in Marion, with a little brick walkway and a flower bed full of daylilies that came up every June whether anybody planted them or not.

I had not seen Patty in person in almost 3 years.

We talked. Not as much as we used to. The kind of cousin relationship where you mean to call and the weeks turn into months. Christmas cards. A birthday text. A long phone call once a year that always ended with one of us saying we needed to do this more often.

The last time I'd talked to her was in May. She'd called on my birthday. We talked for 38 minutes. She told me Glen had retired in March and they were thinking about driving out to see his sister in North Carolina. She said her knees had been bothering her. She said she'd been feeling tired in a way she couldn't explain. I asked if she'd been to the doctor and she said yes, her cholesterol was a little high, they'd put her on something, she was fine.

She said she was fine.

I let her say she was fine because she'd always been fine and there was no reason to push.

The next time I would have heard from Patty was that Christmas card I sent in November.

The card came back in February.

I called my mother that night. My mother is 81 and lives in an assisted living place in Lima. She didn't know. Nobody in our family knew. Glen had not called anyone. I have wondered a lot about that since, what was happening with Glen, who Patty had been to him, why he didn't pick up the phone. I don't have answers to any of those questions and I don't think I'm going to get them.

What I found out later, through Patty's sister-in-law on Glen's side who I tracked down through Facebook, was that Patty had a heart attack at home on a Saturday morning in late January. She was 53 years old. She was making coffee. Glen was outside.

By the time he came back in, she was on the kitchen floor.

That was the call. That was the entire story. A coffee pot still going on the counter. A mug she'd already gotten out of the cabinet. A sister-in-law who answered my Facebook message at 11:47 at night and gave me the details I had no other way of getting.

I sat on the edge of my bed in the dark with my phone in my hand for an hour.

I want to say something here, because I think it's the heart of why I'm writing this.

Patty and I were the same person, biologically.

That is not me being dramatic. We had the same maternal grandparents. Our mothers were sisters. Both of those sisters had heart issues, late in life, and our grandmother Loretta died of a heart attack at 67. Our family had a chart. My mother had drawn it out for us once at Thanksgiving in 2009, on the back of a paper placemat, with little arrows showing who'd had what.

I was on the same branch as Patty.

I had the same blood pressure tendencies as her. I had the same cholesterol issues as her. I had been told by my own doctor for the past 4 years that my numbers were "borderline" and that we'd "keep an eye on them." I had been keeping an eye on them by going in for a panel once a year, looking at the printout, frowning at it, putting it in a drawer with the other ones, and going on with my life.

Patty had been doing the same thing.

She had been one step further down the road. She'd been on a low dose statin for about 18 months. Her sister-in-law told me Patty had complained about feeling foggy on it, like her thoughts moved slower, but she'd been told that was unrelated, and to keep taking it, and her doctor had increased the dose at her last visit.

My doctor had not put me on anything yet. My doctor had said we could try some lifestyle changes first. I had tried. I had cut out the half and half in my coffee. I had walked at lunch a few times a week. My next appointment was in March.

The appointment was 5 weeks away when I got the card back.

I made the appointment for the next morning instead.

I went in on a Thursday and I sat across from a doctor I'd been seeing for 11 years and I told him my cousin had died of a heart attack at 53, in her kitchen, on a Saturday morning, with the same family history I have. I told him my numbers had been borderline for 4 years. I asked him what we were actually going to do.

He pulled up my chart.

He looked at it for a long time.

He said the standard thing, which is that he wanted to put me on a statin. He said the statin would lower my LDL number by about 30%. He said that was the standard of care for someone in my situation, and that he should have probably suggested it sooner, given my family history.

I asked him a question I had never thought to ask before.

I asked him what the LDL number actually meant. Like, the actual mechanism. What happens with the cholesterol that becomes a problem.

He blinked at me a little. I think he wasn't used to that question. He answered it though. He explained that LDL by itself isn't really the issue. The issue is when LDL gets oxidized inside your blood vessels. Oxidized LDL is what gets stuck on the artery walls and starts the plaque process. Regular LDL just does its job. It's the oxidation that turns it dangerous.

I said, so the statin lowers the LDL number, but does the statin do anything about the oxidation.

He said, well, no. The statin lowers the production. It doesn't address oxidation directly.

I said, so we're lowering the total amount but we're not really addressing the part that becomes dangerous.

He said, that's one way to put it.

I said, what addresses the oxidation.

He said, antioxidants. Diet. Lifestyle. There are things in the research, he said, but most of them don't have the kind of clinical track record that prescription medications do.

I left with the prescription.

I filled it. I took the first one. I am not telling you not to listen to your doctor and I am not telling you to throw out your medication.

What I'm telling you is that I went home, and I sat at my kitchen table, and I started reading.

I read for 4 nights in a row.

Most of what I read was beyond me, frankly. I was a billing supervisor, not a biochemist. But I read enough to understand the basic chain. Cholesterol becomes a problem when it gets oxidized. Oxidized cholesterol is what builds up. The standard medical approach is to lower the total amount. The other approach, which doesn't get talked about as much in a regular doctor's office, is to address the oxidation itself.

The thing I kept running into, in different articles and forum posts and a few research summaries I read 3 times each before I felt like I followed them, was a fruit called amla. Indian gooseberry. It contained a class of compounds called emblicanins, and those compounds appeared to do something I hadn't seen attributed to anything else I'd read about.

They appeared to help protect cholesterol from oxidation in the bloodstream.

The research I was reading wasn't anecdotal. There were actual clinical trials. People with elevated lipids, given amla extract, twice a day, for 12 weeks. The results showed improvements in total cholesterol, in LDL specifically, in triglycerides, and in markers of oxidative stress.

That last part is what got me. Markers of oxidative stress.

That was the piece my doctor had said wasn't really being addressed.

I kept going. I read about the cycle, which I'd never had explained to me before. When your cells are under chronic oxidative stress, your body actually produces more cholesterol as a kind of repair signal. It's trying to patch damage. So oxidation drives cholesterol production. And then that new cholesterol is also vulnerable to oxidation. And then more is needed. And the whole thing feeds itself.

If you only lower the production, you've turned down one side of the loop.

If you can also reduce the oxidation, you start to turn down the other side.

That made sense to me in a way the pamphlet at the doctor's office never had.

I ordered Alevia Amla on a Sunday night. It came on Wednesday. I took my first 2 capsules with my coffee on Thursday morning, the same morning I took my statin. I'm telling you that part on purpose. I did not stop my prescription. I'm not a doctor. I'm a 57 year old woman whose cousin had just died, and I was going to use everything I could responsibly use.

I want to tell you what changed and I want to be honest about it.

The first 3 weeks, I didn't notice anything.

I'd read the trials. I knew this stuff was supposed to work over months, not days. So I wasn't expecting the world. I just kept taking the capsules and writing the date on a sticky note on the fridge so I'd know when I'd started.

Around week 4, my morning energy was different.

I'd gotten used to a kind of low grade fog in the mornings that I'd been blaming on being 57 and on the statin and on a hundred other things. That fog started to lift. Not all at once. Just less. I'd be at my desk at work and realize at 11 in the morning that I had not yet thought about needing more coffee, which was not normal for me.

Around week 6, my husband Tom said something at dinner.

He said, "You're laughing more lately."

I said, am I.

He said yes. He said it had been a while.

I sat with that for the rest of the evening. I had not realized I'd stopped laughing. I had not realized I had been quieter for the last year or two. The kind of quieter that you don't notice from the inside but the people who live with you do.

Around week 10, I went in for a follow up panel.

My doctor came in with the printout and he sat down and he said, what are you doing.

I told him.

He said, well, keep doing it.

My total cholesterol had come down 38 points. My LDL specifically had come down 27 points. My triglycerides had come down even further. My HDL had ticked up 4 points, which he said was small but real and which he said was "not nothing."

He said the statin alone did not usually get those numbers in 10 weeks.

He said he was going to make a note in my chart.

He said he had not personally suggested amla to a patient before but that he had read about it in 2 of the medical newsletters he subscribed to.

He said, "Whatever you're doing is working."

I drove home from that appointment and I cried in my car in the parking lot for about 15 minutes. I cried because I was relieved. I cried because Patty wasn't here. I cried because I have a younger brother named Mark who is 51 and who has the same family history and who has been ignoring his own numbers for 6 years and I was going to send him a bottle that night when I got home.

I cried because I almost didn't read that night I got the card back. I almost just put the card in a drawer. I almost just made the next March appointment and gone in and accepted the prescription and gone home and put the bottle on the shelf next to my multivitamin and lived another 4 years on borderline numbers.

I had been one good ignored Christmas card away from being Patty.

I am telling you this because I think there are a lot of women like me out there.

You have a family chart that scares you a little. You have a doctor who looks at your numbers and tells you they're borderline. You have a drawer full of past printouts that you don't want to look at again. You have a cousin or a sister or an aunt or a mother whose story is sitting in the back of your mind and you don't say it out loud, but you wonder sometimes.

I want to tell you that there is more to this conversation than a single number on a piece of paper.

Your body produces cholesterol on purpose. It's a transporter. It's a building material. It only becomes the kind of cholesterol that hurts you when it gets oxidized in your bloodstream by stress and inflammation and damage. The standard medical approach is to lower the production. That works, partially. It moves the number. But it doesn't address the oxidation that turns the cholesterol you do have into the dangerous version.

Amla appears, based on the research that exists right now, to address the part the medication doesn't.

That's not me telling you to stop your medication. I haven't stopped mine. That's me telling you there's another rung on the ladder that nobody talks about in a 15 minute appointment.

Alevia Amla is what I take. I take 2 capsules every morning with my coffee. I have been taking them for 4 months. My cholesterol is the lowest it has been in 8 years. My morning energy is back. I have been laughing more. My husband noticed it before I did.

The company offers a 90 day money back guarantee. 90 days. That was 3 months. It was the same window of time the trials I read about had used. If it doesn't do anything for you, you call them, you send the bottle back, and you get a refund. There's no risk. There's just a chance.

I want to tell you something else.

I sent a bottle to my brother Mark in February, the day after my doctor visit, with a note that said, please.

He has been taking it for 6 weeks. He's not a Facebook person. He doesn't talk about supplements. But last week on the phone, he said he'd had his blood drawn at his last physical and his doctor had asked him what he'd changed. He said he'd told his doctor about the amla, and his doctor had said, hm.

That was the whole story. His doctor had said, hm.

That was enough for me.

I keep the Christmas card I mailed to Patty in a folder in my desk drawer. The one with the yellow DECEASED sticker on the front. I don't know why I kept it. I think I keep it because I don't want to forget what it felt like to stand at that counter with the groceries on my elbow and realize I had been one number away from the same thing.

I kept it because I'm 57 and I have a husband who needs me and 2 sons who need me and a mother who needs me and a brother who needs me and a future I want to be in.

I kept it because the next card I send, I want to come to me, signed.

That's all I have.

If you have a chart. If you have a number. If you have a cousin. If you have a feeling.

Don't wait until February.
