I'm not exaggerating. I've made it for every birthday in this family since 1987. My son's birthdays. My daughter's birthdays. My husband Carl's birthdays. My grandkids. My in laws. My church. My neighbors when their dogs died. My friend Diane after her hysterectomy in 2003.

200 times. At least.

Cream the butter and the sugar for 8 minutes until it's white and fluffy. Add the eggs one at a time. Sift the flour with the salt and the baking powder. Add it in three parts, alternating with the buttermilk, starting and ending with the flour. Fold in the vanilla and the lemon zest at the end.

I could do it with my eyes closed. I have done it with my eyes closed, on a dare, at my sister's bridal shower in 1991.

Last Thursday, I creamed the butter and the sugar. I added the eggs. I picked up the flour. I stood there with the bag in my hand.

And I couldn't remember if I sifted it first or added it straight.

I stood there for what felt like 5 minutes but was probably 30 seconds. The Kitchenaid was still running. I could hear it humming. The afternoon sun was coming through my kitchen window, the one that faces the dogwood tree my husband planted in 2001.

I put the flour bag down on the counter.

I sat down on the kitchen floor with my back against the cabinets.

And I cried like I haven't cried since my mother died in 2014.

I'm Maxine Whitfield. I'm 58 years old. I live in a 1960s ranch on Pulaski Avenue in Athens, Georgia, two blocks from the high school where I taught English Literature for 26 years.

My grandson Marcus turns 6 next Saturday.

That cake was for him.

I want to tell you who I was before this started.

I was the woman in our family who remembered everything. Every birthday. Every anniversary. Every name of every cousin's new baby. The first day of school for all 4 of my grandkids. The order of the songs at my own wedding in 1989.

I was the woman my friends called when they couldn't remember the name of the actor in that movie they saw 6 years ago. I was the woman who taught Beowulf and Chaucer to 17 year olds for almost 3 decades, and I never used notes. The poem was just in me.

I won the spelling bee in my district 3 years in a row in middle school. My maiden name is on a plaque in the gymnasium of W.E.B. DuBois Middle School in Macon, Georgia.

That woman.

That's who I was.

That's who I have been my whole life, all the way up to about 2 years ago.

It started small. The way these things always start small.

I was at the grocery store on Alps Road, the Kroger, in the spring of 2023. I was standing in the produce section holding a bag of yellow onions and I couldn't remember why I needed them. I stood there for 4 or 5 minutes trying to retrace my morning. I'd written a list. The list was at home on the kitchen counter.

I put the onions down and I went home.

When I got home, I looked at the list. Onions for the gumbo I was making that night.

I laughed about it. I told Carl over dinner. He laughed too. He said "welcome to my world, baby." He's 60. He's been losing his keys since the Carter administration. We laughed.

But it kept happening.

I'd walk into a room and stand there. I'd open the refrigerator and forget what I was looking for. I'd start a sentence in the middle of telling Diane a story and I'd just stop. The next word wouldn't come. I'd stand there with my mouth open and Diane would gently feed me the word and I'd thank her and move on.

I started writing things down.

I bought a planner from the Target on Atlanta Highway in August of 2023. A real one. Spiral bound. With pages for each week. I started writing every single thing I had to do that day, including things like "call Carl to remind him about the trash" and "take out the chicken to thaw."

The planner became my brain.

If something wasn't in the planner, it didn't exist.

I lost the planner once, in October, and I sat in my car in the Publix parking lot for 20 minutes trying to remember what I was supposed to do that day.

I want to tell you what I was telling myself this whole time.

I was telling myself it was just menopause. I was telling myself it was just stress. I was telling myself it was just the new cholesterol medicine my doctor put me on after my numbers came back high in 2022. I was telling myself it was just because I'd retired from teaching in 2021 and I wasn't using my brain the way I used to.

I was telling myself a lot of things.

Carl was telling me the same things. So was Diane. So was my son Andre, who lives in Atlanta and calls every Sunday. So was my daughter Jasmine, who lives in Decatur with the grandkids.

"Mom, you're fine. You taught Beowulf for 26 years. Your brain is fine."

But here's the thing. I was the one inside my head. I was the one who knew.

I was the one who couldn't follow the recipe I'd made 200 times.

I went to my doctor in November. Dr. Wilson. Black woman, my age, sharp as a knife. I love her. I've been seeing her since 2009.

She listened. She did some blood work. She did one of those little memory screening tests where they ask you to remember 3 words and then ask you again 5 minutes later.

I remembered all 3 words.

She said my screening was normal. She said it was probably perimenopause settling in. She said she could refer me to a neurologist if I wanted, but she didn't think it was necessary.

I didn't take the referral.

I went home and I told myself I was being dramatic.

I went home and I bought a bigger planner.

I want to fast forward to last Thursday.

Last Thursday, I was making the pound cake for Marcus.

The kitchen smelled like butter and sugar. The Kitchenaid was humming. The dogwood tree was in bloom outside the window. I had a cup of cold coffee on the counter from breakfast that I kept meaning to dump.

I'd made the cake the day before. The first one. The cream of tartar and baking soda one. The one with the lemon glaze. Marcus loves the lemon glaze.

I'd brought it to my husband at the dinner table, because Carl always tastes the first one to make sure it's right. It's our ritual. It's been our ritual for 36 years.

He took a bite.

He chewed.

He looked up at me and he said, very gently, "Max, baby. There's no salt in this."

I had forgotten the salt.

I had been creaming butter and sugar and sifting flour for that recipe for 38 years and I had never once forgotten the salt.

I stood there at the dinner table looking at Carl looking at me and something in my chest got very, very cold.

I went back into the kitchen. I started over the next morning.

That's the cake I was making at 2:14 PM last Thursday.

The redo.

That's the cake I was 4 ingredients into when I forgot whether I sifted the flour first or added it straight.

That's why I was sitting on my kitchen floor crying.

I sat there until 2:54.

Carl came home from his Thursday afternoon golf game with his brother. He found me on the floor. He didn't say anything. He just sat down next to me on the linoleum and put his arm around me.

He said "Max, what is going on."

I told him.

I told him about the onions. I told him about the planner. I told him about the words that wouldn't come. I told him about the salt the night before.

I told him I was scared.

I told him I was scared I was disappearing in pieces, and that the woman who taught Beowulf for 26 years and remembered every birthday in our family was already half gone, and that one day soon I wouldn't even remember that I used to be her.

Carl held me.

He didn't tell me I was being dramatic.

He didn't tell me it was menopause.

He didn't tell me my brain was fine because I taught Beowulf.

He just held me.

And then he said something I didn't expect.

He said, "Max, my sister Phyllis went through this in 2019. Don't you remember? She was forgetting things. She was getting scared. And then she found that thing she takes."

I looked up at him.

Phyllis is Carl's older sister. She's 62. She lives in Augusta. She used to be a nurse at the VA. She had been struggling for about 18 months back then with what she was calling "the fog." I remembered her telling me about it at Thanksgiving in 2018. She said she was forgetting medication names. She said she'd looked at a chart at work and her own handwriting hadn't made sense to her.

I hadn't seen her in 4 years. We don't get up to Augusta the way we used to.

I called her that night.

Phyllis answered on the second ring. She sounded like Phyllis. Sharp. Loud. Laughing at something her dog did before she even said hello.

I told her what was happening.

She got quiet.

And then she said, "Maxie, you remember when I was going through the fog?"

I said I remembered.

She said, "I want you to listen to me, because I tried to tell my doctor about it for 2 years and she kept telling me it was menopause and stress and getting older. And I almost just accepted that. I almost just bought a bigger planner."

She said, "Then my friend Loretta from church told me about something her son had been reading about. A fruit. From India. Called Amla."

I'd never heard the word.

I'm an English teacher. I read everything. I've read fruit names in dozens of languages. I'd never heard Amla.

She said Loretta's son was a research librarian at Fort Valley State and he'd been deep in studies about something called oxidative stress and inflammation in the brain. About how a lot of what we call "brain fog" and "memory slipping" in middle age isn't necessarily the start of something terrible. It's often the buildup of damage at the cellular level. Damage that interferes with how the cells in our brains and our nervous systems do their job.

She said Loretta gave her a bottle. She said she didn't expect anything.

She said it took about 5 weeks.

She said she's been on it for 4 years now and the fog never came back.

I sat on the edge of my bed with the phone in my hand and I cried again.

I want to tell you what I learned, after I got off the phone with Phyllis.

Because I went to the laptop and I started reading until 1 in the morning. Carl brought me tea. Then he brought me crackers. Then he went to bed and told me to come find him when I was ready.

I'm not going to pretend I understood every word of every study I read. I'm an English teacher, not a biochemist. But you give me enough text and I can find the pattern. That's the whole job of literary analysis. You read enough and you start seeing what the text is doing.

And the pattern that started forming as I read was something I had never been told before.

The cells in your brain and your nervous system are some of the most demanding cells in your body. They burn through enormous amounts of energy. They run all day, every day, with no breaks. Every thought you have. Every memory you pull up. Every word you reach for. All of it is happening at the cellular level, and all of it requires power.

That power gets made inside little structures in every cell called mitochondria. Mitochondria are like tiny power plants. They turn what you eat and breathe into the fuel your cells run on.

But mitochondria don't run clean forever. As we get older, and as we live our lives, the mitochondria in our cells start to wear down. Years of inflammation, years of stress, years of processed food, years of just being alive in 2026, all of it builds up.

When mitochondria don't run clean, two things happen.

One, they produce less power. The cells they live in don't have what they need to do their job. In your brain, that can show up as fog. As reaching for a word that won't come. As forgetting a recipe you've made 200 times.

Two, they produce more waste. A specific kind of waste called oxidative stress. Free radicals that bounce around and damage things inside the cell. In your brain, that damage adds up. It interferes with how cells communicate. It makes the fog worse.

It's a cycle.

Less power, more damage, less power, more damage.

And nothing in my whole long life of pamphlets and doctor's visits and well-woman exams had ever told me about it.

I read until I couldn't read anymore.

And the question I kept coming back to was the simplest one.

If the mitochondria are running dirty, what helps them run cleaner?

If the brain cells are getting hit with damage, what helps protect them?

That's where Amla came back into the picture.

Amla is a small green fruit, about the size of a golf ball, that grows on a tree native to India. They've been using it in their traditional medicine for over 3,000 years. The old translation of its name is something like "the nurse," because of how broadly it supports the body.

But what stopped me, sitting at my kitchen table at 11:30 at night, was what the research has been finding about it at the cellular level.

Amla is loaded with compounds called emblicanins, which research suggests are some of the most potent natural antioxidants ever measured. Antioxidants are molecules that can help neutralize the free radicals that build up as oxidative stress. They help clean up the damage before it accumulates.

Amla has also been associated with activating something called AMPK. AMPK is one of the master switches inside your cells. When AMPK is active, it tells your cells to clean up. To clear out damaged components. To support the mitochondria. To run cleaner.

And research suggests Amla's compounds may help support how cells throughout the body, including in the brain and nervous system, manage inflammation and protect themselves from oxidative damage.

When the cells in your brain are better supported, they can do their job. They can communicate. They can pull up the word. They can remember the order of the recipe. They can be the woman who taught Beowulf for 26 years, instead of the woman sitting on a kitchen floor crying.

I'm not telling you Amla is a miracle. I'm an English teacher. I don't believe in miracles. I believe in small, careful, well chosen words and patient sentences that build on each other.

But for the first time in 2 years, I had a frame for what was happening to me that wasn't "you're getting old, buy a bigger planner."

The frame was, the engines in the cells of your brain are running dirty, and there's something that supports them.

I bought a bottle of Alevia Amla that night. From my laptop, on my kitchen table, at 12:47 AM, while Carl snored down the hall.

It came in 4 days. Two capsules a day, with breakfast.

I want to tell you what's happened since, but I want to be careful. I don't want to be the woman on Facebook telling you a fairy tale. I'm a literature teacher. I know fairy tales. They have very specific structures and they are not what is happening in real life.

But here's what I noticed.

The first 3 weeks, almost nothing. I felt a little less foggy in the late afternoon. That was it. I almost gave up. I called Phyllis. She told me to stay with it.

In the second month, I noticed I'd stopped writing certain things in the planner. The chicken to thaw. The trash reminder for Carl. They just stayed in my head again.

Around week 6, Diane and I had lunch at the Mama's Boy Cafe on Cherry Street. I told her a story about my niece's wedding in 2017. The whole story. Names, dates, the song they walked down the aisle to, the joke the best man told. I told it without stopping. Without reaching. Without that little click in my brain where a word should have been.

When I finished, Diane was looking at me funny.

She said, "Max. Where did you go just now?"

I said, "What do you mean?"

She said, "You sounded like you. You sounded like you used to."

I sat there with my Caesar salad in front of me and I felt my eyes get hot and I just nodded at her.

In the third month, I made my grandmother's pound cake again.

Marcus had a half birthday celebration his mother had cooked up because he was disappointed about something at school. Jasmine called me on a Wednesday and asked if I could make the cake.

I made it. From memory. No planner. No phone notes.

The whole thing.

The salt was in it.

I brought it to the table. Carl took the first bite. He chewed. He looked up at me.

He didn't say anything.

He just nodded.

And I went into the bathroom in the hall and I closed the door and I looked at myself in the mirror.

The woman looking back at me was the woman who taught Beowulf.

She was a little older. She was tired. She had grey at her temples she hadn't bothered to dye in months.

But she was there.

She was all the way there.

I want to tell you about Marcus's actual birthday. Last Saturday.

I made the cake the night before. I made it from memory. The kitchen smelled like butter and sugar and lemon zest and I knew exactly what I was doing every step of the way. I sang along to Anita Baker on the radio while I was sifting the flour.

Marcus came in on Saturday wearing a cape. He's 6. He's at the cape stage. He saw the cake on the counter and he ran to me and he wrapped his arms around my legs and he said, "Grandma. You made me the cake."

I said, "I made you the cake, baby."

He said, "Did you remember to put the lemon on top this time?"

I laughed.

I picked him up. He's getting heavy. I held him on my hip the way I used to hold his mother. I showed him the cake.

I said, "I remembered everything, baby."

He said, "Grandma, you always remember everything."

I said, "That's right. Grandma always remembers."

And I want to say something to you, if you're still reading.

If you're a woman in your 50s or your 60s, and you've been losing words and forgetting why you walked into rooms and quietly buying bigger planners, and you've been telling yourself it's menopause or stress or just getting older, I want you to think about what I learned at my kitchen table that night.

"Just getting older" is sometimes a story we tell ourselves about something that has a different name underneath.

The cells in your brain need power to do their job. The engines in those cells need to run clean. Sometimes they need support.

I'm not your doctor. I'm not telling you anything is wrong with what you're doing. Talk to your doctor. Show her this if you want.

But the thing I wish I'd known 2 years ago, when I stood in the produce section of Kroger holding a bag of yellow onions, is that there are answers out there besides "buy a bigger planner."

If you've been losing pieces of yourself, and you've been told it's just menopause, I want you to at least look at it.

We sat on my back porch after the kids went home and we drank sweet tea and we watched the dogwood tree and we didn't say much. We didn't need to. She knew what I was thinking. scripts.body_meta:
The phone rang at 2:47 in the morning and I knew before I picked it up.

You know that thing your body does. That cold thing in your chest before your brain has caught up. I knew. I just didn't know what yet.

It was Memorial Hospital. A woman named Patricia who I will remember for the rest of my life because she said my name three times before I could form a sentence. Mrs. Vega. Mrs. Vega. Mrs. Vega.

Your husband was brought in by ambulance about an hour ago. He's stable. We need you to come down.

I asked her what happened.

She said the words "hypertensive event" and I said okay even though I didn't know what that meant. I'd been a dental hygienist for 22 years. I cleaned teeth. I didn't know what a hypertensive event was. I just knew it had a word for it and that meant it was real.

I drove from our house in Mesa to the hospital in 14 minutes. The speed limit is 45. I don't remember a single light. I don't remember my hands on the steering wheel. I remember pulling into the visitor parking lot and sitting in the car for 30 seconds because I couldn't make my legs work.

His name is Daniel. We've been married 28 years.

I'm going to tell you what happened that night and what happened in the 6 weeks after, because I made a promise to myself sitting in a hospital chair at 4 in the morning that if my husband came home alive I was going to tell other women what nobody told me. And he came home alive. So here I am. Typing this on a Sunday afternoon while he's outside in the garage doing something with the lawnmower.

My name is Diana. I'm 54 years old. I clean teeth at a small dental practice off Southern Avenue. I have two grown sons, one in Tucson and one in Reno, and a granddaughter named Mia who is 4 and calls me Nana with two syllables, like Na Na. I've lived in Mesa, Arizona for 31 years. My husband Daniel sells commercial real estate. He drinks too much coffee. He used to smoke and quit in 2009. He grew up in a small town in New Mexico and he says yes ma'am to women in their 70s the way his mother taught him to.

He turned 56 in February.

I'm going to back up because I want to tell this right.

Daniel had been off for a while. I don't know how long exactly. That's the part that haunts me. You live with somebody for 28 years and you don't notice the thing changing because you see them every day and the change is slow.

He'd been getting headaches. He told me about them in November. Said they came on around 4 in the afternoon and felt like a band tightening across the back of his head. I told him to drink more water. He laughed and said he drinks a gallon a day. I told him to go to the doctor. He said he had an appointment in January for his physical and he'd bring it up then.

January came. He went. He told me his blood pressure was a little elevated. The doctor wanted him to lose 10 pounds and watch his salt and come back in 6 months.

That was January. The phone rang in March.

In between January and March, this is what I noticed and didn't say anything about.

He started waking up in the middle of the night to pee. Not unusual for a 56 year old man, I told myself. He was getting winded walking from the parking lot to his office building. The building has 18 stairs. He used to take them two at a time. By February he was taking the elevator and lying about it. He started skipping his Saturday morning bike ride with his friend Greg. He told Greg he was busy. He wasn't busy. He was sitting on our patio drinking coffee and looking out at the yard.

His face had been a little puffy. His ankles had been a little swollen at night. He told me one Sunday in February that he felt "weird" and I asked what kind of weird and he said "just weird" and we changed the subject.

I want you to understand something. I am not a stupid woman. I work in healthcare. I knew what those things meant. I just didn't put them together because he's my husband and I love him and you don't always want to see what you're seeing.

The night it happened, Daniel had gone to bed at 10:15. I'd stayed up to finish a book. I went to bed around 11:30. He was already asleep. I noticed his breathing sounded heavier than usual but I told myself I was being paranoid.

At 1:42 AM I woke up because he was sitting up in bed. I asked if he was okay. He said his head was hurting and he was going to take some Tylenol. He got up. I heard the bathroom faucet. I heard the medicine cabinet. Then I heard him say my name in a voice I'd never heard before.

"Diana. Something's wrong."

I got out of bed. He was sitting on the edge of the bathtub. His face was grey. Not pale. Grey. The color of wet cement. He was sweating through his t-shirt. His hands were shaking.

I called 911 from the bathroom floor.

The paramedics took 9 minutes. I let them in. They put him on a stretcher. One of them asked me what medications he was on and I said none, he doesn't take any medications, and the paramedic looked at me like I'd given the wrong answer.

His blood pressure when they got there was 217 over 124.

I rode in the back of the ambulance. I held his foot through the blanket because I couldn't reach his hand. I kept saying his name. He kept saying mine.

At the hospital they took him back. I sat in the waiting room. A woman came out at 2:47 AM and that's when she called me.

She was a nurse. She said he was stable. She said he hadn't had a stroke or a heart attack but he'd been very close to having one or the other. She said the word "hypertensive crisis" and explained it to me like I was a child, which I appreciated, because at 2:47 in the morning I needed to be talked to like a child.

She said his blood pressure when he came in was higher than they liked to see. She said they'd brought it down and he was responding well to medication. She said I could see him in about an hour.

I sat in a chair in the hallway and I called both of my sons. The one in Tucson answered on the second ring. The one in Reno answered on the fourth. I tried to be calm. I wasn't calm.

At 4:15 AM they let me into his room.

He was lying in a hospital bed in a gown. There were wires coming out of him in 6 different places. His face was less grey but his eyes were tired in a way I'd never seen them. He looked at me and he said, "I'm sorry, baby."

I want to tell you what he said next because I think about it every single day.

He said, "I knew. I knew something was wrong. I just didn't want to know."

I sat down in the chair next to his bed and I held his hand and I didn't say anything for a long time. Because I knew too. I'd known since November. I'd known and I hadn't pushed. I'd let him not go back to the doctor. I'd let him not bring up the headaches when his number was elevated. I'd let him take the elevator and pretended I didn't notice.

I'd let him because I was scared. Same as him.

They kept him for 3 days. They sent him home with three new prescriptions and a sheet of paper with diet recommendations on it that we both knew he wasn't going to follow. They told him to come back in 2 weeks.

That's when the second part of this story starts.

Daniel went back to work after a week. He didn't want to. His boss told him to take more time. Daniel said he'd go crazy sitting in the house. He was right. He would have. He's not built for stillness.

He started taking the medications. Lisinopril for the blood pressure. Hydrochlorothiazide which is a water pill. Amlodipine which I'd never heard of. He took them every morning with a glass of water and he didn't complain.

The medications brought his number down. Within a week his readings at home were 134 over 86. The doctor said that was a huge improvement. The doctor was happy.

Daniel was not happy.

He was tired all the time. The kind of tired where he came home from work at 5:30 and sat on the couch and didn't move until I put a plate in front of him. He started having a dry cough that wouldn't go away. The water pill made him pee 8 times a day, which doesn't sound like a big deal until you're a grown man in a real estate office trying to sit through a closing. His feet got cold. His hands got cold. I'd reach for his hand at night and it would be cold the way feet are when they've been outside in winter.

He said one night, "I'm alive, but I don't feel alive."

We were sitting on the patio. It was the first week of April. The mountains looked purple the way they do in Mesa at sunset. He said it without drama. He said it like he was reporting weather.

I didn't sleep that night. I went into the kitchen at 1 in the morning and I sat at the counter with my laptop and I started reading.

I want to tell you what I read because I think it matters.

I wasn't looking for an alternative to his medication. I was looking for something that might support what his medication was doing without taking more from him than it had already taken. He was already on three pills. Each pill came with side effects. Each side effect was making him feel less like himself. I'd watched a man I'd known for 28 years collapse in 2 hours and then I'd watched the medications that saved his life slowly drain something else out of him.

There had to be more to the story than that.

I started reading about blood pressure. Why it goes up. What's actually happening in the body. The doctor at the hospital had used the words "vascular health" and I'd nodded but I didn't really know what that meant.

Here's what I learned, in plain language. Your blood vessels are not just plumbing. They're alive. The inside of your blood vessels is a thin layer of cells called the endothelium and that layer is supposed to flex and dilate and respond to what your body needs at any given moment. When you're exercising it should let more blood through. When you're resting it should relax. When you're under stress it should manage the pressure without staying clamped down.

When your endothelium isn't healthy, it stops doing those things well. It gets stiff. It gets inflamed. It can't dilate the way it's supposed to. And your heart has to push harder to move blood through it. That's what high blood pressure actually is. It's not just a number. It's a sign that the inside of your blood vessels isn't working the way it should.

Medications can help bring the number down. They do it by relaxing your vessels chemically, or by reducing the volume of fluid in your body, or by slowing your heart rate. They work. Daniel's medications worked. He was alive because of them.

But what they don't do is repair the underlying issue. They manage the number. They don't address what's making the number go up in the first place.

That's when I started reading about Amla.

I'd never heard the word. Amla. It's a small green fruit that grows on trees in India. The English name is Indian gooseberry. People have been using it as food and medicine in South Asia for over 3,000 years.

What got my attention was a study I read where researchers had given Amla extract to people with metabolic syndrome and watched what happened to their endothelial function over 12 weeks. The reflection index, which is a measure of how well your blood vessels are working, improved. Their nitric oxide levels went up. Nitric oxide is what your blood vessels use to dilate. Their inflammation markers went down. Their blood pressure responded.

I read for 4 hours. I read studies. I read summaries of studies. I read medical journal articles I had no business reading at 1 in the morning. And what I kept finding was that Amla seemed to support the very things Daniel's medications couldn't address. The vessel health itself. The inflammation underneath the number. The oxidative stress that ages blood vessels faster than the calendar should.

scripts.main_pain_point: A 31-year framing-crew owner's chronic back has reduced him to crawling in a parking lot, and his doctor's only counsel is the useless 'manage it.'
scripts.hook_line: I almost didn't make it through my son's rehearsal dinner.
scripts.body_meta:
I almost didn't make it through my son's rehearsal dinner.

Not because of nerves. Not because of cold feet, his or mine. Not because of the open bar or the speech I'd been writing in my head for 6 weeks on every long drive between Birmingham and the job sites my crew was working over in Tuscaloosa.

I almost didn't make it because at 2:47 PM that Friday afternoon, 4 hours and 13 minutes before I was supposed to walk into the Iron City Grill in downtown Birmingham and stand up in front of 60 people and toast my only son's marriage, my back went out so hard in the parking lot of a Publix on Highway 280 that I had to crawl, and I mean crawl, on my hands and knees from the back of my truck to the driver's side door while a woman pushing a cart full of grocery bags pretended not to see me.

I want to tell you what happened that night.

Because what happened at the dinner that night, and the conversation I had at 11:30 PM with a woman I'd never met before, the mother of the girl my son was about to marry, is the reason I can sit here at my kitchen table at 6:08 in the morning and write this with both hands working and a back that doesn't feel like it's full of broken glass.

My name is Curt. I'm 62 years old. I've lived in the same little town outside Birmingham my whole life, a place called Helena, which is far enough out that you can still hear coyotes at night but close enough that I can be at a job site downtown in 35 minutes if traffic is decent, which it never is.

I run a small framing crew. Have for 31 years. We do residential framing, mostly custom homes up in the Highland Lakes area and the Greystone neighborhoods. 4 guys including me. We've been the same 4 guys for 14 years now, with one rotation when my old foreman Hank retired and his nephew Bobby took his spot. We've framed maybe 700 houses in 3 decades. I can walk through any of them, even ones I haven't seen since 1998, and tell you exactly where the load bearing walls are.

I have one son. His name is Rhett. He's 28. He's an architect, of all things, which still cracks me up because I spent his whole childhood telling him to put down the Legos and come help me hang sheetrock and he'd just stare at me with the same look his mother used to give me when she was disappointed and go back to his Legos. He went to Auburn. Got his degree. Now he draws the houses I would have framed, except he's working at a firm in Atlanta and I'm slowing down and the houses he draws are getting framed by guys 25 years younger than me.

He was getting married to a girl named Ainsley. Sweet girl. From Mountain Brook, which if you don't know Birmingham is one of the wealthier zip codes in the state. Her father was a cardiologist. Her mother, Patty, ran a small interior design firm out of the front rooms of the house they'd lived in for 30 years.

The rehearsal dinner was at the Iron City Grill. 7:00 PM that Friday. I had a navy blazer pressed and hanging on the back of my closet door. I had a speech printed on three index cards in 14 point font because my reading glasses were getting harder to deal with. I had a pair of dress shoes I'd bought at a Belk in 2009 that I'd polished the night before with a tin of Kiwi polish I found under the bathroom sink.

I had everything ready.

What I did not have ready was my back.

My back had been a problem for 6 years. Started right around the time I turned 56. Lower back, mostly, but it would creep up between my shoulder blades on bad days and one time it went all the way down into my left leg and I lost feeling in my big toe for almost a week. The kind of back that makes you sit on the edge of the bed for 20 minutes in the morning before you can stand up. The kind that makes you decline coffee with the guys at the diner because the booth is too low and you can't get out of it without putting both hands on the table and grunting like an old man.

My doctor, Dr. Whitfield, had run an MRI on it back in 2022. Showed me pictures of my own spine on a screen. Said the words "degenerative disc" and "facet arthropathy" and "consistent with your age and the kind of work you've done for 30 years." Gave me a prescription for muscle relaxers I didn't take because they made me too foggy to operate a saw. Gave me a referral to a physical therapist I went to twice and quit. Gave me the most useless advice I've ever heard out of a doctor's mouth, which was, and I'm quoting him, "Curt, at your age and in your line of work, this is just how it's gonna be. Manage it."

Manage it.

I'd been managing it for 6 years. I'd been managing it with ibuprofen at the level where my pharmacist had quietly mentioned my kidneys to me twice. I'd been managing it with a heating pad I plugged in next to the couch and forgot about so often my wife Karen kept it in a drawer where I couldn't find it without asking her. I'd been managing it by paying my guys an extra 4 dollars an hour so they'd handle the loads I used to handle.

I'd been managing it by becoming smaller. By saying no to things. By skipping my niece's wedding 2 years ago because the thought of a 4 hour reception in a folding chair made me feel sick. By not picking up my granddaughter, Rhett's daughter from a previous relationship, who is 5 and weighs 41 pounds and who I have not lifted off the ground in 18 months.

So that Friday afternoon, 4 hours before the rehearsal dinner, I went to Publix to pick up a bouquet of flowers for Patty. Karen had told me twice. Yellow roses. Patty's favorite. I had it on a sticky note on the dashboard.

I went into the store. Picked out the flowers. Paid. Walked back to my truck. Opened the back to set the flowers on the bench seat.

And as I leaned in, something in my lower back popped.

I want to be clear about what kind of pop. This wasn't a twinge. This wasn't the usual morning stiffness. This was the kind of pop that sounds like a tree branch breaking inside your body. I went down. Right there, in the parking lot of a Publix, between my Ford F-250 and a silver Honda Pilot.

I was on the asphalt for I don't know how long. Could have been 30 seconds. Could have been 5 minutes. The flowers had landed on the ground next to me and a yellow petal blew under the truck.

A woman with a cart full of grocery bags walked past about 10 feet away. Slowed down. Looked at me. I made eye contact with her. She looked away and kept pushing her cart. I'll never forget that. I don't blame her. People don't know what to do anymore.

I crawled. On my hands and knees, around the back of the truck, to the driver's side door. Pulled myself up using the door handle. Got in. Sat in the driver's seat sweating through my shirt. Looked at the clock. 2:47 PM.

I drove home. I will not tell you how I drove home because I don't want to think about it. I drove home.

Karen took one look at me coming through the door and said, "Curt, what happened?"

I told her.

She said, "We're calling Patty. We'll have to send Rhett alone."

I said no.

I said, "Get me the heating pad and the ibuprofen and a glass of bourbon. I'm going to that dinner if I have to be carried in."

She started crying. I wasn't expecting that. Karen doesn't cry. She's a retired ICU nurse, 35 years at UAB, she's seen things you wouldn't sleep again if you knew about. She doesn't cry. But she stood there in the kitchen and she said, "I'm so tired of watching you disappear, Curt."

That stopped me.

I didn't have anything to say back to her. So I just went into the bedroom and I laid on my back on the floor with the heating pad under me and I stared at the ceiling for an hour and tried to do the breathing exercise the physical therapist had taught me 4 years ago that I'd quit on after 2 sessions.

At 5:30 PM I stood up. It took 4 minutes.

I put on the navy blazer. The dress shoes from Belk. I took 4 ibuprofen and one of the muscle relaxers I'd been hoarding for emergencies. I drank a finger of Maker's Mark from the bottle Karen kept above the fridge.

I drove to the Iron City Grill. Karen drove behind me in her own car so she could watch in case I had to pull over.

I made it through the dinner.

I will not pretend I made it gracefully. I gripped the back of my chair through the entire toast like it was the railing on a fishing boat in rough water. My voice was steady but my legs were not. I sweated through the navy blazer. I made eye contact with my son and I read the words off my index cards and I told him about the day he was born and the day he hit a home run in Little League and the day he showed me his college acceptance letter and the kind of man I knew he was already and the kind of husband I knew he'd be. I sat down before my legs gave out. The room clapped. Rhett came over and hugged me and I tried not to flinch.

After dinner, Karen helped me out to the back patio of the Iron City Grill. There's a little stone wall there where they let smokers go and I'm not a smoker but I needed to sit on something low and not move. It was 11:30 at night. Birmingham in late October. The kind of warm that hangs in the air after the sun's been gone for hours.

Patty came out about 10 minutes later. Sat down on the wall next to me. Karen had quietly gone back inside.

Patty was 64. I knew that because Karen had told me. She had grey hair she didn't dye, cut short, and the kind of warm tan that women in Mountain Brook seem to keep year round. She'd spent the whole evening floating around her own party making everyone feel welcome, the kind of host I wouldn't know how to be if you held a gun to my head.

She sat down. She didn't say anything for a long time. She just looked out at the parking lot.

Then she said, "Curt, can I ask you a question that's gonna sound nosy?"

I said, "Sure."

She said, "How long has your back been like this?"

I told her. The truth, not the polite version. 6 years. The MRI. The doctor. The "manage it." The crawling in the Publix parking lot at 2:47 that afternoon.

She nodded slowly. Looked at her hands.

Then she said, "My husband, Tom, was a cardiologist for 38 years. He retired last year. And the last 5 years of his career, he was in pain every single day. His shoulders, mostly. From standing over patients, from the way cardiologists hold their bodies during procedures. He was on the same path you're on. The pain pills, the muscle relaxers, the 'just manage it.' I watched the man I married disappear into a recliner."

She turned and looked at me.

"I want to tell you what happened. I'm not selling anything. I'm not in a pyramid scheme. I'm a 64 year old woman whose husband got his life back, and I notice when somebody else is on the same road we were on, and it's my son in law's father, and I'm gonna tell you about it whether you want to hear it or not."

I almost laughed. Almost. My back wouldn't let me.

I said, "Tell me."

She told me about a friend of hers, a woman named Beverly, who'd been a research librarian at UAB. Beverly had a younger sister who'd married into an Indian family in Houston, and the family kept feeding her this fruit Beverly had never heard of. After a few years the sister, who had been a frail kind of person her whole life, started showing up to family events looking different. More color in her face. Walking faster. Sleeping better.

Beverly asked her about it. The sister told her it was a fruit called amla. Indian gooseberry. They'd been using it in Ayurvedic medicine for thousands of years. The sister had started taking a standardized extract a friend had recommended.

Beverly, being a research librarian, did what research librarians do. She spent 6 months reading the actual studies. The real ones, not the marketing copy.

What she found, Patty told me, was that amla wasn't a magic pill. It wasn't a painkiller. It wasn't replacing anything. What it was, was a fruit that seemed to do something quietly useful at the cellular level for the kind of slow, grinding, low grade inflammation that builds up in a body over decades of work and stress and living.

Patty had started giving it to Tom about 18 months before that night.

She said, "He's 67 now. He woke up this morning at 5:45 and went for a 3 mile walk before the rehearsal. He's inside laughing right now at a joke my brother told. 18 months ago he was a man I was watching turn into a piece of furniture."

I didn't say anything for a while.

She said, "I'm gonna text you the name of it. The brand we use. Look it up tomorrow. Don't take my word for anything. Just look it up."

She did. My phone buzzed in my blazer pocket.

I drove home that night feeling more wrung out than I'd ever felt in my life. Karen and I didn't talk on the drive. I lay on the floor again when I got home with the heating pad. I fell asleep there.

The next morning, the morning of the wedding, I read about amla for 2 hours before Karen even woke up.

Here is what I came to understand, and I want to explain it the way I'd explain framing a wall to a new guy on the crew, because that's how I think.

When you've got chronic pain like I had, especially the kind that gets worse over years and that doctors shrug at and call "wear and tear," what's actually happening inside you is a long, slow story about inflammation. Not the acute kind, like when you smash your thumb with a hammer and it swells up. The slow kind. The kind where your body's inflammatory signals never quite turn off. They stay on at a low level. Year after year after year.

That low level inflammation does damage to your joints, your tendons, the soft tissue in your spine, and the blood vessels that feed all of those things. It also does damage at the cellular level, to the little engines inside your cells that produce energy, called mitochondria. When those engines get sluggish, you don't just feel pain. You feel tired. You feel old. You feel like you're moving through molasses.

Most things you're handed for chronic pain go after the symptom. Painkillers numb the signal. Muscle relaxers loosen the spasm. Steroids shut down the inflammation acutely but with consequences. None of those things address what's actually going on at the level that matters, which is the cellular environment your tissues live in every day.

Amla is interesting because the research on it suggests it works on that environment. It's been associated with reductions in inflammatory markers like hs-CRP. It's a powerful antioxidant, partly because of its naturally high vitamin C content but also because of compounds called polyphenols and tannins that show up in good standardized extracts. And it appears to support healthy mitochondrial function, which is the cellular energy piece.

In plain English: it doesn't numb the pain. It works on the soil the pain is growing in.

That distinction matters because it explains why ibuprofen had been doing less and less for me over the years. Ibuprofen is a Band-Aid on a wound. The wound was getting worse underneath the Band-Aid. Amla, from what I read, was something more like working on the wound itself. Slowly. Quietly. Over weeks and months.

I ordered it that morning. I took my first 2 capsules with breakfast on the day of my son's wedding.

I got through that wedding. I want to be clear, I got through it on muscle relaxers and ibuprofen and willpower. The amla didn't save the wedding. The amla hadn't even started working yet.

But I had something I hadn't had at 2:47 PM the day before. I had a direction. I had a thing to try that wasn't "manage it."

Week 1, I felt nothing.

Week 2, I noticed I was getting out of bed in the morning in 6 minutes instead of 20.

Week 3, I picked up my granddaughter.

I want to tell you about that one because it's the moment I knew. It was a Saturday afternoon. Rhett and Ainsley had brought her over for lunch. She came running across the kitchen at me the way 5 year olds do, full speed, no concept of physics, and I caught her under the arms and lifted her up and put her on my hip the way I'd done a hundred times when she was 2 and 3 and the way I'd stopped doing when she got to 4. I didn't even think about it. I just did it. She put her arms around my neck and she said, "Pop Pop, I missed your big arms."

Karen was watching from the sink. I caught her eye. She turned around so I couldn't see her face.

Week 6, I was carrying lumber on the job site again. Not the way I had at 35. I'm not crazy. But I was carrying 2x6s and not just pointing at where I wanted them put.

Week 9, I called Patty.

I called her on a Tuesday afternoon and she picked up on the second ring and I said, "Patty. It's Curt. I just wanted to say thank you."

She said, "Curt. Is it working?"

I said, "I haven't taken an ibuprofen in 17 days."

She was quiet. Then she said, "I'm gonna tell Tom. He's gonna be glad to hear that."

I'm 9 months in now.

I'm not pain free. I want to be straight with you. I'm 62 years old and I've been swinging hammers for 31 years. There are mornings my back tells me what the weather is gonna do before the news does. But the floor of my pain has come up. The bottom isn't where it used to be. The crawling in the Publix parking lot, that's not who I am anymore.

I picked up my granddaughter at the wedding reception last weekend, the 1 year anniversary party Rhett and Ainsley threw at their house in Atlanta, and I held her on my hip for the entire 4 minute song they played for the first dance. Karen took a picture of it. It's on the fridge.

If you've been managing it for years, I see you.

If you've been told it's just your age, I see you.

If your wife has cried in the kitchen because she's tired of watching you disappear, I see you.

There's a fruit called amla. The brand I take is called Alevia. The product is Alevia Amla. It's made in the United States. It's 2 capsules a day. It's not a painkiller. It's not replacing anything your doctor has you on. It's not a miracle.

It's just a quiet, well researched, gentle thing from the other side of the world that decided to be kind to my body when not much else was being kind to it.

scripts.hook_line: My dad couldn't open the register at the pizza shop last Tuesday and I had to pretend I didn't see it.
scripts.body_meta:
My dad couldn't open the register at the pizza shop last Tuesday and I had to pretend I didn't see it.

He's been opening that register since 1987.

It's the same brass-plated NCR my grandfather bought when he opened Marino's on Wyoming Avenue in Scranton, and it has a key that turns about a quarter inch and a drawer that pops out hard. You have to brace your other hand against the counter or it'll knock the wind out of you.

My dad's name is Frank Marino Sr. He's 67. He's been making pizza for 51 years. He has hands that could palm a 16 inch dough ball when he was 30 and now he can't grip the key.

I watched him try three times. His thumb just slid off it.

He looked up and saw me looking and he laughed it off and said the lock was sticky and went into the back to start the sauce.

I stood there pretending to count the cannolis in the case and I felt something crack open in my chest that I haven't been able to close since.

I'm Frank Jr. I'm 54. I've been running the front of the shop with my dad since I was 19, and I've been waiting my whole adult life for the day he hands me the keys and goes home and watches the Phillies in his recliner like he earned. That's the deal. That's the deal every son makes with his father in a family business. You work shoulder to shoulder for 30 years and then one day he tells you it's yours and he goes home.

But I don't want him to go home like this.

I don't want him to go home a man who can't open his own register.

So I went home that night and I did something I've never done in my life. I opened my laptop at the kitchen table and I started reading.

My wife Donna was already in bed. The dog, a 12 year old beagle named Pepper who sleeps on the heating vent, was snoring under the radiator. I had a cup of decaf I didn't drink and I sat there and I typed in the search bar:

"Why are my dad's hands getting weak."

I want to back up.

Because what I found that night, and what I'm about to tell you, only makes sense if you understand what my dad was like before.

This is a man who used to walk from our house on Mulberry Street to the shop every morning at 4:30 AM. In the snow. In July heat. In a thunderstorm so bad in 1998 that a tree fell on the Buick across the street. He walked.

He could carry a 50 pound sack of 00 flour on each shoulder up the basement stairs. He used to bench press the chest freezer with my uncle Joey at Christmas as a joke. He once broke up a fight outside the shop between two construction guys twice his size, with one hand, holding a slice of sausage in the other.

That was 12 years ago.

Today he can't open a jar of olives. My mom opens them for him in the kitchen and pretends she doesn't, and he pretends he doesn't see her doing it, and they've been doing this little dance for about two years now.

It started small. He stopped going up on the roof to clean the gutters at the shop. Said his shoulder. Then he stopped lifting the flour sacks. Said his back. Then he started sitting down between orders. Said his hip.

Then his memory started slipping.

He'd forget the names of regulars he's known for 30 years. Vinny Petrocelli walked in one Sunday and my dad called him Tony. Vinny laughed about it and my dad laughed too but I saw his eyes and he didn't know.

He'd lose his train of thought halfway through a sentence. Stop in the middle of mixing dough and stare at the bowl like he forgot why he was holding the spoon.

His balance got bad. He tripped on the floor mat at the front door three different times last winter.

We took him to his doctor.

His doctor is a nice man. Dr. Ahmed. We've been going to him for years. He ran some blood work and he said everything looked good, except the cholesterol. He said the cholesterol was a little elevated, and at my dad's age, with his family history, it would be smart to put him on something to keep it down.

My dad has been on a statin for 11 years.

The dose has been raised twice.

His cholesterol numbers, on paper, look beautiful. His LDL is, in Dr. Ahmed's words, "a textbook number." Dr. Ahmed shows my dad the chart at every annual visit and says "Frank, you're doing everything right."

And my dad nods and smiles and goes home and can't open a jar of olives.

I didn't know any of this was related.

I thought it was age. Everyone thinks it's age. My mom thinks it's age. My dad thinks it's age. He says "I'm 67, Frankie, what do you want from me." He says it with a little smile and he walks back to the dough station.

But I'm telling you, the man I watched try to open that register on Tuesday is not a 67 year old man. My uncle Joey is 71 and he's still hauling cinder blocks for his retaining wall in the backyard. My dad's friend Sal Rinaldi is 69 and he plays softball on Sundays with a senior league at McDade Park. My dad has aged 20 years in 8.

Something is wrong.

So I sat at the kitchen table that Tuesday night until almost 2 in the morning. And what I found, I'm not going to pretend I understood all of it. I'm not a doctor. I make pizza. But I can follow a pattern. I've been reading the same yeast packets and flour bags and tomato can labels for 35 years. I know how to read.

And the pattern I started seeing was something my dad's doctor never told him. Something my doctor never told me. Something I think a lot of men our age have never been told.

Here's what I learned.

Your body makes cholesterol on purpose.

It's not a glitch. It's not a flaw. Every cell in your body has cholesterol in its outer wall. Your brain is something like 25 percent cholesterol. Your hormones are made out of it. Your nerves are wrapped in it. When the doctor tells you "your cholesterol is high," he means one number on one chart is above one line, and the standard move is to push that number down with a pill.

But here's the thing nobody had ever explained to me.

Not all LDL cholesterol is the same.

Regular, normal LDL is just doing its job. Carrying material around your body, repairing cells, building things. It's only a problem when it gets damaged. When it gets oxidized.

Oxidation is what happens when free radicals attack a molecule. It's the same thing that turns a sliced apple brown on the counter. It's the same thing that rusts a wrench in a shed. Your body is dealing with oxidation every minute of every day, from stress, from processed food, from pollution, from just being alive.

When your LDL gets oxidized, it changes. It becomes sticky. It starts grabbing onto the inside walls of your arteries. That's what builds plaque. That's what causes the trouble.

Regular LDL doesn't do that. Oxidized LDL does.

But the standard cholesterol test? It doesn't tell you how much of your LDL is oxidized. It just counts all of it. Good and damaged, lumped together. If the total number is high, you get a prescription.

And here's where it got me.

The pill that lowers your cholesterol doesn't sort the good from the damaged. It can't. It just shuts down your body's ability to make cholesterol in the first place. All of it. The kind your brain needs. The kind your nerves need. The kind your muscles need to keep their walls intact.

It uses the same pathway your body uses to make something called CoQ10. CoQ10 is the molecule that lives inside your mitochondria. Your mitochondria are the little engines inside every cell that turn food into energy. They run everything. Your heart, your muscles, your brain, your hands.

When you shut down that pathway, the cholesterol number drops.

But the CoQ10 drops with it.

And when CoQ10 drops, the engines in your cells run slower. They produce less energy. The cells that use the most energy, your heart, your muscles, your brain, are the ones that feel it first.

I sat there at the kitchen table and I thought about my dad's hands.

I thought about the jar of olives.

I thought about the register.

I thought about him stopping mid sentence at the dough station, staring at the bowl.

I thought, oh my God.

I'm not saying the pill caused all of it. I'm not a doctor. I'm not telling you what to do with your medicine. But I sat there at 1:30 in the morning and for the first time in 8 years, I had a frame for what was happening to my dad. And the frame wasn't "he's old." The frame was "the engines in his cells are running on fumes."

So I kept reading.

And the question I kept coming back to was the simplest one in the world.

If the real problem is oxidized LDL, what stops the oxidation in the first place?

What protects the LDL from getting damaged before it ever has a chance to stick to anything?

That's where I found Amla.

I'd never heard the word before. I'm a guy from Scranton. The most exotic thing in our pantry is the dried oregano my aunt sends from her cousin in Calabria. Amla is a fruit. It's a small green fruit, about the size of a golf ball, that grows on a tree in India. They've been using it for over 3,000 years in their traditional medicine. The translation of its old name is something like "the nurse," because of how broadly it supports the body.

But what stopped me cold was what the research has been finding about it.

Amla has been studied for its effects on lipid handling and oxidative stress in ways most fruits haven't. It's loaded with compounds called emblicanins, which are some of the most potent natural antioxidants ever measured. And research suggests these compounds work on the actual mechanism of LDL damage. Not the number on the chart. The damage to the particle itself.

Studies have looked at how Amla extract influences the same pathway in the liver that the standard pills target, the HMG-CoA reductase pathway, but in a more gentle, modulating way. Not by shutting it down. By dialing it. The body keeps making the cholesterol it needs. The liver keeps clearing what it doesn't.

It's also been associated with supporting LDL receptor activity. Those are the little docks on your liver cells that pull LDL out of your bloodstream. The more active they are, the more your liver clears on its own.

And here's the part that hit me hardest, sitting there at 1:47 in the morning.

Because Amla works upstream of the damage, it doesn't deplete CoQ10. Your mitochondria keep their fuel. Your cells keep their power. Your hands stay strong. Your memory stays sharp. Your balance stays under you.

That's the difference.

One approach forces a number down by shutting off the factory. The other approach supports the factory and protects the product so it doesn't get damaged in the first place.

I'm not a doctor. I want to keep saying that. I'm a guy who runs a pizza shop. But once I saw the picture, I couldn't unsee it.

I went to bed at 2:15 that morning. I didn't sleep much. I lay there next to Donna and I thought about the register.

Two days later, on a Thursday, I drove to my dad's house after lunch service. He was in his recliner watching a Phillies replay from 1980. He always watches the 1980 World Series. Tug McGraw on the mound, ninth inning. He's seen it a thousand times. He says it relaxes him.

I sat down on the couch and I told him what I'd found.

I didn't tell him to stop his medicine. I'm not crazy. I told him I wanted him to talk to Dr. Ahmed about adding something. About supporting his system underneath what the pill was doing. I told him about the oxidation. About the mitochondria. About CoQ10. About Amla.

He listened. My dad is a quiet man. He listens with his whole face.

When I was done he said, "Frankie, I trust you."

That's all he said.

He talked to Dr. Ahmed the next week. Dr. Ahmed didn't have any objection. He said it was reasonable. He said a lot of his patients are taking it now.

So my dad started taking Alevia Amla.

Two capsules in the morning, with his coffee, before he walks to the shop.

I want to be careful here, because I don't want to oversell this. I don't want to be the guy on Facebook telling you about a miracle. There are no miracles in my family. We're Italian and we're tired.

But here's what I've watched happen over the last 4 months.

The first month, I didn't notice anything. Honestly. I almost stopped buying him the second bottle. Donna said give it time.

In the second month, my mom called me on a Wednesday and said "your father carried the laundry basket up the stairs yesterday." I said okay. She said "Frankie, he hasn't carried the laundry basket up the stairs since the Bush administration."

He just nodded.

And I had to walk into the back and stand by the walk in cooler for about 5 minutes before I could come back out.

Last week, on a Sunday, my dad and my uncle Joey hauled the new chest freezer down the basement stairs of the shop. I tried to help. They told me to get out of the way.

I want to tell you about a moment from yesterday.

He was telling a story to Vinny Petrocelli about a delivery run he made in 1991 in a snowstorm where the car slid into a snowbank and he had to walk the pies the rest of the way.

He told the whole story. Start to finish. He didn't lose the thread once.

Vinny was laughing. My dad was laughing. I was standing by the oven pretending to check a pie that didn't need checking.

I want to say something to you, if you're still reading.

If you have a father, or a husband, or a brother, or you yourself are a man over 50 who's been told for years that everything is fine because the numbers on the chart look good, but the man you used to be is fading anyway, I want you to think about what I learned that night at the kitchen table.

The damage to the particle, not the count of the particle, is what matters.

And the engines in your cells need their fuel to keep running.
